This direct, crude shortcut lets the amygdala trigger a startle or freeze response milliseconds before slower cortical processing reaches conscious awareness, the evolutionary logic being that it is safer to react to a stick mistaken for a snake than the reverse.
2016-179: IEPs flow from the Education for All Handicapped Children Act of 1975, later renamed IDEA, which guarantees a free appropriate public education in the least restrictive environment. Unlike a Section 504 plan (from the 1973 Rehabilitation Act), which only provides accommodations, an IEP for a qualifying disability can modify the curriculum and academic requirements themselves, offering specialized instruction rather than mere access.
2016-18: Benzodiazepines like lorazepam raise the seizure threshold and shorten ECT seizure duration, undermining treatment efficacy, so they are typically tapered or held before ECT. Their anticonvulsant action is the same reason they are first-line for status epilepticus—useful there, counterproductive here. When sedation is unavoidable, ultra-short agents or flumazenil reversal have been used to preserve adequate seizure quality during the procedure.
2016-180: Huntington disease results from an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat in the HTT gene on chromosome 4, identified in 1993 by the Huntington's Disease Collaborative Research Group after a long hunt aided by Nancy Wexler's work with affected families around Venezuela's Lake Maracaibo. The expansion explains anticipation, worsening across generations, and direct repeat-length testing definitively confirms the diagnosis George Huntington described in 1872.
2016-181: National child-fatality surveillance has consistently shown that the youngest children bear the greatest risk of dying from abuse, with infants and toddlers under three or four years overrepresented in fatality reviews. Their physical fragility, total dependence, and inability to flee or report make them especially vulnerable; head trauma such as abusive head trauma (formerly 'shaken baby syndrome,' a term advanced by radiologist John Caffey in the 1970s) is a leading mechanism.
2016-182: 'Little Hans' was the pseudonym for Herbert Graf, a five-year-old boy with a fear of horses whom Freud analyzed largely through the boy's father, publishing the case in 1909. Freud interpreted the equine phobia as displaced Oedipal anxiety, making it his foundational account of how phobias form and a cornerstone of psychoanalytic child theory. Graf later became a renowned opera stage director.
2016-183: Kin selection explains how genes promoting altruism toward relatives can spread, since helping kin propagates shared genes. The formal theory was developed by W. D. Hamilton in 1964, whose 'Hamilton's rule' (rB > C) quantifies when altruism pays off. J.B.S. Haldane reputedly quipped he would lay down his life for two brothers or eight cousins, capturing the same logic of inclusive fitness.
2016-184: Carbohydrate-deficient transferrin rises with sustained heavy alcohol intake, as ethanol impairs glycosylation of the iron-transport protein transferrin. Introduced as a biomarker in the 1980s, CDT is prized for relative specificity to chronic heavy drinking and normalizes within weeks of abstinence, making it useful for monitoring relapse, often paired with GGT for added sensitivity.
2016-185: Huntington disease preferentially destroys GABAergic medium spiny neurons of the striatum (caudate and putamen) early in its course, releasing the thalamus from inhibition and producing chorea. The disorder was described by George Huntington in 1872; the causative CAG trinucleotide expansion in the HTT gene on chromosome 4 was identified in 1993, making it a landmark of human genetics.
2016-186: Shaping was central to B. F. Skinner's operant conditioning, in which successive approximations toward a target behavior are reinforced step by step. Skinner famously demonstrated it by training pigeons to peck and even guide missiles during World War II ('Project Pigeon'). The technique remains foundational in behavior therapy and animal training, rewarding closer and closer attempts until the full behavior emerges.
2016-187: ECT-related memory impairment, particularly retrograde amnesia, is influenced by electrode placement, stimulus dose, and treatment frequency. Spacing treatments further apart reduces cumulative cognitive burden. The technique itself dates to 1938, when Ugo Cerletti and Lucio Bini administered the first electroconvulsive treatment in Rome; modern practice favors unilateral or right-sided placement and individualized scheduling to minimize amnestic effects.
2016-188: Vivid, fully formed visual hallucinations occurring with visual pathway lesions or eye disease in cognitively intact people characterize Charles Bonnet syndrome, but lesions of the occipital/posterior cerebral artery territory can produce 'release hallucinations' along the deafferented visual cortex. The Swiss naturalist Charles Bonnet described the phenomenon in 1760 after his grandfather, nearly blind, saw detailed images of people and patterns.
2016-189: Epigenetics describes heritable changes in gene expression without altering DNA sequence, typically via DNA methylation and histone modification. Allelic exclusion and X-inactivation both silence one copy while leaving the sequence intact. The term 'epigenetics' was coined by Conrad Waddington in the 1940s; Mary Lyon proposed random X-chromosome inactivation in 1961, now called Lyonization.
2016-19: Case management's strongest, most replicated benefit in substance use treatment is improved retention—keeping patients engaged—rather than direct reductions in use. By linking clients to housing, benefits, and medical care and reducing practical barriers, case managers keep people in treatment long enough for other interventions to work. This evidence helped cement case management as a core component of comprehensive addiction services.
2016-190: Object permanence, the understanding that objects continue to exist when out of sight, was a hallmark of the sensorimotor stage in Jean Piaget's developmental theory. Piaget studied it by hiding toys from his own children and watching whether they searched, concluding the concept consolidates around eight to twelve months. Later researchers argued infants grasp it even earlier than Piaget believed.
2016-191: Long-term follow-up studies, including a large Swedish cohort published by Dhejne and colleagues in 2011, found that even after gender-affirming surgery transgender individuals continued to show elevated rates of certain general health and psychiatric morbidities relative to the general population. Such findings are interpreted as reflecting persistent minority stress and stigma rather than the surgery itself, which generally reduces gender dysphoria.
2016-192: Grapefruit juice inhibits intestinal cytochrome P450 3A4, reducing first-pass metabolism and raising blood levels of many drugs. The effect was discovered serendipitously in the late 1980s by David Bailey, who used grapefruit juice to mask the taste of ethanol in a drug-interaction study and was surprised by markedly elevated drug concentrations. Furanocoumarins in the juice are the responsible compounds.
2016-193: In Ivan Pavlov's framework, food triggers salivation automatically as an unconditioned response. Pavlov, a Russian physiologist studying dog digestion, noticed dogs salivating before food arrived and systematically mapped reflexive learning, earning the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine (for digestion). His bell-and-food experiments became the archetype of classical conditioning, distinguishing innate reflexes from learned associations.
2016-194: This reflects the Donabedian model of quality, which divides care into structure, process, and outcome. Avedis Donabedian, a physician at the University of Michigan, articulated this triad in a landmark 1966 paper. Process measures capture what is actually done to or for patients, such as engagement or screening rates, bridging the resources of structure and the results of outcome.
2016-195: Antiphospholipid antibodies, including lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin, are most consistently linked to neuropsychiatric manifestations of systemic lupus erythematosus, likely through a prothrombotic, microvascular thrombotic mechanism. They define antiphospholipid syndrome (Hughes syndrome), described by rheumatologist Graham Hughes in the 1980s, and are associated with stroke, cognitive dysfunction, and recurrent pregnancy loss.
2016-196: Sudden irresistible sleep attacks with shortened REM latency on sleep study point to narcolepsy, treated with wake-promoting agents such as modafinil. Narcolepsy was named by French physician Jean-Baptiste Gelineau in 1880. A major advance came around 1999-2000 with discovery that loss of hypocretin (orexin) neurons underlies type 1 narcolepsy with cataplexy.
2016-197: Recognizing mortality and the finitude of personal time is the defining midlife task in adult-development theory. Psychoanalyst Elliott Jaques coined the term 'midlife crisis' in a 1965 paper, describing how confronting one's own death reshapes creativity and priorities in middle age. Erik Erikson framed the same era as the struggle of generativity versus stagnation.
2016-198: Broad, population-wide messaging aimed at everyone regardless of individual risk is a universal intervention in the Institute of Medicine's prevention framework (Mrazek and Haggerty, 1994). This scheme refined Gerald Caplan's older primary/secondary/tertiary model by sorting preventive efforts into universal, selective, and indicated tiers based on the targeted population's risk level rather than disease stage.
2016-199: Vertical and horizontal nystagmus, hypertension, and striking analgesia with agitated, violent behavior are classic for phencyclidine intoxication. PCP was synthesized in the 1950s by Parke-Davis as the anesthetic Sernyl, but emergence delirium and dissociation ended its medical use; it then surfaced as the street drug 'angel dust.' Its dissociative action stems from NMDA-receptor antagonism.
2016-2: Object relations theory grew out of the British psychoanalytic school, with Melanie Klein, W.R.D. Fairbairn, and D.W. Winnicott as central figures. Its core idea is that the psyche is structured around internalized "objects"—mental representations of self and significant others—formed in early relationships, shifting Freud's drive-based model toward a relational one. The term "object" is Freud's own, referring to the target of a drive, but these theorists made internalized relationships, not drives, the organizing principle of mental life.
2016-20: Point mutations are small-scale DNA changes—single-base substitutions or tiny insertions and deletions—as opposed to large structural changes like copy number variations spanning thousands of bases. A famous example is the single adenine-to-thymine substitution in the beta-globin gene that causes sickle cell disease, traced to a single amino-acid change by Vernon Ingram in the 1950s, the earliest molecular disease ever defined.
2016-200: Lithium augmentation has the strongest and longest-standing evidence among add-on strategies for antidepressant non-response, supported by numerous controlled trials since the early 1980s. The STAR*D effectiveness trial in the 2000s further examined sequenced augmentation steps. Lithium's antidepressant-potentiating effect was pioneered largely by Claude de Montigny and colleagues, building on its mood-stabilizing legacy from John Cade's 1949 discovery.
2016-201: Self-help groups differ from formal group psychotherapy in that they target a shared specific problem and do not analyze intragroup dynamics or aim at personality change. Alcoholics Anonymous, founded in 1935 by Bill Wilson and Dr. Bob Smith, is the prototype, relying on peer support, shared experience, and mutual aid rather than a professional leader interpreting group process.
2016-202: The hippocampal dentate gyrus is the best-established site of adult neurogenesis in humans. Joseph Altman reported new neuron formation in adult rodents in the 1960s, but the field was transformed by Peter Eriksson and Fred Gage's 1998 study using BrdU labeling in cancer patients, providing direct evidence that the adult human hippocampus generates new neurons throughout life.
2016-203: Williams syndrome arises from a microdeletion on chromosome 7q11.23 spanning roughly two dozen genes, including ELN (elastin). First described by cardiologist J.C.P. Williams in 1961, it produces a distinctive 'elfin' face, supravalvular aortic stenosis, intellectual disability, and a famously sociable, hyperverbal personality with relative strength in language alongside marked visuospatial deficits.
2016-204: Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia causes osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis), producing the dreaded 'locked-in' picture of flaccid quadriparesis, dysarthria, dysphagia, and ophthalmoplegia. The entity was described in 1959 by Raymond Adams and colleagues. Current guidelines limit sodium correction to roughly 8-10 mEq/L per 24 hours to prevent it.
2016-205: Frantic efforts to avoid real or imagined abandonment is the first listed DSM criterion for borderline personality disorder. The term 'borderline' originated with analyst Adolph Stern in 1938 for patients on the border between neurosis and psychosis. Otto Kernberg later developed borderline personality organization, and Marsha Linehan created dialectical behavior therapy specifically targeting these patients' instability.
2016-206: A partial hospitalization program offers intensive structured daytime treatment while the patient lives at home, bridging the gap between outpatient care and full inpatient or residential placement. It represents a step-up in intensity appropriate when standard outpatient treatment stalls but there is no acute safety crisis, embodying the least-restrictive-environment principle in the continuum of behavioral health care.
2016-207: Placing the webcam near the patient's on-screen image approximates eye contact, which is crucial for rapport and emotional attunement in telepsychiatry; the mismatch between looking at the screen versus the camera otherwise reads as gaze aversion. Telepsychiatry dates to the late 1950s at the Nebraska Psychiatric Institute, among the earliest applications of two-way video in medicine.
2016-208: The efficacy-effectiveness gap is a central critique of randomized controlled trials: their strict inclusion criteria and controlled conditions measure how an intervention works in ideal settings (efficacy) but may not predict real-world performance in heterogeneous clinical populations (effectiveness). This distinction motivated pragmatic and effectiveness trials such as CATIE and STAR*D in psychiatry.
2016-209: New-onset hallucinations several days into an otherwise smooth post-operative course should raise suspicion for alcohol withdrawal, since delirium tremens classically emerges around 48-96 hours after the last drink, a timeline easily unmasked by hospitalization. The term derives from Latin for 'trembling delirium'; untreated DTs carry significant mortality, making prophylactic benzodiazepines essential.
2016-21: Neurofibromatosis type 2 is defined clinically by bilateral vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas), making progressive hearing loss a hallmark feature. It is caused by mutations in the NF2 gene on chromosome 22, which encodes the tumor suppressor merlin. NF2 is far rarer than NF1 (von Recklinghausen disease) and is distinguished by these schwannomas and meningiomas rather than the café-au-lait spots and skin neurofibromas of NF1.
2016-210: An ipsilateral 'down-and-out' eye with ptosis and a blown pupil (oculomotor palsy) plus contralateral hemiparesis localizes to the midbrain, classically Weber syndrome from infarction of the cerebral peduncle involving the exiting CN III fascicles and the corticospinal tract. It is one of the named crossed brainstem syndromes attributed to nineteenth-century English physician Hermann Weber.
2016-211: Pramipexole is a non-ergot dopamine agonist that preferentially targets D3 receptors, approved by the FDA for Parkinson disease in 1997 and later for restless legs syndrome in 2006. The dopaminergic basis of RLS traces to the observation that levodopa and dopamine agonists relieve symptoms, while a key complication, augmentation (paradoxical worsening and earlier onset of symptoms with chronic dopaminergic use), has shifted many clinicians toward alpha-2-delta ligands like gabapentin enacarbil as alternatives.
2016-212: A prior withdrawal seizure or history of delirium tremens reflects the kindling phenomenon, a concept borrowed from epilepsy research by Robert Post and others, in which repeated detoxifications progressively sensitize the brain so that each subsequent withdrawal becomes more severe. The benzodiazepine-based protocols that prevent these complications grew from recognizing that abrupt cessation in a GABA-depleted, glutamate-sensitized brain produces autonomic storm and seizures.
2016-213: Psychomotor disturbance, whether retardation or agitation, has long been viewed as a marker of severe, biologically driven, melancholic depression. Emil Kraepelin emphasized psychomotor changes in his descriptions of manic-depressive illness, and observable motor slowing is one of the few signs in depression that an examiner can witness directly rather than rely on self-report, historically predicting better response to ECT and somatic treatments.
2016-214: The consumer-run mental health movement grew out of the ex-patient and psychiatric survivor activism of the 1970s, emphasizing peer support and self-determination over professional hierarchy. Research on these organizations highlights psychological sense of community, a construct formalized by community psychologist Seymour Sarason in 1974 and later operationalized by McMillan and Chavis, as central to members stepping into leadership rather than remaining passive recipients of services.
2016-215: The link between orbitofrontal cortex damage and disinhibited, risky behavior is immortalized by Phineas Gage, the railroad foreman whose 1848 tamping-iron injury destroyed ventromedial and orbitofrontal regions, transforming his personality. Antonio Damasio later revived the case and, with the Iowa Gambling Task, showed that such patients lose the somatic-marker signals that normally steer decisions away from disadvantageous, high-risk choices.
2016-216: Fluoxetine and fluvoxamine are potent inhibitors of CYP enzymes, and fluoxetine strongly inhibits CYP2D6, the pathway that clears risperidone. Blocking it raises risperidone and its active metabolite, intensifying tuberoinfundibular dopamine blockade and prolactin elevation, hence galactorrhea. This is a classic pharmacokinetic interaction example, a reminder that risperidone is among the most prolactin-elevating second-generation antipsychotics.
2016-217: The Mini-Mental State Examination was published in 1975 by Marshal Folstein, Susan Folstein, and Paul McHugh at Johns Hopkins as a brief bedside cognitive screen. A score around 21-24 of 30 typically signals mild impairment, though interpretation must adjust for education and age. The test's popularity led to copyright enforcement decades later, spurring development of free alternatives like the MoCA.
2016-218: Genetic linkage analysis rests on the principle that loci physically close on a chromosome tend to be co-inherited because recombination rarely separates them, a concept rooted in Thomas Hunt Morgan's fruit-fly work and Alfred Sturtevant's first genetic map in 1913. Linkage studies trace disease alleles through families by tracking co-segregation with known markers, the dominant gene-mapping strategy before genome-wide association studies.
2016-219: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis was first characterized by Josep Dalmau and colleagues in 2007, often in young women with ovarian teratomas. The classic arc, psychiatric symptoms and psychosis progressing to catatonia, dyskinesias, autonomic instability, seizures, and antipsychotic intolerance, was popularized for the public by Susannah Cahalan's memoir Brain on Fire. Antibodies target the GluN1 subunit of the NMDA receptor.
2016-22: REM sleep behavior disorder, first characterized by Carlos Schenck and Mark Mahowald in Minnesota in 1986, is defined polysomnographically by REM sleep without atonia—loss of the normal muscle paralysis of dreaming. Patients physically act out vivid dreams, sometimes injuring themselves or bed partners. It predominantly affects older men and is a powerful early marker of synucleinopathies, with many cases later converting to Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia.
2016-220: The serotonin hypothesis grew from 1960s observations that reserpine depleted monoamines and caused depression, and that low CSF 5-HIAA, serotonin's metabolite, correlated with impulsivity, aggression, and completed suicide in studies by Marie Asberg and others in the 1970s. Serotonergic projections from the raphe nuclei modulate mood, sleep architecture, and impulse control, the triad this question highlights.
2016-221: DHEA, an adrenal steroid and the most abundant circulating hormone in humans, is co-released with cortisol during stress but exerts anti-glucocorticoid and neuroprotective effects. Research, including studies in combat-exposed soldiers, found that a higher DHEA-to-cortisol ratio predicted resilience and less severe PTSD, supporting the idea that the balance between these two adrenal steroids, not cortisol alone, shapes stress outcomes.
2016-222: Attachment theory was founded by John Bowlby and operationalized by Mary Ainsworth, whose Strange Situation procedure in the 1970s classified infant attachment patterns. Ainsworth's Baltimore studies identified maternal sensitivity, the caregiver's prompt and appropriate responsiveness to infant signals, as the key determinant of secure versus insecure attachment, a finding the NICHD child-care studies later echoed.
2016-223: Paramnesia denotes a distortion of memory in which fantasy and real experience are confused; deja vu, French for already seen, is the classic example. The term was popularized by French scholar Emile Boirac in the late 19th century. Related paramnesias include jamais vu and confabulation, distinguishing these memory falsifications from disorders of mood or perception.
2016-224: Clozapine, synthesized in the 1950s and reborn after the landmark 1988 Kane trial showing efficacy in treatment-resistant schizophrenia, is uniquely associated with reduced substance use and increased abstinence in dually diagnosed patients. Naturalistic data, much of it from Robert Drake and colleagues, suggest clozapine's broad receptor profile may dampen the reward circuitry dysfunction underlying comorbid addiction, an effect not seen with typical antipsychotics.
2016-225: Immanuel Kant's moral philosophy, especially the categorical imperative and the principle of treating persons as ends rather than means, supplies the deontological foundation of modern clinical ethics, underpinning respect for autonomy and informed consent. His 1798 work Anthropology from a Pragmatic Point of View also offered early reflections on mental disorder, but his enduring contribution to psychiatry is ethical rather than diagnostic.
2016-226: A large verbal-versus-nonverbal (performance) discrepancy on IQ testing, a concept dating to David Wechsler's scales first published in 1939, can signal a learning disability, neurological insult, or sensory deficit rather than a uniform intellectual level. Because the composite score can mask such scatter, a significant split between index scores flags the need for deeper neuropsychological evaluation.
2016-227: The picture of severe headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual loss, a markedly elevated ESR, and proximal stiffness (polymyalgia rheumatica) is giant cell (temporal) arteritis, and temporal artery biopsy remains the diagnostic gold standard. The disease's dread complication is irreversible blindness from ischemic optic neuropathy, so steroids are started empirically before biopsy results return.
2016-228: Bazett's formula, published by physiologist Henry Cuthbert Bazett in 1920, corrects the QT interval by dividing it by the square root of the RR interval. Because this correction is nonlinear, it overcorrects at fast heart rates, overestimating QTc in tachycardia, and undercorrects in bradycardia. This bias matters in psychiatry given the QT-prolonging potential of many antipsychotics.
2016-229: Epigenetics, the heritable change in gene function without alteration of the DNA sequence, was coined by developmental biologist Conrad Waddington in the 1940s, who pictured the epigenetic landscape of cell fate. Mechanisms include DNA methylation and histone modification. Michael Meaney's rat maternal-care studies famously showed that early nurturing alters glucocorticoid receptor methylation, linking environment to lasting gene regulation.
2016-23: After a clinically suspicious "worst headache of my life," a normal CT does not exclude subarachnoid hemorrhage, especially after several hours, so lumbar puncture is the next step. The classic LP finding is xanthochromia—yellowish CSF from bilirubin as red cells break down—which distinguishes true bleeding from a traumatic tap. Modern high-sensitivity CT within six hours has reduced but not eliminated the role of LP in this workup.
2016-230: The overlap of frontotemporal dementia and ALS was unified by the 2011 discovery of the C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat expansion, the most common genetic cause of both conditions. The shared pathology is TDP-43 protein inclusions, identified in 2006, establishing a clinical and molecular spectrum in which behavioral-variant FTD and motor neuron disease frequently coexist.
2016-231: Self-regulation, the capacity to manage attention, emotion, and impulse, predicts social competence and life outcomes, a link dramatized by Walter Mischel's marshmallow experiments at Stanford beginning in the late 1960s, in which preschoolers who delayed gratification later showed better adjustment. The construct connects to executive function and the developing prefrontal cortex.
2016-232: The shift of death toward home and hospice and away from acute care hospitals reflects the modern hospice movement founded by Dame Cicely Saunders, who opened St. Christopher's Hospice in London in 1967, and the U.S. Medicare Hospice Benefit established in 1982. Tracking the site of death has become a key quality metric in end-of-life care.
2016-233: The brightly colored, flamboyant dress and expansive, grandiose mood describe a classic manic presentation. The grandiose delusion of being loved by a famous person is erotomania, also called de Clerambault syndrome after French psychiatrist Gaetan Gatian de Clerambault, who described it in 1921. Such delusions can appear in mania as well as in primary delusional disorder.
2016-234: Early, intense depressive symptoms shortly after a loss predict complicated bereavement, a distinction sharpened by Sigmund Freud's 1917 essay Mourning and Melancholia separating normal grief from pathological depression. DSM-5 controversially removed the bereavement exclusion in 2013, and later editions recognized prolonged grief disorder, reflecting that early depressive intensity flags risk for lasting impairment.
2016-235: Subacute progressive limb clumsiness with intention tremor, dysmetria, and dysdiadochokinesia localizes to the cerebellum, specifically the lateral hemispheres that coordinate ipsilateral appendicular movement. The cerebellum, Latin for little brain, was central to Joseph Babinski's early 20th-century characterization of asynergy and dysmetria as the hallmark signs of cerebellar dysfunction.
2016-236: Prescription opioid pain relievers consistently top national surveys, such as the SAMHSA National Survey on Drug Use and Health, as the most misused class of prescription drugs. This pattern fueled the U.S. opioid epidemic, whose roots are often traced to aggressive 1990s marketing of OxyContin, leading the CDC to declare a prescription overdose crisis.
2016-237: Erik Erikson's eight-stage model of psychosocial development, laid out in Childhood and Society (1950), places the final stage, ego integrity versus despair, in late life, when a person reviews their life and either finds coherent meaning and acceptance or sinks into regret. Erikson, who also coined the term identity crisis, framed wisdom as the virtue of this stage.
2016-238: Neglect is consistently the most common form of child maltreatment in U.S. data, such as the Child Maltreatment reports from the Children's Bureau, accounting for the majority of substantiated cases. Often called the neglect of neglect because it draws less attention than dramatic physical or sexual abuse, it nonetheless carries profound developmental and attachment consequences.
2016-239: Synaptic pruning, the experience-dependent elimination of excess synapses, peaks in the prefrontal cortex through adolescence into the mid-twenties, refining circuits for abstract reasoning and executive control. Peter Huttenlocher's postmortem studies in the late 1970s documented this rise-and-fall of synaptic density, and the protracted maturation of frontal cortex underlies adolescent impulsivity versus adult judgment.
2016-24: Supportive psychotherapy is the treatment of choice for patients with fragile ego function—poor reality testing, primitive defenses, impulsivity—because it shores up existing strengths rather than uncovering conflict. It bolsters defenses and provides structure instead of inducing the regression that insight-oriented work can trigger. This ego-supportive versus ego-uncovering distinction traces to the structural model and to analysts who adapted technique to a patient's ego strength.
2016-240: Velocardiofacial syndrome, caused by a 22q11.2 microdeletion and also known as DiGeorge or Shprintzen syndrome, classically combines cleft palate, cardiac anomalies, and characteristic facies. It carries one of the highest genetic risks for schizophrenia, with roughly a quarter of affected individuals developing a psychotic disorder, making it a key model linking copy number variation to psychiatric illness.
2016-241: The ventromedial hypothalamus earned the nickname the 'satiety center' from classic mid-20th-century animal lesion studies: bilateral destruction of this nucleus in rats produced ravenous hyperphagia and dramatic obesity. The complementary lateral hypothalamic 'feeding center,' when lesioned, caused aplasia and starvation. This dual-center model of appetite, articulated in the 1940s-1950s, remains a durable teaching framework, and tumors such as craniopharyngiomas pressing on the ventromedial region recapitulate the experimental obesity in humans.
2016-242: Shortened REM latency is one of the most replicated biological findings in major depression, characterized in sleep laboratories beginning in the 1970s by researchers including David Kupfer at Pittsburgh. Depressed patients enter their first REM period unusually quickly after sleep onset, alongside increased REM density and reduced slow-wave sleep. Kupfer proposed REM latency as a potential biological marker of depression, and these EEG signatures became a cornerstone of the biological psychiatry literature.
2016-243: Selection bias arises when the way subjects are recruited makes them systematically unrepresentative of the population of interest. Pulling anxiety patients from a specialty clinic captures more severe, treatment-seeking, or comorbid cases, a classic example sometimes called Berkson's bias after biostatistician Joseph Berkson, who in the 1940s showed how hospital-based sampling distorts disease associations. It remains a foundational concept in clinical epidemiology and a frequent flaw in psychiatric research design.
2016-244: Thomas Szasz published The Myth of Mental Illness in 1961, arguing that since 'disease' properly refers to bodily lesions, conditions without demonstrable physical pathology are better understood as 'problems in living.' A libertarian psychiatrist at SUNY Upstate, Szasz became a central figure in the antipsychiatry movement and co-founded a group opposing coercive treatment. His provocative thesis remains a touchstone in psychiatric ethics and the philosophy of mental illness.
2016-245: Hemispheric language dominance was first localized through Paul Broca's 1860s case studies of patients with left frontal lesions. While the overwhelming majority of right-handers are left-dominant for language, left-handers are more variable: roughly 70 percent are still left-dominant, with the remainder showing right or bilateral representation. The Wada test, developed by Juhn Wada in the 1940s, became the classic method for confirming language lateralization before neurosurgery.
2016-246: Genome-wide association studies, which took off after the HapMap project and the first major GWAS around 2005-2007, repeatedly found that most disease-associated single-nucleotide polymorphisms lie outside protein-coding exons, in intronic and intergenic regions. This surprising pattern shifted attention toward regulatory DNA, reinforced by the ENCODE project's findings that much non-coding genome influences gene expression. It reframed how psychiatric geneticists think about how risk variants actually act.
2016-247: Oxcarbazepine, a keto-analog of carbamazepine introduced to reduce its enzyme-induction and toxicity burden, never accumulated the robust mania trials its parent compound has. Carbamazepine, divalproex, and several atypical antipsychotics carry FDA approval and strong evidence for acute mania, whereas oxcarbazepine's controlled data are sparse and inconsistent. It illustrates the principle that a structural cousin of an effective agent does not inherit its evidence base by default.
2016-248: The principle that agitation in dementia often signals unmet needs, especially untreated pain, became central to person-centered dementia care promoted by researchers like Tom Kitwood. Because patients with advanced Alzheimer disease cannot reliably report pain, behaviors such as aggression may be the only signal. Guidelines emphasize searching for treatable medical causes, including pain, infection, and constipation, before resorting to psychotropics or restraints, which carry significant harm in this population.
2016-249: This vignette turns on cultural transference and the danger of mistaking culturally normative wariness or unfamiliarity with a clinician of differing background for paranoid psychopathology. The DSM-5 formalized attention to such issues with the Cultural Formulation Interview, building on decades of work in cultural psychiatry warning that misreading cultural distance produces diagnostic error and overpathologizing, particularly of minority and insular religious communities.
2016-25: Cerebellar hemispheric lesions disturb skilled, coordinated movements on the same (ipsilateral) side, because cerebellar pathways effectively cross twice. The lateral hemispheres govern limb coordination, producing dysmetria, intention tremor, and dysdiadochokinesia, whereas midline vermis lesions chiefly affect trunk, posture, and gait. Joseph Babinski coined "dysmetria" and "adiadochokinesia" in the early twentieth century to describe these cerebellar signs.
2016-250: The uncinate fasciculus is a hook-shaped white-matter tract (its name comes from Latin uncus, 'hook') linking the anterior temporal lobe with the orbital and ventral prefrontal cortex. One of the last tracts to fully myelinate, often into the third decade, it has drawn intense interest in psychiatry for abnormalities reported in social-emotional processing, antisocial traits, and conditions like temporal lobe epilepsy and frontotemporal dementia.
2016-251: Praising partial progress reflects motivational interviewing, developed by William Miller and Stephen Rollnick in the 1980s-1990s, originally for addiction treatment. Its core spirit emphasizes affirmation, rolling with resistance, and eliciting the patient's own motivation rather than confrontation or shaming. Empirical work showed that confrontational, disappointed responses tend to increase resistance, while affirming incremental change supports continued behavior change, a finding that reshaped substance-use counseling.
2016-252: Adolescent smoking prevention research consistently shows that distant, abstract harms like heart disease or dementia decades away poorly motivate teenagers, whose decision-making weighs immediate social consequences. Appeals to short-term, appearance-related effects such as bad breath and stained teeth align better with adolescent developmental priorities around peer acceptance and self-image, a principle that informed anti-tobacco campaigns like the 'truth' campaign launched around 2000.
2016-253: The split between administrative and clinical roles in handling physician impairment reflects a deliberate ethical safeguard. The administrative psychiatrist, often working with a hospital or licensing structure, is not bound by the confidentiality of a treating relationship because no doctor-patient relationship exists. This separation, codified in professional guidelines, protects the impaired physician's eventual treatment relationship from being contaminated by reporting and disciplinary functions.
2016-254: Excessive synaptic pruning has emerged as a unifying mechanism linking Fragile X syndrome and schizophrenia. Irwin Feinberg proposed in 1982 that schizophrenia might stem from faulty adolescent synaptic elimination, and Fragile X, caused by FMR1 silencing, disrupts the protein regulating synaptic maturation. Modern work implicating the complement gene C4 in schizophrenia-related pruning, published around 2016, dramatically revived this developmental hypothesis.
2016-255: Behavioral activation traces to the behavioral model of depression articulated by Charles Ferster and later Peter Lewinsohn in the 1970s, who argued that reduced contact with positive reinforcement perpetuates low mood and withdrawal. The approach was revived as a stand-alone treatment after Neil Jacobson's 1996 component-analysis study suggested activation alone matched full cognitive therapy. It works by scheduling rewarding, mastery-building activities to break cycles of avoidance and inactivity.
2016-256: An illusion is a misperception of a real external stimulus, distinguishing it from a hallucination, which is a perception without any stimulus. The word derives from Latin illudere, 'to mock or play with.' Karl Jaspers, in his 1913 General Psychopathology, was central to formalizing these descriptive distinctions, separating affect-driven illusions, completion illusions, and pareidolia, terms still used in the mental status examination today.
2016-257: School-based mental health care addresses a long-recognized access gap: the majority of children needing services never reach a clinic. By embedding services where students already are, this model removes transportation, stigma, and parental-arrangement barriers. The approach gained federal momentum in the U.S. through expanded school-based health center funding, and large surveys repeatedly found schools to be the de facto primary mental health provider for many American youth.
2016-258: Cortisol secretion follows a pronounced circadian rhythm, peaking in the early morning around awakening (the cortisol awakening response) and falling to a nadir near midnight, driven by the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and the suprachiasmatic nucleus master clock. This rhythm underlies the dexamethasone suppression test and the long-studied HPA-axis dysregulation in depression, where the normal diurnal pattern and suppression are often blunted.
2016-259: Dressing apraxia is the inability to carry out the learned motor task of dressing despite intact strength, sensation, and comprehension. The term apraxia (Greek, 'without action') was elaborated by Hugo Liepmann around 1900, who localized praxis to the left hemisphere. Dressing apraxia specifically is classically associated with non-dominant (right) parietal lobe lesions and is a useful bedside sign of parietal dysfunction.
2016-26: Female orgasmic disorder, per DSM-5, cannot be diagnosed when the difficulty is better explained by an external stressor such as intimate partner violence, severe relationship distress, or another non-sexual cause. This contextual exclusion reflects a deliberate shift in DSM-5 sexual dysfunctions toward requiring that symptoms not be fully attributable to partner factors or situational stress—protecting against pathologizing a normal response to an abusive situation.
2016-260: Guidance to answer young children's questions about anatomical sex differences simply, accurately, and matter-of-factly reflects developmental and psychosexual theory dating to Freud's stage model and refined by later child development research. Three-year-olds are in a normal phase of bodily curiosity, and clinicians advise honest, age-appropriate naming rather than evasion, shaming, or deferral, which can convey that the body or the question is taboo.
2016-261: Countertransference refers to the analyst's own emotional reactions to the patient, originally described by Freud around 1910 as an obstacle to be overcome. Later analysts, notably Heinrich Racker and Paula Heimann in the 1950s, reconceived it as a valuable clinical instrument: the therapist's feelings could illuminate the patient's inner world. This shift from contaminant to diagnostic tool reshaped psychodynamic technique.
2016-262: The triad of excessive daytime sleepiness with cataplexy, sudden emotion-triggered loss of muscle tone causing head drop or knee buckling, points to narcolepsy. The hallmark polysomnographic and Multiple Sleep Latency Test finding is sleep-onset REM. Narcolepsy with cataplexy was later linked to loss of hypocretin (orexin)-producing hypothalamic neurons, a discovery around 1998-2000 that revolutionized understanding of the disorder.
2016-263: This presentation, headache, jaw claudication, age over 50, and a markedly elevated ESR, is classic giant cell (temporal) arteritis, a medical emergency because of the risk of irreversible blindness from ophthalmic artery involvement. High-dose corticosteroids must be started immediately, even before biopsy confirmation. The condition was described by Horton in the 1930s, and the ESR threshold popularized as part of later classification criteria.
2016-264: Clozapine's low affinity for the D2 receptor underlies both its near-absence of extrapyramidal side effects and its status as the prototype 'atypical' antipsychotic. Synthesized in the 1950s-1960s, it challenged the dogma that strong D2 blockade was required for efficacy. Its 1975 withdrawal after agranulocytosis deaths in Finland, then dramatic 1988 reinstatement following the Kane trial, made it one of psychiatry's most storied drugs.
2016-265: Clozapine is the only medication with an FDA indication for reducing suicidal behavior, granted in 2002 on the strength of the InterSUICIDE Prevention Trial (InterSePT), published 2003, which compared clozapine with olanzapine in patients with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder at high suicide risk. This made clozapine uniquely evidenced for an outcome that drives much of the excess mortality in schizophrenia.
2016-266: Lithium is well known to prolong seizure duration during ECT and can produce prolonged or tardive seizures, as well as heightened post-ictal confusion and neurotoxicity. Because of this interaction, clinicians often hold or reduce lithium around ECT courses. The concern reflects lithium's broad effects on neuronal excitability and its narrow therapeutic index, long a caution in combining the two treatments.
2016-267: Voluntariness is one of the three pillars of informed consent, alongside disclosure and capacity, and is violated when consent is obtained through coercion or undue inducement. Promising expedited discharge in exchange for taking medication constitutes coercion. The doctrine of informed consent crystallized after cases like Canterbury v. Spence (1972) and is anchored in the ethical principle of respect for autonomy.
2016-268: Genome-wide association studies are designed to scan the genome for common variants, typically single-nucleotide polymorphisms with population frequencies above roughly one to five percent, testing their statistical association with disease across very large samples. This 'common disease, common variant' strategy, enabled by the HapMap and high-throughput genotyping in the mid-2000s, contrasts with sequencing approaches that hunt for rare mutations or copy-number variants.
2016-269: This is transient global amnesia: an abrupt, isolated, anterograde memory loss with repetitive questioning, preserved identity and motor function, and full resolution typically within 24 hours, often under several hours. First named by Fisher and Adams in the 1960s, it is benign, rarely recurs, and despite mimicking stroke is not associated with significant vascular risk or lasting deficit, with imaging usually normal or showing only tiny transient hippocampal changes.
2016-27: For patients with multiple, shifting, medically unexplained somatic complaints, the evidence-based management strategy is regular, scheduled visits with a single physician and a brief examination at each one—decoupling care from symptom escalation. This approach, rooted in classic work on somatization by Smith and colleagues in the 1980s, reduces unnecessary testing, ER visits, and costs by giving the patient predictable attention rather than confrontation or dismissal.
2016-270: Research on U.S. military families intensified during the prolonged Iraq and Afghanistan deployments, with studies from the late 2000s documenting increased anxiety, behavioral, and emotional symptoms in children during and after a parent's deployment, plus elevated maltreatment risk around reintegration. Effects vary by the child's developmental stage. This literature shaped military family-support programs and screening recommendations for this vulnerable population.
2016-271: Cognitive behavior therapy is the backbone of modern sex-offender treatment, typically combined with relapse-prevention models borrowed from addiction work by G. Alan Marlatt in the 1980s. The aim is to identify cognitive distortions, restructure deviant arousal patterns, and build coping skills to interrupt the offense chain. Many programs operate under the 'Risk-Need-Responsivity' framework developed by Canadian psychologists Andrews and Bonta, which holds that CBT-based interventions matched to risk level reduce recidivism.
2016-272: HIPAA, enacted in 1996, carves out a 'law enforcement exception' allowing covered entities to disclose limited protected health information to police without patient consent under specific circumstances, including providing notification of a patient's discharge. Crucially, no court order, written request, filed charges, or patient notification is mandated for these permitted disclosures. The rule reflects the Privacy Rule's attempt to balance confidentiality against legitimate public-safety and law-enforcement needs.
2016-273: Acculturation difficulty appears in the DSM as a 'V-code' (other condition that may be a focus of clinical attention) rather than a disorder. The term 'acculturation' was popularized in early-20th-century anthropology by figures like Redfield, Linton, and Herskovits to describe the changes that occur when cultural groups come into continuous contact. In clinical use it captures distress from adapting to a new culture or value system, including the intergenerational gap between family-of-origin expectations and an individual's emerging identity.
2016-274: The mesolimbic dopamine pathway, projecting from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens, is the final common reward pathway for virtually all drugs of abuse. Roy Wise and colleagues advanced the 'dopamine hypothesis of reward' in the 1970s-80s, and James Olds and Peter Milner's 1954 brain-stimulation experiments in rats first revealed these reward circuits. Nearly every addictive substance, whatever its initial target, converges on increasing accumbens dopamine.
2016-275: The distinction between upper and lower facial weakness is a classic localization pearl: the upper face (forehead) receives bilateral cortical innervation, so a central (stroke) lesion spares the forehead, whereas a peripheral seventh-nerve lesion like Bell palsy weakens the whole hemiface. Bell palsy is named for Scottish anatomist Sir Charles Bell, who described the facial nerve's motor function in the early 1800s. Forehead involvement therefore points away from stroke and away from tPA.
2016-276: Separation anxiety disorder was reclassified in DSM-5 (2013), moving out of the childhood-disorders chapter into the anxiety disorders so it could be formally diagnosed in adults. The construct grew from John Bowlby's attachment theory and the early observations of childhood 'school refusal.' The hallmark is excessive fear of separation from major attachment figures, with the panic-like episodes tied specifically to being away from the attachment figure rather than occurring out of the blue.
2016-277: The American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology, founded in 1934, structures its Maintenance of Certification around the ACGME/ABMS core competencies. Of those, medical knowledge is universally required and assessed through continuing education and examination. The shift from lifelong certificates to time-limited certification and ongoing MOC began in the 1990s, reflecting a broader medical-profession move toward demonstrating continued competence rather than relying on a one-time board pass.
2016-278: The Multiple Sleep Latency Test, developed by Mary Carskadon and William Dement in the 1970s, objectively quantifies daytime sleepiness through a series of scheduled daytime nap opportunities. In narcolepsy it shows a short mean sleep latency plus two or more sleep-onset REM periods (SOREMPs), the diagnostic signature reflecting the disorder's intrusion of REM into wakefulness. It is always performed after a preceding overnight polysomnogram to ensure adequate prior sleep.
2016-279: Dendritic spines, the tiny protrusions where most excitatory synapses form, were first drawn by Santiago Ramón y Cajal using the Golgi stain around 1888; he suspected they were real structures, not artifacts, decades before microscopy could confirm it. Their rapid formation, retraction, and reshaping underlies synaptic plasticity and learning. Abnormal spine density and morphology are now implicated in conditions ranging from intellectual disability and fragile X syndrome to schizophrenia.
2016-28: Global mental health is distinguished from much of global medicine by how heavily culture shapes the way distress is conceived, expressed, and diagnosed, since psychiatric diagnoses lack biomarkers and rest on behavior and meaning. "Idioms of distress" and culture-bound syndromes mean symptom presentation and explanatory models vary far more than for, say, an infectious disease. Arthur Kleinman's concept of "explanatory models" underscores this challenge in exporting Western diagnostic categories.
2016-280: Functional MRI relies on the BOLD (Blood-Oxygen-Level-Dependent) signal, discovered by Seiji Ogawa at Bell Labs around 1990. Deoxyhemoglobin is paramagnetic while oxyhemoglobin is not, so neural activity—which transiently increases local oxygenated blood flow and lowers the relative deoxyhemoglobin concentration—alters the magnetic signal. Linus Pauling had described hemoglobin's magnetic properties back in 1936, work that fMRI would exploit decades later to image the working brain noninvasively.
2016-281: 'ICU psychosis' is an older, somewhat misleading label for what is almost always delirium—an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness with a medical cause. The DSM has steadily clarified delirium's criteria, emphasizing inattention and an underlying physiological etiology over the term 'psychosis,' which wrongly implies a primary psychiatric illness. Recognizing the syndrome as delirium matters because it prompts a hunt for reversible causes rather than antipsychotic management alone.
2016-282: Electroconvulsive therapy is a recognized treatment for neuroleptic malignant syndrome, particularly refractory cases or when the catatonia-NMS overlap makes the two hard to separate. NMS itself was described by French clinicians (Delay and Deniker's group) in the early 1960s soon after chlorpromazine's introduction. Because NMS and malignant catatonia share features and ECT is the definitive catatonia treatment, ECT became a logical rescue therapy when dantrolene and bromocriptine fail.
2016-283: Pyromania, from the Greek 'pyr' (fire) and 'mania' (madness), was among the early 'monomanias' described by French alienist Jean-Étienne Esquirol in the 1830s. It is classified among the impulse-control disorders, defined by deliberate fire-setting on more than one occasion, tension or arousal beforehand, fascination with fire, and relief or gratification afterward—without motives of profit, revenge, or concealment. It is a diagnosis of exclusion, distinct from arson driven by other goals.
2016-284: The insanity defense's modern form descends from the M'Naghten Rules, set down by English judges in 1843 after Daniel M'Naghten shot the Prime Minister's secretary while delusional. The standard asks whether, due to mental disease, the defendant did not know the nature of the act or that it was wrong. Crucially, whether a defendant meets the legal standard is a question for the trier of fact—typically the jury—not the testifying experts.
2016-285: Interpersonal psychotherapy, developed by Gerald Klerman and Myrna Weissman in the 1970s for depression, is structured into distinct phases. The initial phase centers on the 'interpersonal inventory'—a systematic review of the patient's significant relationships—and on framing the depression within one of four problem areas: grief, role disputes, role transitions, or interpersonal deficits. This relationship survey anchors the focused, time-limited work that follows.
2016-286: Regression analysis is the workhorse for modeling the relationship between an outcome and multiple predictor variables simultaneously. The term 'regression' was coined by Sir Francis Galton in the 1880s when he observed 'regression toward mediocrity' (the mean) in the heights of offspring relative to their parents. Multiple regression lets researchers examine several putative risk factors at once while estimating each one's independent contribution.
2016-287: Menarche in girls and the first nocturnal emission (spermarche) in boys are the conventional markers signaling reproductive capacity, distinct from earlier secondary sexual characteristics. The staging of pubertal development was formalized by James Tanner, whose 'Tanner stages' from work in the mid-20th century remain standard. Earlier signs like breast buds, testicular enlargement, and pubic hair indicate that puberty has begun but not yet that fertility has been achieved.
2016-288: Carotid sinus syncope results from a hypersensitive carotid baroreflex—pressure on the neck (a tight collar, head turning, shaving) triggers a reflex drop in heart rate and blood pressure. Brief 'convulsive' jerks from cerebral hypoperfusion (convulsive syncope) can mimic seizure. The carotid sinus reflex was characterized by Heinrich Hering in the 1920s, and the sinus nerve carrying its afferents is still sometimes called Hering's nerve.
2016-289: The hypothesis that physical activity protects against cognitive decline draws on decades of epidemiologic and trial data; despite variable study quality, most evidence favors a benefit, likely mediated by improved cerebral perfusion, neurotrophic factors like BDNF, and vascular health. Aerobic exercise has been linked to larger hippocampal volume in older adults in randomized work. Exercise also independently reduces depression risk, making it a broadly beneficial recommendation.
2016-29: The Trail Making Test, developed for the U.S. Army in the 1940s and later incorporated into the Halstead-Reitan battery, measures set-shifting and cognitive flexibility in its Part B, where the examinee alternates between numbers and letters. Performance is a classic index of executive functioning, mediated by prefrontal circuitry. Deficits here in depressed adolescents point to impaired executive control rather than memory or simple processing speed, which Part A captures.
2016-290: Genomic imprinting—where a gene is expressed depending on whether it was inherited from mother or father—works through differential DNA methylation that silences one parental allele. If the active allele is then deleted or mutated, there is no backup, producing disease. The classic illustration is the chromosome 15q11-13 region: defects yield Prader-Willi syndrome when of paternal origin and Angelman syndrome when of maternal origin, a striking demonstration of parent-of-origin effects.
2016-291: Large randomized trials, including data from cardiovascular and cognition studies, have generally failed to show that omega-3 fatty acid supplementation prevents cognitive decline or dementia in older adults. Early enthusiasm came from observational links between fish consumption and lower dementia rates, but those associations did not hold up in controlled supplementation. Omega-3s may still offer cardiovascular or triglyceride-lowering benefits, so the honest answer separates proven from unproven claims.
2016-292: Self psychology was founded by Heinz Kohut, who broke from classical Freudian drive theory in the 1970s with works like 'The Analysis of the Self.' He argued that healthy development requires empathic responsiveness from 'selfobjects'—usually parents—who provide mirroring, idealization, and twinship. Failures of this empathic attunement, rather than repressed drives, were Kohut's explanation for narcissistic injury and disturbances in the sense of self-worth.
2016-293: STAR*D, the largest real-world antidepressant effectiveness trial, enrolled over 4,000 patients and ran in the early 2000s. Its sobering headline finding was that only about a third of patients achieved remission with the first SSRI (citalopram), with cumulative remission climbing only modestly across subsequent treatment steps. The study reshaped clinical expectations about depression treatment, underscoring that many patients need multiple sequential trials to get well.
2016-294: This scenario illustrates the principle of veracity and honesty in medical documentation. Falsifying a chart to claim ongoing suicidality—even with the benevolent aim of securing care—is unethical primarily because it misrepresents the clinical rationale, corrupting the record that other clinicians and payers rely upon. Professional ethics codes, including the AMA's and APA's, treat truthful documentation as foundational; good intentions do not justify deception that distorts the stated basis for treatment.
2016-295: This addresses operant conditioning principles applied at the bedside: positive reinforcement to shape adaptive behavior. The framework derives from B.F. Skinner's mid-20th-century work on operant learning, later formalized into 'behavior modification' and 'contingency management' programs. Rewarding self-feeding reinforces independence and recovery, whereas hand-feeding inadvertently reinforces regression and dependency—a common dynamic in medically ill patients under stress.
2016-296: This reflects the 'authoritative' parenting style, identified by developmental psychologist Diana Baumrind in the 1960s. She distinguished authoritative (high warmth plus firm, reasoned limits) from authoritarian (high control, low warmth) and permissive (high warmth, few limits) styles. Her longitudinal research consistently linked the authoritative approach—validating the adolescent's feelings while still enforcing consequences—to the best long-term outcomes in competence and self-regulation.
2016-297: The amnestic versus nonamnestic distinction in mild cognitive impairment was advanced largely by Ronald Petersen and colleagues at Mayo Clinic. Amnestic MCI, marked by prominent memory loss, carries the highest risk of conversion to Alzheimer disease, the prototypical amnestic dementia. The MCI construct itself crystallized in the 1990s as researchers sought to capture the transitional zone between normal aging and dementia, creating a target for early intervention trials.
2016-298: The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex is the canonical seat of working memory and executive function. Patricia Goldman-Rakic's elegant primate experiments in the 1980s-90s showed individual DLPFC neurons firing to hold spatial information 'online' during a delay—the cellular substrate of working memory. Damage or dysfunction here impairs planning, set-shifting, and holding information in mind, deficits prominent in schizophrenia and frontal-lobe injury.
2016-299: The Affordable Care Act's Section 2703 created Medicaid 'health homes' in 2010 to coordinate care for beneficiaries with chronic conditions. The model rests on a 'whole-person' philosophy that integrates physical health, behavioral health, and links to community, social, and family supports rather than treating them as siloed services. It reflects the broader patient-centered medical home movement aimed at better outcomes and lower costs for complex, high-need populations.
2016-3: Tangentiality describes replies that veer off and never return to the point, contrasted with circumstantiality, where the speaker eventually arrives at the goal after excessive detail. Both terms were sharpened in the descriptive psychopathology tradition associated with Eugen Bleuler and later formalized in American phenomenology. A useful mnemonic: a tangent line touches a circle and shoots off forever, while a circumstantial speaker circles the point before landing on it.
2016-30: Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures, formerly "pseudoseizures," are distinguished from true generalized tonic-clonic seizures partly by the absence of a postictal serum prolactin rise. Genuine generalized convulsions transiently elevate prolactin within roughly 10 to 20 minutes via hypothalamic discharge, whereas nonepileptic events typically do not. This biomarker, studied since the late 1970s, supplements video-EEG, which remains the actual gold standard for telling the two apart.
2016-31: The idea that infants differ in how they handle stimulation comes from the landmark New York Longitudinal Study begun in the 1950s by Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess, which defined temperament dimensions like threshold of responsiveness and reactivity. Hypersensitive, low-threshold infants startle and cry easily because ordinary stimuli feel overwhelming. This work introduced the now-classic categories of the easy, difficult, and slow-to-warm-up child and the concept of goodness-of-fit between child and caregiver.
2016-32: DSM-5's Criterion A for schizophrenia requires at least one of the three 'positive' core symptoms: delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech. This was a deliberate tightening from DSM-IV, which had allowed two bizarre delusions or special hallucinations alone to suffice. The notion of disorganized thought traces to Eugen Bleuler, who in 1911 coined 'schizophrenia' and ranked loosening of associations among his fundamental symptoms.
2016-33: Adenosine is the body's built-in sleep pressure signal, accumulating in the basal forebrain during wakefulness and inhibiting arousal-promoting neurons. Prostaglandin D2 is one of the most potent endogenous sleep-promoting substances and acts in part by raising extracellular adenosine. The practical hook is caffeine: it produces alertness precisely by blocking adenosine A1 and A2A receptors, reversing this drowsiness signal.
2016-34: With normal aging the brain loses dopaminergic neurons and dopamine receptors, leaving older adults with diminished nigrostriatal reserve. Because antipsychotics work by blocking D2 receptors, this reduced baseline means even modest blockade can tip patients into parkinsonism, dystonia, and other extrapyramidal symptoms. The principle 'start low, go slow' in geriatric prescribing follows directly from this narrowed therapeutic window.
2016-35: The bilateral medial temporal and orbitofrontal involvement, temporal periodic discharges on EEG, and acute encephalopathy are the classic signature of herpes simplex encephalitis, the most common sporadic fatal viral encephalitis. Because outcomes hinge on early antiviral therapy, the teaching mantra is to start acyclovir empirically before PCR confirmation. Untreated HSV encephalitis carries roughly 70% mortality, which acyclovir dramatically reduces.
2016-36: Dissociative identity disorder, called multiple personality disorder until DSM-IV in 1994, features amnestic gaps, identity discontinuity, depersonalization, and intrusions such as hearing a child's voice. It became a cultural touchstone through cases like 'Sybil' and 'The Three Faces of Eve,' and remains one of psychiatry's most debated diagnoses. DSM-5 added that the disruption may be self-reported or observed and can include possession-like presentations across cultures.
2016-37: Factitious disorder is defined by the deliberate falsification of physical or psychological symptoms in the absence of obvious external reward, distinguishing it from malingering. Its most dramatic form was named Munchausen syndrome by physician Richard Asher in 1951, after Baron Munchausen, the 18th-century teller of wildly exaggerated tall tales. DSM-5 renamed the imposed-on-another variant 'factitious disorder imposed on another,' formerly Munchausen by proxy.
2016-38: Primary prevention aims to stop disease before it ever starts by reducing risk factors, here controlling hypertension, diabetes, and lipids to prevent vascular cognitive decline. The classic public-health framework of primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention was articulated by Hugh Leavell and E. Gurney Clark in the 1950s. The memorable distinction: primary prevents onset, secondary catches it early via screening, and tertiary limits disability once disease exists.
2016-39: Asking a patient to explain their own illness draws on Arthur Kleinman's 'explanatory model' interview, introduced in his influential 1978 work and 1988 book The Illness Narratives. Kleinman, a psychiatrist and anthropologist, distinguished 'disease' (the biomedical entity) from 'illness' (the lived, culturally shaped experience). DSM-5's Cultural Formulation Interview operationalized these questions to elicit how patients understand cause, course, and meaning of their suffering.
2016-4: Central pontine myelinolysis, now often called osmotic demyelination syndrome, was first described by Adams, Victor, and Mancall in 1959, originally in malnourished and alcoholic patients. It results from overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia, which dehydrates and demyelinates pontine neurons, classically producing a delayed "locked-in" quadriparesis. The clinical teaching mantra is to raise serum sodium no faster than the guideline-recommended limits per day—"from low to high, your pons will die."
2016-40: Epigenetics, a term coined by developmental biologist Conrad Waddington in the 1940s, refers to heritable changes in gene expression without alteration of the DNA sequence, via mechanisms like DNA methylation and histone modification. It elegantly explains why genetically identical twins diverge phenotypically as environment marks their genomes differently. Waddington's image of the 'epigenetic landscape,' a ball rolling down branching valleys, remains the field's iconic metaphor.
2016-41: Memantine, FDA-approved in 2003 for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease, is an uncompetitive NMDA-receptor antagonist that dampens glutamate excitotoxicity, a mechanism entirely distinct from cholinesterase inhibitors like donepezil. Because the two act on different systems, they are commonly combined as disease progresses. Memantine's lineage is unusual: it derives from amantadine, originally an antiviral and antiparkinsonian agent.
2016-42: Cortical acetylcholine receptors include both ionotropic nicotinic and metabotropic muscarinic subtypes, producing effects that can be excitatory or inhibitory depending on the receptor and circuit. The neurotransmitter was the first ever identified, isolated by Otto Loewi in his famous 1921 'frog heart' experiment, reportedly conceived in a dream, which won him the 1936 Nobel Prize. Cholinergic loss in the nucleus basalis underlies Alzheimer cognitive decline.
2016-43: The triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia is Wernicke encephalopathy, caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency and named for Carl Wernicke, who described it in 1881. It is a medical emergency because untreated cases can progress to irreversible Korsakoff amnesia. The crucial clinical pearl is to give thiamine before glucose, since a carbohydrate load can precipitate or worsen the syndrome in deficient patients.
2016-44: Interpersonal psychotherapy, developed by Gerald Klerman and Myrna Weissman in the 1970s and 1980s, ties depressive symptoms to current relationships and frames recovery around four problem areas: grief, role transitions, interpersonal disputes, and interpersonal deficits. Assessing the quality of social connections is central from the outset. IPT was rigorously manualized and tested in the NIMH Treatment of Depression Collaborative Research Program in the 1980s.
2016-45: This maps to the Institute of Medicine's six aims for quality care from its landmark 2001 report Crossing the Quality Chasm: care should be safe, timely, effective, efficient, equitable, and patient-centered. Verifying identity before treatment prevents wrong-patient errors, squarely a safety aim. The IOM's earlier 1999 report, To Err Is Human, famously estimated tens of thousands of annual deaths from preventable medical error, galvanizing the patient-safety movement.
2016-46: The strongest gene-environment interaction for aggression involves the MAOA gene and childhood maltreatment, demonstrated in Avshalom Caspi and Terrie Moffitt's influential 2002 Science study of a New Zealand birth cohort. Maltreated boys with the low-activity MAOA variant were far more likely to develop antisocial behavior. Sensationalized press coverage dubbed it the 'warrior gene,' a label researchers consider an oversimplification of a true interaction effect.
2016-47: Chronotherapy treats circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders by progressively shifting bedtime to reset the internal clock, an approach formalized by Charles Czeisler and colleagues around 1981 for delayed sleep phase syndrome. It exploits the body's tendency to drift later, advancing sleep around the clock until the desired schedule is reached. Modern circadian management increasingly pairs or replaces it with timed bright light and melatonin.
2016-48: Naming an object felt in the left hand but not the right reflects a disconnection syndrome of the corpus callosum, the great fiber bundle linking the hemispheres. Left-hand sensation projects to the right hemisphere, and without a callosum that information cannot reach the left-hemisphere language centers to be named. Roger Sperry's split-brain studies of callosotomy patients illuminated these effects and earned him the 1981 Nobel Prize.
2016-49: This cluster of overeating, weight gain, hypersomnia, and leaden paralysis defines depression 'with atypical features,' whose hallmark is mood reactivity, the capacity to brighten in response to positive events. The 'atypical' label is historical, coined when these patients were noted to respond preferentially to MAO inhibitors rather than tricyclics. Despite the name, atypical depression is quite common, particularly in younger patients.
2016-5: Using one object to stand for another—a banana as a telephone—is symbolic or pretend play, a hallmark Jean Piaget placed in his preoperational stage, beginning around age two. He called it the semiotic or symbolic function: the dawning capacity to let a mental symbol represent something absent. This same representational leap underlies language and deferred imitation, which is why its absence is a red flag for autism spectrum disorder.
2016-50: This reflects the ethical hazard of dual agency: a treating psychiatrist cannot serve as both healer and forensic evaluator without compromising the therapeutic alliance. The American Academy of Psychiatry and the Law and commentators like Larry Strasburger and Thomas Gutheil warned in a noted 1997 paper against the treating clinician offering forensic opinions on causation, damages, or disability. The treater may appropriately describe clinical presentation and observed treatment course.
2016-51: Performing a behavior to avoid an unpleasant outcome (the time-out) is negative reinforcement, where removing or preventing an aversive stimulus strengthens behavior. The term comes from B.F. Skinner's operant conditioning framework of the 1930s, and the persistent confusion is that 'negative' means subtraction, not punishment. Reinforcement always increases behavior; punishment decreases it, regardless of the positive/negative sign.
2016-52: The picture of restlessness, flushing, fasciculations, tachycardia, and racing thought and speech is caffeine intoxication, here from energy drinks that can pack hundreds of milligrams per can plus added stimulants. Caffeine intoxication is a formal DSM diagnosis, and the syndrome reflects adenosine-receptor blockade and adrenergic activation. Adolescent energy-drink overconsumption became a recognized public-health concern, prompting emergency department surveillance reports in the 2010s.
2016-53: Among second-generation antipsychotics, paliperidone (the active metabolite of risperidone, marketed as Invega from 2006) carries specific FDA labeling cautioning about QTc prolongation. QTc prolongation reflects delayed cardiac repolarization, typically via blockade of the hERG potassium channel, and raises risk of torsades de pointes. Among first-generation agents, intravenous haloperidol and thioridazine are the classic offenders flagged for the same concern.
2016-54: Hemispatial neglect of the left side localizes to the right parietal lobe, particularly the inferior parietal region, reflecting the right hemisphere's dominance for spatial attention. Because the right side directs attention to both hemifields while the left attends mainly rightward, right-sided damage leaves the left world unattended with no left hemisphere to compensate. Classic bedside signs include leftward errors on clock drawing and line bisection.
2016-55: Hyperuricemia with cognitive impairment, choreoathetosis, and compulsive self-mutilating biting describes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, an X-linked recessive disorder first reported in 1964 by medical student Michael Lesch and his mentor William Nyhan. It results from deficiency of the purine-salvage enzyme HGPRT, leading to massive uric acid overproduction. The self-injurious lip and finger biting is its haunting and distinctive behavioral hallmark.
2016-56: The Stroop Test, naming the ink color while ignoring the printed word, was published by John Ridley Stroop in 1935 and remains one of psychology's most replicated paradigms. The 'Stroop effect' is the interference and slowing that occurs when word and color conflict, making it a sensitive measure of selective attention and inhibitory frontal-executive control. It is among the most cited experiments in cognitive science.
2016-57: Reliability is consistency, whether an instrument yields the same result across raters (inter-rater) or over repeated administration (test-retest), as opposed to validity, which asks whether it measures the true target. The distinction was sharpened during DSM-III's 1980 development, when fixing psychiatry's notoriously poor diagnostic reliability became a central goal, aided by tools like the kappa statistic to quantify agreement beyond chance.
2016-58: A clouded or fluctuating sensorium, impaired attention and altered consciousness, is the cardinal sign of delirium and points strongly toward an underlying medical or toxic cause rather than a primary psychiatric disorder. This emphasis on level of consciousness as the key discriminator dates to the foundational work of George Engel and John Romano on delirium in the 1950s, who linked it to diffuse cerebral metabolic disturbance reflected in EEG slowing.
2016-59: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is caused by the JC virus, named for the patient initials John Cunningham from whom the polyomavirus was isolated in 1971. It is a latent infection that reactivates and destroys oligodendrocytes only under severe immunosuppression, as in advanced AIDS or with immunomodulators like natalizumab. That latter association reshaped multiple sclerosis drug monitoring after PML cases emerged in the mid-2000s.
2016-6: Paroxetine has the shortest half-life among the common SSRIs (roughly a day) and, unlike fluoxetine, no long-acting active metabolite, so blood levels drop fast when doses are missed. It is also a potent anticholinergic and inhibits its own metabolism via CYP2D6, compounding withdrawal. The classic discontinuation acronym is FINISH: Flu-like symptoms, Insomnia, Nausea, Imbalance, Sensory disturbances ("brain zaps"), and Hyperarousal. Fluoxetine's long half-life makes it the least likely to cause this.
2016-60: Neurosyphilis in its tertiary form, general paresis of the insane, produces psychosis, grandiosity, and gait disturbance, and once filled asylum beds. In 1917 Austrian psychiatrist Julius Wagner-Jauregg pioneered malariotherapy, deliberately inducing fever to kill the spirochete, earning the 1927 Nobel Prize in Medicine, the only psychiatrist so honored. Penicillin's arrival in the 1940s rendered the fever cure obsolete.
2016-61: Socratic questioning takes its name from Socrates, the ancient Greek philosopher who famously taught not by lecturing but by asking probing questions that led pupils to examine their own assumptions (the 'Socratic method'). Aaron Beck adopted this collaborative, guided-discovery style as the engine of cognitive therapy in the 1960s and 70s, using gentle questioning rather than direct disputation to help patients test the evidence for their automatic negative thoughts.
2016-62: The false-belief task became the gold-standard test of 'theory of mind,' the ability to attribute mental states to others. The classic 'Sally-Anne' version was devised by Simon Baron-Cohen, Alan Leslie, and Uta Frith in a landmark 1985 study showing that many children with autism failed it. The phrase 'theory of mind' itself was coined earlier, by Premack and Woodruff in 1978 in their work asking whether chimpanzees possessed it.
2016-63: Continuous quality improvement grew out of the industrial total-quality-management movement, with roots in W. Edwards Deming's statistical process-control work that helped rebuild postwar Japanese manufacturing. Healthcare imported the philosophy in the 1980s-90s, shifting focus from blaming individuals to improving systems and processes. Tracking patient satisfaction over time for accreditors like the Joint Commission is a quintessential CQI activity: ongoing measurement aimed at iterative betterment rather than one-time inspection.
