Pre-trauma vulnerabilities such as prior childhood adversity, psychiatric history, and lack of social support emerged as robust predictors. Notably, peritraumatic factors and the trauma's severity often predicted PTSD even more strongly than static pre-trauma traits.
2017-222: Quetiapine exemplifies the 'loose binding' or fast-off-D2 hypothesis advanced by Philip Seeman, which holds that some atypicals dissociate rapidly from the dopamine D2 receptor and need only transient, low-affinity occupancy. This weak D2 affinity explains quetiapine's very low risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and its prominent sedating, antihistaminergic profile, making it behave clinically quite differently from high-affinity agents like risperidone or paliperidone.
2017-223: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial frontal lobe and the leg area of the motor homunculus, which is tucked along the interhemispheric fissure. Hence an ACA stroke classically spares the arm and face but weakens the contralateral leg, and damage to medial frontal and orbitofrontal regions produces apathy, abulia, and personality change. The homuncular map was charted by Wilder Penfield through intraoperative cortical stimulation.
2017-224: The distinction between a boundary crossing and a boundary violation was crystallized by Glen Gabbard and Eric Lazarus in the 1990s. A boundary crossing is a benign, often helpful departure from the usual therapeutic frame that serves the patient, whereas a violation is exploitative and harms the patient. Graciously accepting a small gift to build alliance with a wary patient is the textbook example of a benign crossing.
2017-225: Selective abstraction is one of the cognitive distortions catalogued by Aaron Beck, the founder of cognitive therapy, who first described these systematic errors while treating depression in the 1960s. Also called 'mental filter,' it involves focusing on a single negative detail while ignoring the larger, more positive context, exactly the pattern of fixating on one critical comment amid glowing reviews. Beck's daughter Judith later helped codify the full list.
2017-226: Alfred Kinsey's mid-twentieth-century research reframed sexual orientation as a continuum, the famous seven-point Kinsey scale, rather than a binary. Adolescence is widely understood as a period of fluidity in which transient same-sex arousal is common and does not fix orientation. Reassuring an adolescent that such feelings are normal and that identity continues to consolidate reflects this developmental, nonpathologizing understanding.
2017-227: Neonatal adaptation syndrome, sometimes called poor neonatal adaptation, describes transient jitteriness, irritability, feeding and respiratory difficulties seen in roughly a quarter to a third of infants exposed to SSRIs late in pregnancy. The FDA added a class label warning in 2004. The syndrome is usually mild and self-limited within days, and clinicians weigh it against the well-documented harms of untreated maternal depression.
2017-228: Structured problem-solving in behavioral couples therapy was systematized by Neil Jacobson and Gayla Margolin in their 1979 text. A core rule is that before any solutions are generated, the listening partner must paraphrase the speaker's stated problem to confirm accurate understanding, only then do the partners brainstorm and evaluate solutions. This reflective-listening step prevents the escalating misattributions that fuel distressed couples' conflicts.
2017-229: Wernicke's aphasia is named for Carl Wernicke, who in 1874, while still in his twenties, described fluent but meaningless speech with impaired comprehension following damage to the posterior superior temporal gyrus. This 'receptive' aphasia complemented Broca's earlier 'expressive' aphasia, and Wernicke presciently predicted the existence of conduction aphasia from a disconnection between the two regions, laying groundwork for disconnection neurology.
2017-23: Clomipramine, a tricyclic with the strongest serotonergic action of its class and a first-line agent for OCD, carries notable seizure risk in overdose owing to its proconvulsant tricyclic properties (sodium-channel blockade and anticholinergic effects). Among antidepressants, tricyclics and bupropion are the most epileptogenic in overdose, whereas SSRIs and SNRIs pose comparatively lower seizure risk.
2017-230: The inflammatory hypothesis of depression, sometimes called the 'macrophage theory' proposed by Ronald Smith in 1991, holds that pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, TNF-alpha, and CRP are elevated in depressed patients. Interferon therapy for hepatitis famously induced depression in many recipients, strengthening the link, and trials of anti-inflammatory agents like infliximab have shown benefit in subgroups with high baseline inflammation.
2017-231: Curiosity about bodies and genitals in preschoolers is a normal, expected feature of psychosexual development, corresponding to Freud's phallic stage with its heightened interest in anatomical differences. Contemporary child development research distinguishes such ordinary exploratory curiosity from concerning sexualized behavior; matter-of-fact questions about body parts in a three-year-old fall squarely within normative development and warrant simple, accurate answers rather than alarm.
2017-232: A widespread myth holds that HIPAA forbids clinicians from talking to one another without a signed release. In fact, the 2003 Privacy Rule explicitly permits disclosures among providers for treatment, payment, and healthcare operations without patient authorization. Coordinating safe prescribing with a primary care provider is a quintessential treatment communication, so a signed consent form is not legally required.
2017-233: A cohort study follows exposed and unexposed groups forward in time to see who develops the outcome, making it the natural design for an exposure-to-incidence question like whether a drug precedes new psychotic symptoms. The Framingham Heart Study, launched in 1948, is the archetypal prospective cohort and gave epidemiology much of its vocabulary, including the very term 'risk factor.'
2017-234: Linkage analysis traces how genetic markers co-segregate with a disease across generations of a pedigree, exploiting the fact that loci near each other on a chromosome are inherited together. The method's triumph was the 1983 localization of the Huntington's disease gene to chromosome 4 by James Gusella using a single large Venezuelan kindred, the first disease mapped by anonymous DNA markers.
2017-235: Duloxetine, a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, gained FDA approval for diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain in 2004, becoming one of the first agents specifically indicated for that condition. Its analgesic effect is attributed to boosting descending noradrenergic and serotonergic pain-inhibitory pathways in the spinal cord, an action shared with older tricyclics but achieved with a cleaner side-effect profile.
2017-236: Large epidemiological surveys of OCD consistently rank contamination obsessions, paired with washing and cleaning compulsions, as the single most common symptom dimension. The disorder's history is captured in the term itself: 'obsession' derives from the Latin obsidere, to besiege, reflecting the experience of intrusive thoughts laying siege to the mind. Samuel Johnson and Howard Hughes are among the famous figures believed to have had contamination-related symptoms.
2017-237: Attributable risk, the simple difference between the incidence in exposed and unexposed groups, quantifies the excess risk directly caused by the exposure. The concept and the broader framework of relative versus absolute risk measures grew out of mid-twentieth-century work, notably the British Doctors Study by Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill linking smoking to lung cancer, which made these risk metrics central to modern epidemiology.
2017-238: The dogma that the adult brain grows no new neurons was overturned by Fred 'Rusty' Gage and Peter Eriksson, who in 1998 used the cell-division marker BrdU in cancer patients' brains to show new neurons forming in the adult human hippocampal dentate gyrus. This adult hippocampal neurogenesis became linked to learning, memory, and the mechanism of antidepressant action, though its extent in humans remains debated.
2017-239: Margaret Mahler's separation-individuation theory, developed from infant observation in the 1960s and 70s, charts the toddler's psychological birth. The rapprochement subphase, roughly fifteen to twenty-four months, captures the conflict at the heart of borderline pathology: the child both darts away toward autonomy and anxiously returns for reassurance. Failure to resolve this push-pull is a classic developmental formulation for borderline patients' fear of both closeness and abandonment.
2017-24: Content validity asks whether a measure adequately samples the full domain it claims to assess. An omitted core element, here failing to ask about a traumatic event when defining PTSD, is a content-validity gap. The concept traces to mid-20th-century psychometrics; Lee Cronbach and Paul Meehl's influential 1955 paper on construct validity helped formalize the distinctions among content, criterion, and construct validity still used today.
2017-240: Genome-wide association studies scan hundreds of thousands to millions of single-nucleotide polymorphisms across many cases and controls to find variants statistically tied to disease, without prior hypotheses about which genes matter. The approach took off after the HapMap project and the first major GWAS around 2005 (age-related macular degeneration), and psychiatric GWAS later required enormous consortia to detect the many small-effect variants behind disorders like schizophrenia.
2017-241: Concern about stimulants and the cardiovascular system intensified after Health Canada briefly suspended Adderall XR in 2005 over reports of sudden death. The FDA subsequently issued warnings, and the AHA recommended cardiac screening for structural heart defects before initiating stimulants in children. Because stimulants raise heart rate and blood pressure, a known underlying cardiac defect is treated as a relative contraindication requiring cardiology input.
2017-242: The MHPAEA, signed by President George W. Bush in October 2008, built on the narrower Mental Health Parity Act of 1996. Its core demand was that quantitative treatment limits like visit caps, copays, and deductibles for behavioral health be no more restrictive than those for comparable medical/surgical care. Notably, it did not by itself mandate that plans cover mental health at all; that universal-coverage piece came later through the Affordable Care Act's essential health benefits.
2017-243: Dextromethorphan, the cough suppressant in countless cold remedies, was approved as a safer non-opioid alternative to codeine after a 1950s Navy-era research program. At high recreational doses it becomes an NMDA-receptor antagonist much like ketamine and PCP, producing dissociation; users describe ascending 'plateaus,' and the slang 'robotripping' derives from Robitussin. This pharmacology is why over-the-counter sales are now age-restricted in many states.
2017-244: DNA methylation is the best-studied epigenetic mechanism linking early adversity to later illness. Michael Meaney and Moshe Szyf's landmark rat studies in the early 2000s showed that low maternal licking and grooming left lasting methylation marks on the glucocorticoid receptor promoter in the hippocampus, altering stress reactivity into adulthood. The term 'epigenetics' itself was coined by Conrad Waddington in the 1940s, long before the molecular machinery was understood.
2017-245: Deinstitutionalization accelerated in the U.S. after chlorpromazine arrived in the mid-1950s and the 1963 Community Mental Health Act, dropping state hospital census from roughly 560,000 to under 100,000. The promised community infrastructure largely failed to materialize, and the unintended result was 'transinstitutionalization': the seriously mentally ill shifted into jails and prisons, which some now call the nation's largest psychiatric institutions.
2017-246: Myasthenia gravis, literally 'grave muscle weakness,' is the classic disorder of fatigable, fluctuating weakness worst at day's end and improved by rest. It results from autoantibodies against the acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction. Mary Walker's famous 1934 observation that physostigmine relieved symptoms launched anticholinesterase therapy, and the variable, asymmetric ocular involvement (ptosis, diplopia) makes it a great mimic of central lesions.
2017-247: Andropause, the gradual age-related decline in testosterone in men, is sometimes called late-onset hypogonadism to distinguish it from the abrupt hormonal drop of female menopause. The change is slow and partial rather than a true 'pause,' affecting erectile rigidity and other parameters over years. The term deliberately echoes menopause for memorability, though the analogy is imperfect.
2017-248: The wraparound process grew out of 1980s child mental health reform, notably the work of John VanDenBerg and Karl Dennis in Alaska and Illinois, and was reinforced by the federal Child and Adolescent Service System Program (CASSP) principles. Its defining feature is that the plan is individualized, family-driven, and youth-guided, wrapping services around the child rather than fitting the child into existing programs.
2017-249: Folic acid supplementation before conception reduces neural tube defects, a finding cemented by the 1991 MRC Vitamin Study in the Lancet showing roughly 70% risk reduction. This is especially relevant for women on antiepileptics like valproate and carbamazepine, which interfere with folate metabolism. The data drove mandatory folic-acid fortification of grain products in the U.S. starting in 1998.
2017-25: Direct, honest disclosure of one's training status reflects the ethical principles of informed consent and truth-telling that govern the physician-patient relationship. The 2017 update to the AMA Code of Medical Ethics emphasizes transparency about the roles of residents and trainees in patient care, and honest self-identification also builds the therapeutic alliance rather than evading or deflecting a reasonable question.
2017-250: Histone acetylation, added by 'writer' enzymes called HATs, neutralizes the positive charge on lysine residues, loosening histones' grip on negatively charged DNA and relaxing chromatin to permit transcription. Vincent Allfrey first linked acetylation to active gene expression in 1964. The opposing HDAC 'erasers' tighten chromatin, and HDAC inhibitors are now studied as potential mood and cognition agents.
2017-251: This reflects Prochaska and DiClemente's Transtheoretical Model, developed in the early 1980s from studying how smokers quit. In precontemplation the person isn't yet considering change, so confrontation or quit-date pushing backfires; the task is gentle consciousness-raising. The stages, precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, and maintenance, became the backbone of motivational interviewing.
2017-252: Physician health programs emerged after the AMA's influential 1973 'Sick Physician' report reframed impairment as a treatable illness rather than a moral failing. Referral hinges on demonstrable impairment of professional functioning, not merely a diagnosis or past hospitalization; observed harm to patient care is the clear trigger. These confidential programs aim to protect patients while rehabilitating the physician.
2017-253: Escitalopram is the S-enantiomer of citalopram, isolated by Lundbeck and approved in 2002. Among SSRIs and SNRIs, sexual dysfunction is a notorious, frequently treatment-limiting class effect, with paroxetine often the worst offender. Drugs acting through other mechanisms, such as bupropion and mirtazapine, are the truly low-risk options, but among the agents listed, escitalopram tends to be the most favorable.
2017-254: Modern bereavement work for children draws heavily on attachment theory and on researchers like J. William Worden, whose Harvard Child Bereavement Study tracked grieving children through the 1990s. The consistent finding is that children mourn adaptively when allowed open, age-appropriate expression of feelings, not when grief is hushed, hurried toward closure, or when the child is parentified into supporting the surviving adult.
2017-255: This describes the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) loop central to Stephen Stahl's model of OCD. Hyperactivity in the loop connecting orbitofrontal/prefrontal cortex, striatum, and thalamus generates intrusive worry, with the thalamus acting as the relay that feeds signals back to cortex. The same circuit underlies the rationale for both SSRIs and ablative procedures like cingulotomy in refractory cases.
2017-256: Psychostimulants like methylphenidate are favored for depression in terminally ill patients because they act within days rather than weeks, a decisive advantage when prognosis is measured in weeks. Methylphenidate was synthesized by Leandro Panizzon at Ciba in 1944 and named Ritalin after his wife Rita. Stimulants also counter fatigue and can have an analgesic-sparing effect in palliative care.
2017-257: Dissociative amnesia, formerly 'psychogenic amnesia,' involves loss of autobiographical memory beyond ordinary forgetting, typically for traumatic material, with intact ability to learn new information and normal imaging and EEG. Its dramatic subtype, dissociative fugue, features sudden purposeful travel with identity confusion, classically captured in the case of Ansel Bourne, the 19th-century preacher William James wrote about.
2017-258: The Trail Making Test originated in the Army Individual Test Battery during World War II and was popularized by Ralph Reitan. Part A requires connecting numbered circles in sequence; the harder Part B alternates numbers and letters, taxing attention, visual scanning, and set-shifting. It is among the most sensitive bedside measures of processing speed and executive function and a staple of neuropsychological screening.
2017-259: Prader-Willi syndrome, described by Andrea Prader and Heinrich Willi in Switzerland in 1956, results from loss of paternally expressed genes on chromosome 15q11-13, often by deletion. It is a classic teaching example of genomic imprinting: the same region lost from the maternal copy instead causes Angelman syndrome. The hallmark switch from infantile failure to thrive to insatiable hyperphagia and obesity is memorable and unique.
2017-26: Fear is among the basic emotions identified by Paul Ekman, whose cross-cultural studies in the 1960s-70s (including with the Fore people of Papua New Guinea) showed facial expressions for a handful of emotions are universally recognized. Self-conscious emotions like shame, pride, and guilt require a developed sense of self and emerge in the second year or later, whereas fear appears within the first year of life.
2017-260: Habituation is the simplest form of learning, a decreasing response to a repeated, inoffensive stimulus. Eric Kandel won the 2000 Nobel Prize partly for dissecting its cellular basis in the sea slug Aplysia, showing it reflects reduced neurotransmitter release at specific synapses. It is distinguished from sensory adaptation because the receptors still fire; the nervous system simply learns to ignore the input.
2017-261: The defining behavioral split is the presence of recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviors. Bulimia nervosa features purging or other compensation such as laxative abuse, self-induced vomiting, or excessive exercise, whereas binge eating disorder, formally added to DSM-5 in 2013 after years as a research category, involves binges without compensation, which is why those patients are more often overweight.
2017-262: Diffusion tensor imaging is an MRI technique that maps white-matter tracts by measuring the directionally constrained (anisotropic) diffusion of water molecules along axons. Developed in the 1990s by Peter Basser and colleagues at the NIH, it enables tractography, the colorful 3D renderings of fiber bundles, and underpins connectome research into how brain regions are wired together.
2017-263: Motor skill (procedural) learning depends on the basal ganglia and cerebellum, not the hippocampus, which is why the famous amnesic patient H.M., who lost his hippocampi to surgery in 1953, could still improve at mirror-drawing day after day while having no memory of ever practicing. This dissociation between declarative and procedural memory is a cornerstone of cognitive neuroscience.
2017-264: The IMPACT trial, led by Jürgen Unützer and published in JAMA in 2002, was a landmark randomized study of collaborative care for late-life depression across many primary care sites. It paired a care manager and consulting psychiatrist with primary clinicians and roughly doubled the rate of meaningful depression improvement compared with usual care, becoming the evidence base for the collaborative care model now reimbursed by Medicare.
2017-265: Migraine with aura, historically 'classic migraine,' features transient neurological symptoms, often a visual scintillating scotoma, that march and resolve before or as the headache builds. The aura reflects cortical spreading depression, a slow wave of neuronal depolarization first described by Aristides Leão in 1944. Sensitivity to light, sound, and smell (photophobia, phonophobia, osmophobia) with nausea rounds out the classic picture.
2017-266: Semantic memory is the store of general facts and meanings, distinct from episodic memory of personally experienced events, a distinction Endel Tulving formalized in 1972. Loss of well-learned conceptual knowledge, like the anatomy underlying a routine procedure, points to semantic rather than episodic impairment, the pattern seen prominently in semantic variant frontotemporal dementia.
2017-267: The blood-brain barrier's selectivity comes chiefly from specialized capillary endothelial cells joined by tight junctions, a feature Paul Ehrlich first hinted at around 1885 when injected dyes stained every organ except the brain. Astrocytic end-feet and pericytes support and induce the barrier, but the endothelial tight junctions are the structural gatekeeper that excludes most drugs and toxins.
2017-268: Propranolol, a nonselective beta-blocker, is the standard treatment for benign lithium-induced postural tremor, an exaggeration of normal physiologic tremor mediated by peripheral beta-2 receptors. Propranolol was developed by James Black in the 1960s, work that earned him a share of the 1988 Nobel Prize; the same antitremor mechanism makes it first-line for essential tremor.
2017-269: Prions are misfolded proteins that template normal proteins into the pathogenic form, the 'protein-only' hypothesis for which Stanley Prusiner coined the term in 1982 and won the 1997 Nobel Prize. Rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus and spongiform change on biopsy is the signature of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, a transmissible agent uniquely resistant to standard sterilization because it contains no nucleic acid.
2017-27: Heinrich Kluver and Paul Bucy described this syndrome in 1939 after bilateral temporal lobectomy in rhesus monkeys produced placidity, hyperorality, hypersexuality, and visual agnosia ('psychic blindness'). The behavioral changes are largely attributed to amygdala damage within the resected temporal lobes. In humans, the full syndrome is rare but can follow herpes simplex encephalitis, trauma, or frontotemporal degeneration.
2017-270: Normal pressure hydrocephalus was described by Salomón Hakim and Raymond Adams in 1965 and is remembered by the triad 'wet, wobbly, and wacky', urinary incontinence, a magnetic shuffling gait, and cognitive slowing. It is one of the few potentially reversible dementias, treatable by ventriculoperitoneal shunting, which makes recognizing the gait-predominant picture clinically crucial.
2017-271: Consistently pairing a defined response with a given behavior to shape functioning is behaviorism, the school launched by John B. Watson's 1913 manifesto and extended by B.F. Skinner's operant conditioning. Applied Behavior Analysis, the dominant evidence-based intervention for autism, descends directly from these principles, with Ivar Lovaas's 1987 study a foundational demonstration of intensive behavioral treatment.
2017-272: The amygdala (Latin/Greek for almond, named for its shape) was first described by anatomist Karl Friedrich Burdach in the early 1800s. Its central role in fear and threat processing was cemented by the Kluver-Bucy syndrome experiments in the 1930s, in which monkeys with bilateral temporal lesions lost normal fear and aggression responses. Volumetric studies linking smaller amygdala volume to heightened trait aggression and psychopathy fit this fear-and-emotion-regulation framework.
2017-273: Bupropion, marketed as Wellbutrin and approved by the FDA in 1985, is a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor with no direct serotonergic action. Its relatively low manic switch and rapid-cycling risk compared with tricyclics and serotonergic-noradrenergic agents made it a preferred antidepressant adjunct in bipolar depression, a distinction highlighted in expert consensus guidelines (such as those from Sachs and colleagues) for managing breakthrough depression on a mood stabilizer.
2017-274: Avoidant personality disorder entered the DSM in 1980 (DSM-III), shaped heavily by psychologist Theodore Millon, who coined the term and conceptualized it around a craving for connection blocked by fear of rejection. The key distinction from schizoid personality is that avoidant patients deeply desire relationships but withdraw from fear of criticism and shame, whereas schizoid patients are genuinely indifferent to closeness.
2017-275: The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test was developed by Esta Berg and David Grant at the University of Wisconsin in 1948 to measure abstract reasoning and cognitive flexibility. The subject sorts cards by an unstated rule that periodically changes, and must shift strategy using only feedback. Perseverative errors on the task became a classic marker of dorsolateral prefrontal cortex dysfunction, popularized in schizophrenia research.
2017-276: Copy number variations, large duplications or deletions of DNA segments, were recognized as a widespread feature of normal human genomes by landmark genome-wide surveys around 2004-2006, which overturned the assumption that healthy people carry nearly identical genomes. Like single-nucleotide polymorphisms, most CNVs are common, benign, and contribute to ordinary human variation rather than disease, though some are pathogenic.
2017-277: This describes serotonin syndrome, a triad of mental status change, autonomic instability, and neuromuscular hyperactivity first systematically characterized in the 1990s. The Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria (2003) later refined diagnosis. Triptans are serotonin (5-HT1) agonists, and the FDA issued a 2006 alert about combining them with SSRIs or SNRIs, though the real-world risk is now considered low; fluoxetine's long half-life heightens concern.
2017-278: National survey data, including the CDC's National Intimate Partner and Sexual Violence Survey, have consistently shown that American Indian and Alaska Native women report the highest lifetime rates of intimate partner violence of any U.S. racial or ethnic group, with more than half reporting such victimization. These disparities are tied to historical trauma, jurisdictional gaps in tribal law enforcement, and socioeconomic factors.
2017-279: Variable-ratio reinforcement was defined by B.F. Skinner through his operant-conditioning experiments in the 1930s-1950s using the Skinner box. He found that rewarding behavior after an unpredictable number of responses produces the highest, most persistent response rate and the greatest resistance to extinction, exactly the dynamic that makes slot machines and other gambling so compelling and habit-forming.
2017-28: DSM-5 (2013) substantially revised anorexia nervosa, dropping the amenorrhea criterion and replacing the rigid 85%-of-expected-weight cutoff with the broader concept of 'significantly low weight,' assessed in children via growth-chart percentiles and failure to make expected gains. Diagnosis hinges on restriction leading to low weight plus fear of weight gain or behavior interfering with gain; the term derives from Greek for 'without appetite,' a historical misnomer since appetite is often preserved.
2017-280: Orexin, also called hypocretin, was discovered independently by two teams in 1998. The name orexin (from the Greek orexis, appetite) was chosen by Masashi Yanagisawa's group for its role in feeding, while Luis de Lecea's group called it hypocretin for its hypothalamic origin. Loss of these lateral hypothalamic neurons was soon shown to cause narcolepsy, transforming sleep neuroscience.
2017-281: The case-control design, which compares people with a disease to those without and looks backward at exposures, is the workhorse for studying rare diseases because a cohort study would need impractically huge numbers to capture enough cases. A defining example is the 1950 study by Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill linking smoking to lung cancer, which used this approach to powerful effect.
2017-282: Broca's aphasia is named for French physician Paul Broca, who in 1861 described a patient nicknamed Tan (he could utter little but that syllable) and at autopsy localized the lesion to the left inferior frontal gyrus, now Broca's area. It is a nonfluent, effortful aphasia with impaired repetition but relatively preserved comprehension, a foundational finding in the history of brain localization.
2017-283: Decades of developmental research, notably Mavis Hetherington's long-term studies of divorce, found that most children of divorce do not show lasting pathology and adjust well when key protective conditions are met: a stable, competently functioning custodial parent, economic security, and low ongoing conflict. The quality of parenting and resources, not family structure alone, drives outcomes.
2017-284: Cortisol follows a robust circadian rhythm driven by the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and the suprachiasmatic nucleus, peaking in the early morning shortly after waking (the cortisol awakening response) and reaching a nadir near midnight. This diurnal pattern is well established in healthy children and adults and underlies the use of late-night cortisol and the dexamethasone suppression test in evaluating HPA-axis disorders.
2017-285: DSM-5 (2013) split the old hypochondriasis category into somatic symptom disorder, defined by distressing physical symptoms, and illness anxiety disorder, defined by fear of having a serious illness with few or no actual somatic complaints. By definition, illness anxiety patients have minimal physical symptoms; their distress centers on the threat of disease rather than the symptoms themselves.
2017-286: This is fragile X syndrome, the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability, caused by a CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome that silences the gene. Named for the constricted, fragile-appearing site on the X chromosome seen under the microscope, it classically presents with macroorchidism, a long face with large ears, and autistic features such as hand-flapping.
2017-287: The mesocortical pathway projects dopamine from the ventral tegmental area to the prefrontal cortex and is central to executive function, working memory, and cognition. The hypothesis that hypofunction of this pathway underlies the negative and cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia, while mesolimbic hyperfunction drives positive symptoms, became a cornerstone of the dopamine theory of schizophrenia.
2017-288: Heinz Kohut introduced self-psychology and the concept of the selfobject in his 1971 book The Analysis of the Self. A selfobject is another person experienced as part of one's own self, fulfilling essential needs such as mirroring (validation) and idealization. Kohut argued that empathic failures in these relationships, especially in childhood, produce the fragile self-esteem of narcissistic disorders.
2017-289: Corticotropin-releasing hormone, isolated and characterized by Wylie Vale and colleagues in 1981, is the apex hormone of the stress response. Secreted by the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus, it triggers pituitary ACTH release and ultimately adrenal cortisol. Its discovery clarified the entire HPA cascade and spurred interest in CRH antagonists as potential antidepressants and anxiolytics.
2017-29: The Global Burden of Disease framework and the disability-adjusted life year (DALY) were developed by Christopher Murray and Alan Lopez in the 1990s for the WHO and World Bank. Their analyses repeatedly rank major depressive disorder among the leading global causes of disability and overall disease burden, a finding that helped reframe mental illness as a major public-health priority worldwide.
2017-290: Sleep paralysis is part of the classic narcolepsy tetrad (along with excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, and hypnagogic hallucinations), all reflecting intrusion of REM-sleep phenomena into wakefulness. The dreamlike hallucinations at sleep onset and the temporary inability to move on waking are essentially the atonia and vivid imagery of REM appearing at the wrong moment, a hallmark of disrupted REM regulation.
2017-291: Evidence and consensus guidelines, including from psycho-oncology bodies, support starting an SSRI for subthreshold or syndromal depressive symptoms in cancer patients rather than waiting for full DSM criteria, since depression worsens quality of life and adherence. SSRIs are favored for their tolerability and relatively low drug-interaction burden, making them a practical first-line choice in medically ill populations.
2017-292: Self-assessment continuing medical education is built around feedback: it presents current best practices, gives learners the correct answers with supporting literature, and benchmarks their performance against peers. This model became central to Maintenance of Certification programs adopted by the American Board of Medical Specialties, reflecting evidence that feedback and comparison drive practice improvement more than passive lectures.
2017-293: Family and twin studies establish a roughly 10 percent lifetime risk of schizophrenia for a person with an affected sibling, compared with about 1 percent in the general population. Risk rises steeply with shared genes: about 50 percent in a monozygotic twin. These gradients, mapped largely through Irving Gottesman's mid-20th-century work, are classic evidence for the strong but polygenic heritability of schizophrenia.
2017-294: Modern neurosurgery for refractory OCD, including anterior cingulotomy, anterior capsulotomy, and deep brain stimulation, targets the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) loops thought to be hyperactive in OCD. Imaging of the orbitofrontal cortex, caudate, and thalamus gave rise to this circuit model, and DBS for OCD received an FDA humanitarian device exemption in 2009.
2017-295: In the face-hand test, a genuinely paralyzed arm will fall and strike the face, since gravity acts regardless of intent. When the hand consistently veers away and avoids the face, it implies preserved purposeful control, pointing toward a functional (psychogenic) rather than organic weakness. This bedside maneuver is a classic, low-tech way to flag conversion or feigned paralysis.
2017-296: The single strongest risk factor for postpartum (puerperal) psychosis is a personal or family history of prior puerperal psychiatric illness, particularly bipolar disorder, reflecting its strong link to the bipolar spectrum. The condition was described as far back as the writings of Marce in the 19th century; the Marce Society for perinatal mental health is named for him.
2017-297: Prader-Willi syndrome typically results from loss of paternally expressed genes on chromosome 15q11-q13, most often a deletion (a pathogenic copy number variant), illustrating genomic imprinting. The mirror-image maternal loss causes Angelman syndrome. First described by Andrea Prader and colleagues in 1956, Prader-Willi features infantile hypotonia followed by hyperphagia, obesity, and intellectual disability.
2017-298: Supportive psychotherapy, distinguished from expressive/psychodynamic and CBT approaches, aims to bolster the patient's self-esteem, adaptive defenses, and functioning rather than interpret transference or assign homework. Gratefully accepting the patient's praise and affirming progress reinforces the alliance and the patient's gains, consistent with the ego-supportive stance described by clinicians such as Pinsker and Winston.
2017-299: The mesolimbic dopamine pathway, running from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens, is the brain's reward circuit and the final common pathway of addiction. Work by James Olds and Peter Milner in the 1950s on intracranial self-stimulation in rats revealed this reward system, and virtually all drugs of abuse converge on increasing dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens.
2017-3: Complex partial seizures (now called focal seizures with impaired awareness in the 2017 ILAE classification) most often arise from the temporal lobe and feature automatisms like lip-smacking, chewing, and purposeless repetitive acts, followed by amnesia for the event. John Hughlings Jackson, the 19th-century English neurologist, first described the 'dreamy state' and uncinate fits of temporal-lobe epilepsy, linking olfactory auras and automatic behaviors to mesial temporal foci.
2017-30: In Aaron Beck's cognitive model, compensatory strategies (like excessive reassurance-seeking) are behaviors that protect against an underlying negative core belief. Beck, who founded cognitive therapy at the University of Pennsylvania in the 1960s, described how schemas of helplessness or unlovability drive such strategies; his daughter Judith Beck later popularized the cognitive conceptualization linking core beliefs, intermediate assumptions, and compensatory behaviors.
2017-31: Heroin (diacetylmorphine) is short-acting, so opioid withdrawal typically begins within 6-12 hours, peaks around 36-72 hours, and largely subsides within about a week. The syndrome, though intensely uncomfortable with lacrimation, rhinorrhea, piloerection, myalgias, and diarrhea, is rarely life-threatening, unlike alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal. The Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) is commonly used to gauge its severity.
2017-32: The orbitofrontal cortex is forever linked to Phineas Gage, the railroad foreman whose 1848 tamping-iron accident drove an iron rod through his frontal lobe. Though he survived, observers famously reported he was 'no longer Gage' — disinhibited, profane, and unable to plan. His skull and the iron remain on display at Harvard, and the case became the founding anecdote of frontal-lobe personality science, illustrating exactly the impulsivity and euphoria seen with orbitofrontal damage.
2017-33: In females the earliest objective sign of puberty is the growth spurt, driven by the reactivation of the hypothalamic GnRH pulse generator. James Tanner, the British pediatrician who in the 1960s codified the staging of sexual maturation that bears his name, documented that linear growth acceleration precedes breast budding (thelarche) and that menarche comes relatively late, typically after peak height velocity has already passed.
2017-34: Conversion disorder traces to Jean-Martin Charcot and Sigmund Freud, who in the late 1800s theorized that psychic conflict was 'converted' into physical symptoms. The classic bedside clue here is navigating obstacles despite reported blindness, reflecting intact visual pathways. DSM-5 renamed it functional neurological symptom disorder and notably dropped the requirement that psychological stressors be identifiable, reflecting modern neurology's view of it as a genuine disorder of brain network function rather than malingering.
2017-35: Daily triptan or analgesic use can paradoxically worsen headaches, a phenomenon called medication-overuse (or rebound) headache. Recognized formally in the International Headache Society classification, it requires regular intake on too many days per month for over three months. The counterintuitive but evidence-based first step is withdrawing the overused acute medication — here sumatriptan — which often dramatically improves the headache pattern that the drug itself was perpetuating.
2017-36: Means restriction is one of the best-evidenced suicide-prevention strategies. On inpatient units, hanging is the leading method of death, so eliminating anchor points (the doors, hooks, and fixtures from which ligatures can be suspended) directly attacks the most lethal means. The Joint Commission and the VA's Mental Health Environment of Care Checklist made ligature-risk reduction a national priority after data showed it lowers inpatient suicide far more reliably than contracts or constant observation.
2017-37: Microglia are the brain's resident immune cells, derived not from neural tissue but from yolk-sac myeloid progenitors that colonize the brain early in development. Pío del Río Hortega, a student of Cajal's school, identified and named them in the 1910s-1920s. When activated by injury or infection they release proinflammatory cytokines like TNF-alpha and IL-1, placing them at the center of modern neuroinflammation research in depression and neurodegeneration.
2017-38: Urine remains the most commonly used drug-testing matrix precisely because it is also the easiest to defeat — through dilution, substitution with synthetic or another's urine, or chemical adulterants. This vulnerability spawned an entire countermeasure industry and, in turn, observed collection, temperature strips, and validity testing. Alternative matrices like hair (offering a months-long window) and oral fluid (collected under direct observation) were developed partly to close these loopholes.
2017-39: Cobalamin (B12) deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, damaging the dorsal columns (vibration/proprioception loss, sensory ataxia) and corticospinal tracts. Pernicious anemia, its classic cause, was a fatal disease until George Minot and William Murphy showed in the 1920s that feeding patients raw liver cured it — work that earned them, with George Whipple, the 1934 Nobel Prize. The neuropsychiatric features can precede anemia entirely.
2017-4: This reflects empathic validation, a cornerstone of the therapeutic alliance. Carl Rogers, founder of client-centered therapy in the 1950s, identified accurate empathy, unconditional positive regard, and genuineness as the core conditions for change. Decades of psychotherapy outcome research, notably by Edward Bordin and later meta-analyses, show the alliance is one of the most robust predictors of outcome across modalities, often outweighing the specific technique used.
2017-40: Patient registries are the population-health backbone of the Collaborative Care Model developed at the University of Washington by Wayne Katon and Jürgen Unützel. Validated in the landmark IMPACT trial for late-life depression, the model's defining feature is treating a whole panel rather than reacting visit-by-visit: a care manager tracks every patient in a registry, flags those not improving, and adjusts treatment toward measurable targets — true measurement-based, population-based care.
2017-41: Leptin, from the Greek leptos ('thin'), was discovered in 1994 by Jeffrey Friedman's lab through positional cloning of the mutated gene in the obese ob/ob mouse. Secreted by adipose tissue in proportion to fat stores, it signals satiety to the hypothalamus. The disappointing twist: most human obesity involves leptin resistance, not deficiency, so leptin therapy works only in the rare cases of congenital leptin deficiency.
2017-42: By elementary-school age, fundamental gross-motor skills like jumping and hopping should be well established (a typical four-year-old hops on one foot). Persistent difficulty with these basic milestones is a red flag for an underlying neuromuscular or developmental disorder, whereas struggling with refined fine-motor or skill-specific tasks like instrument playing falls within normal variation. Developmental screening emphasizes that gross-motor delays generally carry more diagnostic weight than fine-motor quirks.
2017-43: MDMA (ecstasy) classically causes hyponatremia through a double mechanism: the drug stimulates antidiuretic hormone release while users, fearing hyperthermia at raves, drink large volumes of water. The resulting dilutional hyponatremia can cause fatal cerebral edema, and several widely publicized deaths of young users in the 1990s — including the UK case of Leah Betts — were attributed to water intoxication rather than the drug's direct toxicity.
2017-44: Major depression shows a roughly two-to-one female predominance, and being married, urban living, and higher socioeconomic status are generally protective. Low socioeconomic status and, in some epidemiologic work, rural residence have been associated with elevated risk. The large community surveys underpinning these risk-factor profiles — the Epidemiologic Catchment Area study and the National Comorbidity Survey — established the modern lifetime-prevalence estimates for mood disorders in the United States.
2017-45: The Bereitschaftspotential, or readiness potential, is a slow EEG buildup over the supplementary motor area that precedes voluntary movement by up to a second. Discovered by Kornhuber and Deecke in 1965 and central to Benjamin Libet's famous free-will experiments, its presence before a 'myoclonic' jerk betrays that the movement was internally generated and voluntary — supporting a functional (conversion) rather than organic origin for the tremor or jerk.
2017-46: The 2010 Affordable Care Act barred insurers from denying coverage or charging more for preexisting conditions — a protection that directly benefited people with prior psychiatric diagnoses, who had previously faced routine denials. Combined with the 2008 Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act and the ACA's designation of mental health and substance-use treatment as an 'essential health benefit,' these reforms substantially expanded behavioral-health access.
2017-47: Aaron Beck, the founder of cognitive therapy, described the depressive 'cognitive triad' in the 1960s: negative views of the self, the world, and the future. Of these, the negative self-schema — beliefs of worthlessness, inadequacy, and being unlovable — is the hallmark of depression, distinguishing it from anxiety disorders, where schemas instead center on threat, danger, and catastrophe. Beck originally trained as a psychoanalyst before this reorientation toward cognition.
2017-48: Clozapine-induced sialorrhea is paradoxical given the drug's potent anticholinergic profile, and it can be socially distressing and a nighttime aspiration risk. Glycopyrrolate, a quaternary-amine antimuscarinic that does not cross the blood-brain barrier, dries secretions peripherally without worsening cognition or sedation — making it a favored treatment. Its CNS-sparing property is exactly why it is also used as a perioperative antisialagogue in anesthesia.
2017-49: The Joint Commission defines a sentinel event as a patient-safety event reaching a patient that results in death, permanent harm, or severe temporary harm — the word 'sentinel' signaling that each one demands immediate investigation via root-cause analysis. The concept and the accompanying RCA framework were introduced in the mid-1990s, reshaping hospital safety culture by treating serious adverse events such as a harmful elopement as system failures rather than individual blame.
2017-5: This landmark work came from Michael Meaney and Moshe Szyf at McGill in the early 2000s, showing that rat pups receiving high maternal licking and grooming had less methylation of the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) gene promoter in the hippocampus, yielding calmer, less stress-reactive adults. Cross-fostering reversed the effect, proving it was environmental epigenetics rather than inherited DNA sequence, a foundational demonstration of behavioral epigenetics.
2017-50: Norepinephrine is synthesized from dopamine by dopamine beta-hydroxylase, a copper-containing enzyme uniquely located inside synaptic vesicles. This is the final committed step in the catecholamine pathway (tyrosine to DOPA to dopamine to norepinephrine to epinephrine) first elucidated by Julius Axelrod, whose work on catecholamine metabolism and reuptake earned him a share of the 1970 Nobel Prize and laid the groundwork for understanding how antidepressants act.
2017-51: Around ages two to three, the child's emerging sense of being a separate, autonomous self drives the normative possessiveness and reduced sharing of the toddler years — Erik Erikson's stage of 'autonomy versus shame and doubt' and the colloquial 'terrible twos.' Asserting ownership ('mine!') is a developmental achievement of selfhood, not mere selfishness, reflecting the toddler's dawning recognition of personal boundaries and will.
2017-52: Across elder-abuse research, victim cognitive impairment (particularly dementia) is the most consistently replicated risk factor, increasing vulnerability through impaired self-protection, dependence on caregivers, and reduced ability to report mistreatment. The National Elder Mistreatment Study and related epidemiologic work also highlight social isolation and caregiver burden, but cognitive impairment stands out as the strongest and most reproducible victim characteristic.
2017-53: Genome-wide association studies test hundreds of thousands to millions of SNPs simultaneously, so without correction many associations will appear significant by chance alone — the multiple-comparisons problem. The field's solution was the stringent genome-wide significance threshold (about 5 x 10^-8), a Bonferroni-style correction. This rigor, plus the requirement for independent replication, is why early 'candidate gene' findings in psychiatry largely failed to hold up under proper GWAS methodology.
2017-54: Shoe-tying is a relatively late-acquired fine-motor and sequencing skill, typically mastered around ages five to six, while running, kicking, tricycle-riding, and zipping are all age-appropriate for a four-year-old. Recognizing normal developmental variation prevents over-pathologizing — a recurring theme in pediatric assessment, where milestone charts like those compiled in the Denver Developmental Screening Test help clinicians distinguish true delay from ordinary timing differences.
2017-55: Assertive Community Treatment (ACT) was created in Madison, Wisconsin in the 1970s by Leonard Stein and Mary Ann Test as the 'Training in Community Living' program. Born of the deinstitutionalization era, it delivers intensive, multidisciplinary, around-the-clock services directly in the community to people with severe mental illness. Decades of controlled trials make ACT one of psychiatry's best-evidenced service models for cutting hospitalization and improving housing stability.
2017-56: Depression is the most common psychiatric sequela of traumatic brain injury, affecting roughly half of patients within the first year and far exceeding general-population rates. It reflects both the neurobiological disruption of frontal-subcortical mood circuits and the psychosocial impact of disability. Recognizing post-TBI depression matters because it independently worsens cognitive recovery and functional outcomes, yet is frequently missed amid the focus on physical rehabilitation.
2017-57: Strong erotic countertransference is an occupational hazard recognized since Freud, who developed the concept after Josef Breuer's unsettling experience with the patient 'Anna O.' The professionally and ethically correct first move is always supervision or consultation — never acting on or disclosing the feelings to the patient. Seeking a trusted colleague's perspective transforms a potential boundary violation into a source of clinical insight and protects the patient.
2017-58: Learned helplessness was described by Martin Seligman and Steven Maier in the 1960s: dogs exposed to inescapable shock later failed to escape even when escape became possible. The behavioral deficits are reversed by antidepressants and by ECT, which is why the paradigm became one of the foundational animal models of depression. Seligman later pivoted from this work to found the positive-psychology movement.
2017-59: The 'fencing posture' — one arm extended, the other flexed, with bizarre bilateral motor activity and preserved awareness — is characteristic of frontal-lobe seizures arising from the supplementary motor area. These seizures are notoriously misdiagnosed as psychogenic because of their brief duration, nocturnal clustering, hypermotor flailing, and frequently normal scalp EEG, making video-EEG monitoring essential to capture the electrographic correlate.
2017-6: Dialectical behavior therapy was developed by Marsha Linehan in the late 1980s for chronically suicidal patients with borderline personality disorder, blending CBT with Zen acceptance. The 'devil's advocate' strategy she described deliberately argues against a too-easy commitment to strengthen the patient's own resolve, embodying DBT's central dialectic of acceptance and change. Linehan later disclosed her own lived experience with the disorder.
2017-60: Monozygotic twin concordance for schizophrenia is roughly 50 percent — high enough to prove strong genetic contribution, but far below 100 percent, proving genes are not destiny. This gap is the cornerstone evidence for a 'two-hit' or diathesis-stress model: inherited vulnerability plus environmental insults (obstetric complications, cannabis, urban upbringing, infection) together produce illness. Classic twin and adoption studies, including the Danish adoption work, established this framework.
2017-61: The Patient Health Questionnaire's nine-item depression module (PHQ-9) is a brief self-report derived from PRIME-MD, developed by Robert Spitzer, Kurt Kroenke, and Janet Williams in the late 1990s with Pfizer support. Mapping directly onto the nine DSM criteria, it takes only a couple of minutes, making it the workhorse instrument for depression screening and measurement-based care in busy primary-care and collaborative-care settings.
2017-62: Fragile X is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability (Down syndrome is more common overall but usually arises sporadically, not inherited). It results from a CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome, silencing production of the FMRP protein. The fragile site was first observed cytogenetically by Herbert Lubs in 1969 as a constriction near the tip of the X, and the gene was cloned in 1991. The classic phenotype includes a long face, large ears, and macroorchidism.
2017-63: The link between severe childhood trauma and dissociative identity disorder anchors the modern post-traumatic model of dissociation. Once called multiple personality disorder, the condition was renamed DID in DSM-IV (1994) to emphasize fragmentation rather than separate 'people.' Surveys of patients across North America and Europe consistently report extremely high rates of childhood physical and sexual abuse, supporting the idea that identity splitting is a defensive adaptation to overwhelming, repeated maltreatment in early life.
2017-64: Lithium is filtered and reabsorbed by the kidney much like sodium, so anything that depletes sodium drives the kidney to retain lithium. Thiazide diuretics like hydrochlorothiazide act at the distal tubule, causing volume contraction that increases proximal reabsorption of both sodium and lithium, reducing lithium clearance and raising serum levels into the toxic range. The classic early signs of toxicity, a coarse tremor and ataxia, distinguish it from the fine benign tremor seen at therapeutic doses.
2017-65: Cortisol secretion follows a strong circadian rhythm orchestrated by the HPA axis, reaching its nadir in the late evening around sleep onset and peaking shortly after morning awakening (the cortisol awakening response). Slow-wave sleep early in the night actively suppresses HPA activity, whereas the early-morning hours bring a surge driven by the suprachiasmatic nucleus. This is why salivary cortisol sampling is timed to specific points across the day, and why late-night cortisol is used to screen for Cushing syndrome.
2017-66: The view that gender identity is most strongly rooted in innate, biologically-influenced feelings rather than rearing was crystallized by the tragic case of David Reimer, raised as a girl after a botched circumcision under John Money's guidance in the 1960s; he reverted to a male identity in adolescence. The case, exposed by Milton Diamond in the 1990s, undermined the 'blank slate' theory of gender and supported the durability of an internally felt gender identity.
2017-67: Trail Making Test Part B requires alternating between numbers and letters (1-A-2-B...), tapping set-shifting, a core executive function mediated by the prefrontal cortex. The test grew out of the Army Individual Test Battery in the 1940s and was popularized by Ralph Reitan as part of the Halstead-Reitan battery. Comparing the slower Part B to the simpler number-sequencing Part A isolates the cognitive flexibility component from basic processing speed.
2017-68: Panic disorder characteristically emerges in late adolescence through early adulthood, with a typical onset in the late teens to mid-twenties. Donald Klein's observation in the 1960s that imipramine blocked panic attacks but not anticipatory anxiety helped carve panic out as a distinct entity, eventually recognized in DSM-III (1980). The bimodal age distribution and this young typical onset are favorite testable details.
2017-69: The 22q11.2 deletion underlies velocardiofacial (DiGeorge) syndrome and carries one of the largest known genetic risks for schizophrenia, with roughly a quarter to a third of carriers developing a psychotic disorder. The region includes COMT, an enzyme degrading dopamine, offering a mechanistic clue. The syndrome was described by Angelo DiGeorge in the 1960s, and its psychiatric significance made it a model for studying the genetics of psychosis.
2017-7: Carbamazepine, introduced in the 1960s and structurally related to tricyclics, is a potent inducer of CYP3A4 and is itself metabolized by it. Erythromycin inhibits CYP3A4, causing carbamazepine levels to spike and producing the classic triad of nausea, ataxia, and diplopia. Carbamazepine also famously autoinduces its own metabolism, requiring dose adjustment after the first weeks of therapy.
2017-70: Paliperidone, the active metabolite of risperidone (9-hydroxyrisperidone), is cleared largely unchanged by the kidneys rather than extensively metabolized in the liver. Because renal excretion dominates, moderate-to-severe renal impairment markedly raises drug exposure, so dosing must be reduced or the drug avoided. Marketed as Invega from 2006, its osmotic extended-release delivery system (OROS) and long-acting injectable forms made it a workhorse, but the renal caveat is its key prescribing limitation.
2017-71: Mental health courts are a diversion innovation dating to the late 1990s, with the first established in Broward County, Florida in 1997. Because entering such a program means foregoing a normal trial, the defendant must knowingly and voluntarily waive constitutional rights, the same competence standard rooted in Dusky v. United States (1960). Capacity here turns on rational understanding of the legal trade-offs, not on insight into one's illness.
2017-72: Orexin (also called hypocretin) was discovered independently by two groups in 1998; the name orexin nods to the Greek 'orexis' for appetite. Narcolepsy with cataplexy is caused by loss of the hypothalamic orexin-producing neurons, so cerebrospinal fluid orexin-A is undetectable or very low. This discovery, linked through dog and mouse models around 1999-2000, transformed narcolepsy from a mysterious sleep disorder into a defined neurodegenerative-like deficiency state and spawned orexin-targeting hypnotics.
2017-73: The frontal-subcortical circuits, mapped influentially by Alexander, DeLong, and Strick in 1986 and elaborated for behavior by Cummings, link the prefrontal cortex through the striatum, globus pallidus, and thalamus. The dorsolateral prefrontal circuit subserves executive function, so traumatic brain injury that shears these connections, especially the vulnerable frontal white matter, produces the classic executive dysfunction of poor planning, perseveration, and impaired set-shifting.
2017-74: The National Comorbidity Survey Replication, led by Ronald Kessler and conducted in the early 2000s, was a landmark epidemiologic study documenting how long Americans wait before treatment. It found long delays between symptom onset and first contact for care across disorders, with mood disorders typically diagnosed several years after onset. These findings highlighted the treatment gap and helped justify early-intervention and screening initiatives.
2017-75: For undifferentiated agitation from an unknown or sympathomimetic intoxicant like synthetic cathinones (bath salts), benzodiazepines such as lorazepam are first-line because they calm agitation, lower sympathetic drive, and do not lower the seizure threshold or worsen hyperthermia the way antipsychotics can. Bath salts surged in the U.S. around 2010-2012, prompting emergency federal scheduling of MDPV and mephedrone in 2011 amid sensational reports of agitated delirium.
2017-76: In Freud's theory the latency stage spans roughly age six to puberty, when libidinal drives are dampened and energy is redirected into school, sports, hobbies, and same-sex peer friendships, exactly the picture of a boy absorbed in basketball who plays mainly with other boys. Freud laid out the oral, anal, phallic, latency, and genital sequence in his 1905 'Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality,' and latency uniquely lacks a focal erogenous zone.
2017-77: Functional imaging like SPECT, which shows regional blood flow, helps distinguish Alzheimer disease from frontotemporal dementia by their characteristic hypoperfusion patterns: temporoparietal in Alzheimer versus frontal and anterior temporal in FTD. FTD itself was historically tied to Arnold Pick's 1892 description of focal lobar atrophy, the eponymous Pick disease, and the functional pattern often diverges before structural atrophy is obvious on CT or MRI.
2017-78: Paroxetine carries the strongest signal among SSRIs for congenital malformations, particularly cardiac septal defects, prompting the FDA in 2005 to reclassify it to pregnancy category D. Its short half-life and potent anticholinergic profile also make it notable for neonatal discontinuation symptoms. This evidence shifted prescribing toward agents like sertraline when an SSRI is needed in pregnancy.
2017-79: HIPAA, enacted in 1996 with its Privacy Rule taking effect in 2003, explicitly permits sharing protected health information among providers for treatment purposes without a separate signed release, so two physicians coordinating a patient's care may discuss the case. A common misconception is that all disclosure requires consent; in fact treatment, payment, and healthcare operations are the carve-outs, though federal Part 2 rules add extra protection specifically for substance-use records.
2017-8: Erik Erikson's eight-stage model of psychosocial development, published in 'Childhood and Society' (1950), framed each life stage as a conflict to resolve. Ego integrity versus despair is the final stage of late adulthood, in which one reflects on life with either acceptance and wisdom or regret over missed chances and 'roads not taken.' Erikson, a student of Anna Freud, coined the term 'identity crisis.'
2017-80: Normal aging brings a stooped (flexed) posture and a slower, shorter-stepped gait, reflecting gradual loss of muscle mass, joint flexibility, and reaction time rather than disease. Distinguishing these benign changes from pathological gaits, such as the resting tremor and shuffle of Parkinson disease or the high-stepping gait of peripheral neuropathy, is a core part of the geriatric neurological exam.
2017-81: Parental criminality is among the strongest replicated risk factors for conduct disorder, a finding cemented by longitudinal cohorts such as the Cambridge Study in Delinquent Development led by David Farrington. The relationship reflects both genetic transmission and adverse environment (harsh or inconsistent discipline, antisocial modeling). Notably, blunted rather than heightened autonomic fear conditioning is associated with antisocial behavior, making low fear reactivity a marker, not a protection.
2017-82: This is dementia with Lewy bodies, where patients show profound neuroleptic sensitivity: typical antipsychotics like haloperidol can trigger severe rigidity, worsening parkinsonism, and even a neuroleptic-malignant-like reaction, so a dramatic worsening after haloperidol actually supports the diagnosis. Frederic Lewy first described the eponymous intracytoplasmic inclusions in 1912, and the core DLB triad is fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism.
2017-83: Ketamine, an NMDA-receptor antagonist developed as an anesthetic in the 1960s by Calvin Stevens, produced rapid antidepressant effects in trials beginning around 2000. A consistent and expected adverse effect is a transient rise in blood pressure and heart rate from sympathetic stimulation, alongside dissociation. This work culminated in FDA approval of the esketamine nasal spray (Spravato) in 2019, the first genuinely novel-mechanism antidepressant in decades.
2017-84: The medial prefrontal cortex is central to both acquiring and extinguishing conditioned fear, work driven largely by Joseph LeDoux and colleagues mapping the fear circuit. The infralimbic region in particular promotes extinction by inhibiting the amygdala, while the prelimbic region drives fear expression. This dual role makes the mPFC-amygdala dialogue the leading neural model for exposure therapy and for understanding PTSD's failure of extinction.
2017-85: Persistent toe-walking beyond about age three is a red flag because most toddlers adopt a heel-to-toe gait by then; continued tiptoeing warrants evaluation for cerebral palsy, tethered cord, muscular dystrophy, or autism spectrum disorder, after idiopathic causes are excluded. The other findings described, including hand dominance not yet fixed and some wobble on a bike, fall within normal four-year-old variation.
2017-86: Botulinum toxin, produced by Clostridium botulinum, is among the most lethal substances known; it blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, causing a descending flaccid paralysis with prominent cranial-nerve and autonomic signs, classically fixed dilated pupils, ptosis, diplopia, and dysphagia with intact sensation. The illness was named from the Latin 'botulus' (sausage) after 19th-century outbreaks from spoiled sausages described by Justinus Kerner; the same toxin is now therapeutic Botox.
2017-87: Beneficence, the duty to act for the patient's good, justifies admitting a person at imminent risk after a suicide attempt even over their refusal, where it outweighs respect for autonomy. The four-principles framework, autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice, was articulated by Tom Beauchamp and James Childress in their 1979 'Principles of Biomedical Ethics,' and acute suicidality is the paradigm case where protective beneficence prevails.
2017-88: Childhood absence epilepsy produces brief staring spells with subtle eyelid flutter and the hallmark generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges on EEG, often provoked by hyperventilation. The French term 'petit mal' was coined in the early 19th century to contrast these minor spells with 'grand mal' convulsions. Ethosuximide, which targets thalamic T-type calcium channels generating the rhythm, remains the drug of choice.
2017-89: Family psychoeducation for schizophrenia grew from research on 'expressed emotion' in the 1960s-70s by George Brown and others, showing that high-criticism, over-involved family environments predicted relapse. Effective programs teach realistic expectations, communication, and crucially support for medication adherence, since nonadherence is a leading cause of relapse. Such interventions are among the best-evidenced psychosocial treatments, reliably lowering rehospitalization.
2017-9: Leon Festinger introduced cognitive dissonance theory in 1957, proposing that inconsistent cognitions create psychological discomfort that motivates change. His famous 1959 experiment with James Carlsmith found that subjects paid only $1 to lie about a boring task later rated it as more enjoyable than those paid $20, because the small reward gave them insufficient external justification, forcing them to alter their attitude to reduce dissonance.
2017-90: In a crossover design each subject receives both treatments in sequence, serving as their own control, which boosts statistical power by removing between-person variability. The wash-out period between treatments is essential to clear carryover effects from the first drug. The approach was formalized in mid-20th-century experimental design, and its self-control feature makes it efficient, though it is unsuitable for conditions that change irreversibly over the study.
2017-91: Oppositional defiant disorder is marked by a persistent pattern of angry, argumentative, defiant behavior toward authority figures, classically most pronounced at home and with familiar people, without the serious rights-violating aggression, theft, or destruction that defines conduct disorder. ODD entered the DSM in 1980 and was reorganized in DSM-5 into anger/irritability, argumentative/defiant, and vindictiveness clusters, emphasizing the affective as well as behavioral dimension.
2017-92: The dentate gyrus of the hippocampus is the textbook home of adult neurogenesis, alongside the subventricular zone. The concept overturned the long-held dogma, attributed to Santiago Ramon y Cajal, that the adult brain produces no new neurons. Pioneering work by Joseph Altman in the 1960s and later studies in the 1990s using bromodeoxyuridine labeling, including a landmark 1998 human study by Eriksson and Fred Gage, revived the field and tied hippocampal neurogenesis to learning, memory, and antidepressant action.
2017-93: Liothyronine is synthetic T3, the active thyroid hormone, used to augment antidepressants. Its role was cemented by the STAR*D trial published in 2006, where T3 augmentation rivaled lithium augmentation but was better tolerated. The idea that thyroid hormone can accelerate or enhance antidepressant response dates to studies from the 1960s and 1970s, and it tends to be favored in patients with fatigue and psychomotor slowing, fitting the classic picture of subclinical thyroid contribution to depression.
2017-94: This reflects the medicolegal principle that clinical judgment, not the insurer's payment decision, governs whether a patient is safe to discharge. The landmark case is Wickline v. State of California (1986), which held that physicians remain liable for discharging a patient who needs further care even when an insurer denies coverage, and that the doctor must protest and appeal an adverse decision rather than passively comply.
2017-95: A bitemporal hemianopia localizes to the optic chiasm, where nasal retinal fibers (carrying temporal visual fields) cross. The classic culprit is a pituitary adenoma pressing upward on the chiasm. The very word chiasm comes from the Greek letter chi, shaped like an X, describing the crossing of the two optic nerves, a structure first carefully described in antiquity and central to understanding visual field localization.
2017-96: Exposure and response prevention (ERP) is the gold-standard behavioral treatment for OCD, developed by Victor Meyer in 1966, who treated hospitalized patients by exposing them to feared stimuli while preventing their compulsive rituals. The approach relies on habituation: anxiety naturally subsides when the ritual is blocked, breaking the negative-reinforcement cycle. Edna Foa later refined and popularized ERP, and it remains the most evidence-supported psychotherapy for OCD.
2017-97: Rapid onset of PTSD symptoms generally predicts better recovery, whereas insidious or delayed onset portends a more chronic course. This mirrors a broader principle in psychiatry, echoing the prognostic rules for psychotic disorders, where acute onset, clear precipitant, and short duration of untreated illness all favor recovery, while gradual, smoldering presentations carry worse outcomes.
2017-98: Eligibility for special education hinges on a documented disability under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), originally passed in 1975 as the Education for All Handicapped Children Act. The law guarantees a free appropriate public education in the least restrictive environment and codifies the Individualized Education Program (IEP). A child must have one of the law's qualifying disability categories and need specialized instruction to benefit from school.
2017-99: The raphe nuclei, a midline cluster running through the brainstem, contain the brain's highest concentration of serotonergic neurons. Their name comes from the Latin raphe, meaning seam or ridge, reflecting their position along the midline suture of the brainstem. From here, serotonergic projections fan out across nearly the entire brain, which is why these small nuclei have outsized influence on mood, sleep, and the action of SSRIs.
2018-1: Alcohol's sedative, anxiolytic, and motor-impairing effects are mediated largely by potentiation of GABA-A receptors, the brain's main inhibitory ionotropic receptors, identified through decades of work on the GABA system following the discovery of GABA as a neurotransmitter in the 1950s. This shared GABA-A mechanism explains the cross-tolerance between alcohol and benzodiazepines and the use of benzodiazepines to treat alcohol withdrawal.
2018-10: The habenula, Latin for 'little rein' (a diminutive of habena, a strap or rein), sits in the epithalamus near the pineal gland and was named for its slender stalk-like appearance. Once obscure, it has drawn intense interest as a hub encoding disappointment and aversion; lateral habenula hyperactivity is now studied as a substrate of depression and may be a target of ketamine's antidepressant action.
2018-100: Investing in a patient's business is a textbook boundary violation because it injects the psychiatrist's financial self-interest directly into the treatment relationship, the classic risk that Glen Gabbard and Eva Lester analyzed in their influential work on boundaries in psychotherapy. The crucial distinction is between boundary crossings—minor, often benign deviations—and violations that exploit the patient. Dual financial relationships are among the most clearly prohibited because they corrupt the physician's fiduciary duty.
2018-101: Fragile X is the prototypical epigenetic disease: a full-mutation CGG repeat expansion (over 200 copies) in the FMR1 gene triggers hypermethylation of the CpG sites in its promoter, silencing transcription and abolishing the FMRP protein needed for synaptic development. Named for the chromosomal 'fragile site' seen on the X under folate-deprived culture, it is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and a leading single-gene cause of autism.
2018-102: Delayed ejaculation becomes more common with age, attributed partly to the loss of fast-conducting peripheral sensory nerves serving the penis and to the decline in sex steroid (testosterone) secretion that accompanies aging. DSM-5 reframed the older 'inhibited male orgasm' under this label. The age-related drop in penile sensory acuity raises the sensory threshold needed to trigger the ejaculatory reflex.
2018-103: The Epidemiologic Catchment Area (ECA) study, launched by NIMH around 1980 across five U.S. sites, was a landmark community survey of psychiatric disorders using the Diagnostic Interview Schedule. Among its findings, people with irritable bowel syndrome showed notably elevated rates of mood and anxiety symptoms—part of the broader recognition of strong psychiatric comorbidity with functional somatic syndromes and the gut-brain axis.
2018-104: Reactive (affective, defensive) aggression is most consistently mediated by a subcortical circuit running from the amygdala to the medial hypothalamus to the periaqueductal gray (PAG) of the midbrain. Walter Hess won the 1949 Nobel Prize for showing that electrical stimulation of the hypothalamus could evoke rage-like attack in cats. The orbitofrontal cortex normally restrains this circuit, so its dysfunction is linked to impulsive violence.
2018-105: Lamotrigine, originally developed as an antiepileptic, became valued in bipolar disorder for preventing depressive episodes—its strength in bipolar II, where depression dominates. It is renal-friendly and weight-neutral, advantages over lithium, divalproex, and the metabolically burdensome atypicals. Its signature hazard is rash, including rare Stevens-Johnson syndrome, which is why it demands slow titration; this risk first emerged during its epilepsy trials.
2018-106: John Bowlby and especially Mary Ainsworth established that infants form a hierarchy of multiple attachments of differing strengths rather than a single exclusive bond. Ainsworth's 'Strange Situation' procedure (1970s) operationalized attachment patterns—secure, avoidant, resistant—and Mary Main later added the disorganized category. Attachment depends on quality and responsiveness of interaction, not merely the quantity of time spent with a caregiver.
2018-107: The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) is the region most reliably engaged when shifting cognitive sets, as on the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, and patients with DLPFC lesions show the classic perseverative errors. Linked to working memory and executive control, the DLPFC is a frequent target in schizophrenia research and a stimulation site for repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) in depression.
2018-108: HIPAA's Privacy Rule, effective in 2003, permits sharing protected health information without specific authorization for treatment, payment, and health care operations (TPO). Research generally falls outside this triad, so disclosing identifiable data to an investigator typically requires patient authorization or an IRB/privacy-board waiver. This is why the epidemiological researcher—unlike the payer, treating provider, or QI administrator—needs explicit consent.
2018-109: Sensitivity is a test's ability to correctly identify those who truly have the disease (true positives), so maximizing it minimizes false negatives—the cases a screening test must not miss. The mnemonic SnNout captures it: a highly Sensitive test, when Negative, rules out disease. Screening prioritizes sensitivity; confirmatory tests prioritize specificity (SpPin).
2018-11: Fasciculations are visible, spontaneous twitches of a single motor unit, from Latin 'fasciculus,' a little bundle of muscle fibers sharing one motor neuron.
