On EMG they appear as discrete, relatively regular motor-unit potentials. While benign fasciculations are common, their pairing with weakness and atrophy is an ominous hallmark of motor neuron disease such as ALS, contrasting with fibrillations, which are subclinical single-fiber discharges only seen on EMG.
2018-110: Tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme converting tyrosine to L-DOPA, the first step in synthesizing all catecholamines, and it is a defining marker of dopaminergic neurons. A neurotoxin that collapses tyrosine hydroxylase levels points to damage of dopamine neurons—echoing MPTP, the contaminant that produced parkinsonism in drug users in the early 1980s and became the standard model of Parkinson disease.
2018-111: The Belmont Report (1979) emerged from the National Commission convened after the Tuskegee syphilis study scandal and laid out three core principles: respect for persons, beneficence, and justice. Respect for persons—honoring individual autonomy and protecting those with diminished autonomy—is the principle that grounds informed consent. The report remains the ethical bedrock of U.S. human-subjects research regulation.
2018-112: Normative childhood sexual behaviors such as self-stimulation and curiosity-driven exhibitionism are most frequent around age five, then decline as children enter the school years and become more aware of social norms and privacy. Much of this developmental data comes from William Friedrich's research on the Child Sexual Behavior Inventory, helping clinicians distinguish age-expected behavior from concerning signs.
2018-113: Sleep spindles—brief 11–16 Hz bursts of thalamocortical activity in stage 2 NREM sleep—decline in density with aging, most prominently over frontal and occipital regions. First described by Alfred Lee Loomis in the 1930s, spindles are generated by the thalamic reticular nucleus and are implicated in memory consolidation and protecting sleep from arousal; their loss parallels the fragmentation of older adults' sleep.
2018-114: Histone acetylation, catalyzed by histone acetyltransferases and removed by histone deacetylases (HDACs), neutralizes the positive charge on lysine residues, loosening chromatin and generally activating transcription—and it is rapidly reversible. This dynamism made HDAC inhibitors attractive in oncology and neuroscience. The 'histone code' concept, proposed around 2000, frames these reversible marks as a regulatory language layered atop the DNA sequence.
2018-115: Sertraline is widely regarded as a preferred SSRI during breastfeeding because infant serum levels are typically very low or undetectable; the guiding principle is that untreated maternal depression poses documented harms to infant development and bonding that generally outweigh the minimal medication exposure. This risk-benefit framing—treating the mother to protect the child—underlies why routine breast-milk or infant blood-level testing is not indicated.
2018-116: Severing the corpus callosum (commissurotomy) to control intractable epilepsy produces the classic split-brain syndrome: an object felt in the left hand projects to the right hemisphere, which lacks language, so the patient cannot name it—yet can name what is seen, routed to the left hemisphere. Roger Sperry's split-brain studies of hemispheric specialization earned him a share of the 1981 Nobel Prize.
2018-117: Pramipexole, a dopamine agonist, is a first-line treatment for restless legs syndrome, reflecting the disorder's link to dopaminergic dysfunction and iron deficiency. RLS was described in 1945 by Swedish neurologist Karl-Axel Ekbom and is sometimes called Ekbom syndrome. A notable caveat with long-term dopamine agonists is 'augmentation,' a paradoxical worsening and earlier onset of symptoms, which has shifted some guidelines toward alpha-2-delta ligands.
2018-118: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome results from thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, classically in chronic alcohol use, and damages the mammillary bodies and the dorsomedial thalamus—lesions tied to the profound anterograde amnesia and confabulation of Korsakoff psychosis. Carl Wernicke described the acute triad (confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia) in the 1880s and Sergei Korsakoff the chronic amnestic state; the mammillary body atrophy is a hallmark autopsy finding.
2018-119: Cognitive behavioral therapy for psychosis (CBTp) targets the positive symptoms—delusions and hallucinations—by helping patients reappraise the beliefs and meaning attached to anomalous experiences. Pioneered largely in the UK by clinicians such as Aaron Beck's intellectual heirs and researchers like David Kingdon and Douglas Turkington, CBTp is endorsed by NICE guidelines as an evidence-based adjunct to antipsychotic medication.
2018-12: Selective abstraction, also called mental filter, is one of the cognitive distortions catalogued by Aaron Beck and later popularized by David Burns in 'Feeling Good' (1980). It means seizing on a single negative detail and dwelling on it while ignoring the larger, mostly positive picture, like fixating on one wrong answer on an otherwise excellent exam. The hook: you abstract one dark thread and let it dye the whole fabric.
2018-120: The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, devised by Esta Berg and David Grant in 1948, requires sorting cards by an unstated rule (color, form, or number) that changes without warning, measuring abstract concept formation and the cognitive flexibility to shift set. Perseverative errors—continuing to sort by an old rule—are a sensitive marker of dorsolateral prefrontal/frontal-lobe dysfunction, making it a staple of executive-function assessment.
2018-121: Neuroinflammation is not purely harmful: the acute 'sickness behavior' driven by microglia releasing cytokines—fatigue, reduced activity, social withdrawal in response to peripheral infection—is an adaptive, energy-conserving response that promotes recovery. Robert Dantzer's work reframed these cytokine-mediated behaviors as a coordinated host-defense strategy, distinguishing this beneficial acute signaling from the maladaptive chronic microglial activation seen after injury or with aging.
2018-122: The National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI)—originally the National Alliance for the Mentally Ill—was founded in 1979 by family members, growing out of grassroots groups of parents seeking support and advocacy as deinstitutionalization moved people with serious mental illness into communities. It became the leading family-focused advocacy and lobbying organization, helping shift public framing away from blaming families toward a brain-disease model.
2018-123: Shortened REM latency, the rapid plunge into dream sleep, became one of the most reproducible biological markers of depression after sleep-lab studies in the 1960s and 1970s, much of it driven by David Kupfer and colleagues at Pittsburgh. Along with reduced slow-wave sleep and increased REM density, it fueled the cholinergic-aminergic imbalance hypothesis of mood disorders and even prompted attempts to use the EEG sleep profile as a diagnostic aid.
2018-124: Velocardiofacial syndrome stems from a microdeletion at chromosome 22q11.2, making it the most common human microdeletion syndrome. Robert Shprintzen described the clinical phenotype in the late 1970s, and it overlaps with DiGeorge syndrome under the umbrella term 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. It carries one of the highest known genetic risks for schizophrenia, with roughly a quarter of affected individuals developing psychosis, making it a prized natural model for psychiatric genetics.
2018-125: A confounder is a hidden third variable correlated with both exposure and outcome that distorts the apparent relationship. The classic textbook example is the spurious link between coffee and lung cancer, actually explained by smoking. Here the rescue benzodiazepines given only to controls confound the antipsychotic comparison. R.A. Fisher's championing of randomization was meant precisely to balance such unmeasured confounders across groups.
2018-126: PET imaging exploits positrons emitted by radiotracers; the workhorse FDG (fluorodeoxyglucose), developed at the University of Pennsylvania and Brookhaven in the 1970s, is a glucose analog that accumulates wherever cells burn glucose, mapping regional metabolism. Because active neurons and tumors are glucose-hungry, FDG-PET reveals both brain function and cancer. The technique grew from Michael Phelps and Edward Hoffman's work building the first human PET scanner.
2018-127: The exome, the protein-coding fraction of DNA, makes up only about 1-2% of the human genome, yet harbors the majority of known disease-causing mutations. The term gained currency with the rise of whole-exome sequencing around 2009, which let researchers cheaply hunt for pathogenic variants by skipping the vast noncoding remainder once dismissed as junk DNA.
2018-128: Histrionic derives from the Latin histrio, meaning actor, capturing the theatrical, attention-seeking quality of the disorder. It is the modern descendant of hysteria, from the Greek hystera (uterus), reflecting ancient and Freudian-era notions that the condition was uniquely female. DSM-III renamed it histrionic personality disorder in 1980 to shed the gendered baggage of the older hysterical label.
2018-129: The standard for competency to stand trial comes from the U.S. Supreme Court's 1960 decision Dusky v. United States, which requires that a defendant have a rational and factual understanding of the proceedings and the ability to consult with counsel with a reasonable degree of rational understanding. Crucially, this is about present functioning at trial, entirely separate from the insanity defense, which concerns mental state at the time of the offense.
2018-13: Mental health courts emerged in the late 1990s, with Broward County, Florida, often credited as launching one of the first in 1997. Modeled on drug courts, they are problem-solving courts that divert defendants with serious mental illness from jail into supervised, community-based treatment. The movement grew from recognition that jails and prisons had become de facto psychiatric institutions after deinstitutionalization, criminalizing untreated mental illness.
2018-130: Guanfacine is a selective alpha-2A adrenergic agonist that dampens noradrenergic tone in the prefrontal cortex. Amy Arnsten's work at Yale showed that alpha-2A stimulation strengthens prefrontal network connectivity, providing the rationale for its use in ADHD. Originally marketed as an antihypertensive, its extended-release form (Intuniv) gained FDA approval for pediatric ADHD in 2009, joining clonidine as a non-stimulant option.
2018-131: Progressive supranuclear palsy was first delineated in 1964 by Steele, Richardson, and Olszewski, and is sometimes called Steele-Richardson-Olszewski syndrome. Its hallmark is a vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, especially impaired downgaze, with the eyes still movable by the oculocephalic (doll's eye) maneuver, confirming the lesion is above the ocular motor nuclei. A tauopathy, it produces early falls, axial rigidity, and the surprised facial expression of frontalis overactivity.
2018-132: Validity, from the Latin validus (strong), asks whether a test measures what it claims to, while reliability concerns consistency of results. A classic teaching device is the dartboard analogy: reliability is tight clustering, validity is hitting the bullseye. The distinction was formalized in early-twentieth-century psychometrics by figures such as Lee Cronbach and is foundational to test construction.
2018-133: Mirror neurons were discovered serendipitously in the 1990s by Giacomo Rizzolatti's group in Parma, who found premotor neurons in macaques firing both when the animal acted and when it watched another act. The insula, a deep cortical island named by Johann Christian Reil, is central to interoception and disgust, and links the mirror system to felt emotional resonance, a proposed neural substrate of empathy.
2018-134: OCD migrated out of the anxiety disorders chapter in DSM-5 (2013) into its own obsessive-compulsive and related disorders category, yet it remains most often comorbid with the anxiety disorders it once kept company with. The reshuffling reflected growing recognition of a distinct neurocircuitry, particularly cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loops, that set OCD apart from classic fear-based conditions.
2018-135: Corticotropin-releasing hormone, isolated and characterized by Wylie Vale's team at the Salk Institute in 1981, is the master initiator of the stress axis. It is synthesized by parvocellular neurons of the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus and released into the hypophyseal portal system to drive ACTH secretion, launching the HPA cascade that culminates in cortisol release.
2018-136: Ultrarapid metabolizers carry gene duplications, multiple copies of the wild-type (functional) allele, so they clear substrates faster than normal and show subtherapeutic drug levels despite adherence. CYP2D6, the enzyme metabolizing risperidone and many antipsychotics, is famous for this copy-number variation; the phenomenon was first dramatically documented for debrisoquine hydroxylation, the founding story of modern pharmacogenetics.
2018-137: Standard developmental milestones place two-word phrases (telegraphic speech such as more milk) at around 24 months, so failure to combine words by age two is a red flag warranting audiologic evaluation, since undetected hearing loss is a leading reversible cause of language delay. Universal newborn hearing screening, now routine in the U.S., grew from advocacy in the 1990s precisely to catch deficits before they derail speech development.
2018-138: In a crossover design each subject serves as their own control, eliminating between-subject variability and thereby boosting statistical precision so fewer participants are needed. The tradeoff is the carryover effect, which is why a washout period is built between treatment arms. The approach traces to agricultural and early clinical experimentation and is prized in studies of stable chronic conditions.
2018-139: The high-affinity alpha-4-beta-2 nicotinic receptor mediates nicotine's rewarding dopamine release in the mesolimbic pathway. This pharmacology inspired varenicline (Chantix), a partial agonist designed to occupy the receptor and blunt both craving and reward, which the FDA approved in 2006 as a purpose-built smoking-cessation drug.
2018-14: This cluster, isolation of affect, intellectualization, and reaction formation, comprises the classic obsessional defenses described in the psychoanalytic tradition stretching back to Freud's writings on obsessional neurosis. Isolation strips feeling from thought, intellectualization retreats into abstraction, and reaction formation converts an unacceptable impulse into its opposite. Together they paint the orderly, controlled, emotionally distant style of the obsessive-compulsive personality, making them a reliable test signature.
2018-140: Disaster research consistently identifies social support, especially peer connection, as among the strongest protective factors against post-traumatic symptoms in children. This echoes Stevan Hobfoll's influential consensus principles for mass-trauma intervention, which emphasize promoting connectedness and a sense of safety, and underlies psychological first aid models that prioritize reuniting children with familiar peers and caregivers over premature formal counseling.
2018-141: Countertransference, the clinician's own emotional reactions projected onto the patient, was named by Freud in 1910 and initially viewed purely as an obstacle to be overcome. Later analysts such as Heinrich Racker and Paula Heimann reframed it as a valuable diagnostic instrument. Here the psychiatrist's unresolved history with an alcoholic parent drives the overinvested insistence on progress, a textbook countertransference enactment.
2018-142: Whole-exome sequencing, by reading only the protein-coding 1-2% of the genome, became the method of choice around 2009-2010 for pinpointing single-nucleotide variants in rare Mendelian diseases. Its first celebrated triumph was diagnosing a child with intractable inflammatory bowel disease (Nicholas Volker), a case that helped usher exome sequencing into routine clinical genetics.
2018-143: Effective transitions at the end of life hinge on continuity and an identified care person who knows the patient's wishes and coordinates communication across settings. This insight underpins the modern hospice and palliative care movement founded by Dame Cicely Saunders, whose St Christopher's Hospice opened in London in 1967 and championed total, person-centered care across the dying trajectory.
2018-144: Voluntary intoxication generally does not excuse criminal responsibility under Anglo-American law, a doctrine reaching back centuries, since the person chose to become impaired. By contrast, the insanity defense (rooted in the 1843 M'Naghten Rules), duress, and legally recognized incapacity can negate culpability. Thus the man robbing for vodka remains responsible, whereas the psychotic or coerced actors may not.
2018-145: Tertiary prevention aims to reduce complications and disability once disease is already established, as opposed to preventing onset (primary) or catching it early (secondary). The three-tier framework was formalized by Hugh Leavell and E. Gurney Clark in the 1940s-1950s. Treating quetiapine-induced diabetes with metformin to forestall its damage is a quintessential tertiary intervention.
2018-146: Linkage analysis tracks how genetic markers and disease traits co-segregate through families, exploiting the fact that loci physically close on a chromosome are inherited together because recombination rarely separates them. The conceptual groundwork was laid by Thomas Hunt Morgan and student Alfred Sturtevant, who in 1913 built the first genetic linkage map using fruit flies, founding the discipline of gene mapping.
2018-147: Collaborative care arose to address a stark capacity gap: most people with mental illness are seen only in primary care, where specialist resources cannot reach everyone. Wayne Katon and Jurgen Unutzer at the University of Washington developed and validated the model, notably in the landmark IMPACT trial for late-life depression published in 2002, embedding a care manager and consulting psychiatrist into primary-care teams.
2018-148: Melanie Klein, the pioneering child analyst, proposed that the infant moves from the paranoid-schizoid position, where the mother is split into idealized good and persecutory bad objects, to the depressive position, where the child integrates these and recognizes one whole mother who is both loved and hated. This achievement, theorized in the 1930s-1940s, brings guilt, concern, and the wish to make reparation.
2018-149: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine 2007 scoring rules renamed the deep slow-wave stage N3, defined by high-voltage delta activity occupying at least 20% of an epoch; it merged the older Rechtschaffen and Kales stages 3 and 4. N3 is the realm of sleepwalking, night terrors, and growth-hormone release, and is hardest to rouse from. Slow eye-rolling movements mark the descent through early NREM sleep.
2018-15: A prospective cohort study identifies groups by exposure status, here lorazepam use, and follows them forward in time to see who develops the outcome. The landmark exemplar is the Framingham Heart Study, begun in 1948, which tracked residents to uncover cardiovascular risk factors. The mnemonic hook: 'cohort' shares its root with the Roman military unit, a band marching forward together; prospective cohorts march forward through time toward the outcome.
2018-150: Intensive case management blends assertive community treatment with low caseloads to support people with severe mental illness. A large 2017 Cochrane review found its clearest, most consistent benefit was reduced length of hospital stay, with effects strongest where baseline hospital use was high, rather than dramatic gains in employment or mortality. It grew from Stein and Test's pioneering ACT work in 1970s Wisconsin.
2018-151: Botulinum toxin, the most lethal poison known by weight, was tamed into medicine when Alan Scott adapted it for strabismus in the 1970s-80s. Injected into the overactive neck muscles, it blocks acetylcholine release and is now first-line for cervical dystonia (spasmodic torticollis). The FDA approved its cosmetic form (Botox) in 2002, but its therapeutic use for dystonia came first.
2018-152: Oppositional defiant disorder is defined by a recurrent pattern of angry, argumentative, defiant behavior directed at authority figures, with outbursts triggered by limits and not getting one's way, distinguishing it from the autonomous mood episodes of bipolar disorder. DSM-5 grouped ODD among the disruptive, impulse-control, and conduct disorders and clarified it as distinct from the more pervasive rule-violations of conduct disorder.
2018-153: Catastrophizing was named by Albert Ellis, founder of Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy in the 1950s, and later elaborated by Aaron Beck within cognitive therapy as one of the classic cognitive distortions. The hallmark is mentally chaining together a worst-case sequence in which one bad outcome cascades into total ruin. Beck's work in the 1960s-70s on systematically cataloguing such distortions became foundational to modern CBT.
2018-154: Histamine neurons cluster almost exclusively in the tuberomammillary nucleus of the posterior hypothalamus and fire fastest during waking, going silent in sleep, which is why classic antihistamines cross the blood-brain barrier and cause drowsiness. This wake-promoting role explains the 2010s development of pitolisant, an H3 autoreceptor antagonist that boosts histamine release to treat narcolepsy. The histaminergic system is a key node in the brain's ascending arousal network.
2018-155: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension, historically called pseudotumor cerebri, presents with raised intracranial pressure and papilledema but normal imaging and CSF composition. It classically strikes young obese women of childbearing age. The diagnostic Modified Dandy criteria are named for neurosurgeon Walter Dandy, who described the syndrome in the 1930s; treatment includes acetazolamide and weight loss to prevent vision loss.
2018-156: Phencyclidine was synthesized by Parke-Davis in the 1950s as the anesthetic Sernyl, but emergence delirium and psychosis ended its human use; it survived as the veterinary agent ketamine's parent compound. As an NMDA-receptor antagonist it produces dissociation, violent agitation, and the near-pathognomonic vertical (or rotary) nystagmus. Its street name 'angel dust' and PCP-induced psychosis became a model for studying schizophrenia's glutamatergic hypothesis.
2018-157: This reflects the principle of facilitation in the medical interview, a foundational technique in patient-centered communication taught since George Engel's biopsychosocial model emerged in 1977. Minimal encouragers and reflective prompts keep a hesitant patient talking without leading or shutting them down, especially around shame-laden topics like sexual dysfunction. The skill rests on tolerating silence rather than rushing to closed questions.
2018-158: Quality improvement methodology insists you measure a problem before assuming its size; the residents only 'predict' missed handoffs, so establishing a baseline prevalence comes first. This reflects the Model for Improvement and the Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle popularized by the Institute for Healthcare Improvement. Handoff safety gained national urgency after duty-hour reforms multiplied shift changes, spawning standardized tools like I-PASS.
2018-159: Shoe-tying is a developmental milestone that typically isn't mastered until around age five or six, well after children manage Velcro, snaps, zippers, and large buttons. Tying requires bimanual coordination, sequencing, and bilateral integration that mature relatively late. Pediatric developmental schedules, descended from Arnold Gesell's mid-20th-century normative work, consistently place complex fasteners like laces last in the dressing sequence.
2018-16: The cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) loop is the leading neurocircuit model of OCD, linking the orbitofrontal cortex, caudate, and thalamus in a self-reinforcing feedback loop thought to generate intrusive thoughts and compulsions. Imaging studies show this circuit becomes hyperactive during symptom provocation and normalizes after successful SSRI treatment or CBT. The model also rationalizes neurosurgical targets like cingulotomy and deep brain stimulation for refractory OCD.
2018-160: The Global Burden of Disease studies, launched in the early 1990s by Christopher Murray and Alan Lopez with WHO and World Bank backing, introduced the disability-adjusted life year and repeatedly rank major depressive disorder among the leading causes of years lived with disability worldwide. Depression's high prevalence combined with substantial disability weight gives it an outsized nonfatal burden, reshaping global health priorities toward mental illness.
2018-161: Repetitive TMS for depression standardly targets the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, a region found hypoactive in depression on functional imaging. The FDA first cleared an rTMS device (NeuroStar) for treatment-resistant depression in 2008. The technique grew from Anthony Barker's 1985 demonstration in England that a magnetic pulse over motor cortex could noninvasively trigger a muscle twitch, proving the brain could be stimulated through the skull.
2018-162: During acute refeeding in severe anorexia, the brain is starved and cognitively rigid, so insight-oriented or cognitive work is premature; supportive coaching and behavioral reinforcement to restore weight come first. This staged approach reflects the principle that 'food is medicine' early in treatment. Clinicians also watch vigilantly for refeeding syndrome, the dangerous hypophosphatemia first widely recognized among liberated WWII prisoners and famine survivors.
2018-163: Transvestic disorder requires that the cross-dressing arousal cause clinically significant distress or impairment, distinguishing the paraphilic disorder from cross-dressing itself. DSM-5 made this distress/impairment threshold explicit across the paraphilias in 2013, depathologizing the behavior absent suffering or harm. The older term transvestic fetishism was narrowed and renamed as the diagnostic framework shifted toward distress-based criteria.
2018-164: Operant conditioning, formalized by B.F. Skinner in the 1930s-40s, holds that behavior is shaped by its consequences, so asking how parents respond probes whether reassurance or escape from the bus is reinforcing the avoidance. This negative-reinforcement loop, escaping the feared situation reduces anxiety and thereby strengthens avoidance, is central to maintaining childhood anxiety. The cure typically involves exposure that breaks the reinforcement cycle.
2018-165: Family-based treatment for adolescent eating disorders, the Maudsley approach developed at London's Maudsley Hospital in the 1980s, mobilizes parents to take charge of refeeding. Landmark trials, notably Lock and Le Grange's 2010 randomized study, showed FBT outperforming individual adolescent-focused therapy at follow-up roughly six to twelve months out. It remains the best-supported intervention for adolescent anorexia nervosa.
2018-166: Paranoid personality disorder is a pervasive, pattern-based distrust and suspiciousness present without the frank delusions, hallucinations, or mood episodes that would point to a psychotic or affective disorder. It sits in DSM-5's Cluster A, the 'odd/eccentric' cluster, alongside schizoid and schizotypal personality disorders. The construct traces back to early-20th-century descriptions of constitutionally suspicious 'paranoid' temperaments by Kraepelin and others.
2018-167: In suspected acute ischemic stroke, the urgent job of non-contrast CT is to rule out hemorrhage before giving thrombolytics, since giving a clot-buster into a bleed is catastrophic. Early ischemia is often invisible on plain CT for hours, so the scan's value is exclusionary. This 'rule out blood first' logic underpins the time-critical stroke protocols built around tPA, approved for stroke in the US in 1996.
2018-168: Bupropion is an norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor that is activating rather than sedating and tends to be weight-neutral or even associated with weight loss, making it ideal for depression with low energy and weight gain. It uniquely lacks sexual side effects among common antidepressants. Originally approved in the 1980s, it was briefly withdrawn over seizure risk, then reintroduced at lower doses and later repurposed as the smoking-cessation aid Zyban.
2018-169: Microglia are the brain's resident immune cells, derived not from neural tissue but from yolk-sac myeloid progenitors, and they mount the CNS's primary inflammatory response. Spanish neuroscientist Pío del Río Hortega first identified and named microglia in the 1910s-1920s using silver staining. Their activation is now central to neuroinflammation hypotheses of depression, neurodegeneration, and the brain's response to injury.
2018-17: Disulfiram (Antabuse), introduced for alcohol use disorder around 1948 after rubber-industry workers exposed to it grew sick when drinking, blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase. The resulting acetaldehyde buildup causes the dreaded disulfiram-ethanol reaction: flushing, throbbing headache, tachycardia, hypotension, and nausea. The aversive misery is the whole therapeutic point, deterring drinking, but it can be dangerous, even fatal, with significant alcohol exposure.
2018-170: Methadone maintenance is continued through pregnancy because abrupt withdrawal risks miscarriage, preterm labor, and fetal distress, and relapse to illicit opioids is far more dangerous than maintenance. This standard dates to the methadone maintenance treatment pioneered by Vincent Dole and Marie Nyswander in 1960s New York. Buprenorphine has since become an accepted alternative; neonatal abstinence syndrome is managed after delivery.
2018-171: The evidence-based stance on mental-health apps is one of cautious appraisal: the clinician reviews the app before endorsing it, because most consumer apps lack peer-reviewed validation and may mishandle data. The American Psychiatric Association responded by publishing an App Evaluation Model, a tiered framework assessing safety, evidence, usability, and privacy, to guide clinicians through an unregulated marketplace.
2018-172: Amnesia for ordinary, everyday events, not just trauma, is a distinguishing feature of dissociative identity disorder, reflecting gaps when different identity states hold the memories. PTSD involves amnesia only for trauma aspects. DID was renamed from 'multiple personality disorder' in DSM-IV (1994) to emphasize fragmentation of identity rather than the existence of multiple people, reframing the core pathology as a failure to integrate consciousness and memory.
2018-173: Histamine H1-receptor blockade drives the sedation and weight gain seen with many psychotropics; potent H1 antagonism is why mirtazapine, quetiapine, and olanzapine are so sedating and appetite-stimulating. The same H1 affinity makes diphenhydramine a sleep aid. Receptor-binding profiling, pioneered by Solomon Snyder's lab in the 1970s, let pharmacologists map these side-effect liabilities to specific receptor affinities.
2018-174: Nonjudgmental, present-moment awareness is the defining stance of mindfulness, distinguishing it from relaxation or cognitive restructuring. Jon Kabat-Zinn brought it into Western medicine in 1979 by founding Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction at the University of Massachusetts, secularizing Buddhist vipassana practice. He famously defined mindfulness as paying attention, on purpose, in the present moment, and nonjudgmentally.
2018-175: Metacognition literally means 'thinking about thinking,' a term coined by developmental psychologist John Flavell in the 1970s. In schizophrenia, metacognitive approaches help patients recognize their own reasoning biases, capacities, and limits to improve social insight. This connects to work on cognitive insight and to metacognitive training, which targets the jumping-to-conclusions bias and other distortions implicated in delusion formation.
2018-176: Australian psychiatrist John Cade discovered lithium's calming effect in 1949 while injecting guinea pigs with lithium urate, chosen partly because lithium salts were already used to dissolve urate in gout and bladder stones. His small open trial in agitated manic patients launched the modern era of psychopharmacology. Lithium remains the gold standard mood stabilizer despite predating randomized trials.
2018-177: Social (pragmatic) communication disorder is a diagnosis new to DSM-5 in 2013, created for children who have the social-communication deficits of autism, trouble with conversational turn-taking, social context, and nonliteral language, but lack the restricted, repetitive behaviors and rigidity required for an autism spectrum diagnosis. It filled a gap left when DSM-5 collapsed Asperger's and PDD-NOS into the single autism spectrum category.
2018-178: Next-generation sequencing, the massively parallel technology that matured in the late 2000s, can read individual base pairs and so detect rare and even private variants that genome-wide association studies, which rely on common tagging SNPs, systematically miss. NGS dramatically dropped the cost of whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing, enabling discovery of rare highly penetrant mutations underlying neuropsychiatric disorders.
2018-179: Cisplatin, a platinum compound whose anticancer activity Barnett Rosenberg serendipitously discovered in the 1960s while studying electric fields on bacteria, classically causes a dose-limiting distal sensory polyneuropathy along with ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity. The neuropathy stems from platinum accumulation in the dorsal root ganglia, producing a length-dependent, stocking-glove sensory loss that can persist or even worsen after treatment ends.
2018-18: Mary Ainsworth devised the Strange Situation in the late 1960s and published it fully in 1978's 'Patterns of Attachment.' In this 20-minute laboratory protocol, an infant experiences separations from and reunions with the caregiver and a stranger, and the infant's reunion behavior classifies attachment as secure, anxious-resistant, or avoidant. Building on John Bowlby's attachment theory, it became the gold-standard empirical measure of the parent-child bond.
2018-180: The entrainment test is a hallmark bedside sign of functional (psychogenic) tremor: when the patient is asked to tap a rhythm with the unaffected hand, the involuntary tremor either disappears, syncs to the new rhythm, or cannot coexist, betraying its voluntary, non-organic origin. Organic tremors maintain their own independent frequency. Distractibility and entrainment are among the most useful clinical clues to functional movement disorders.
2018-181: Gerstmann syndrome, the tetrad of agraphia, acalculia, right-left disorientation, and finger agnosia, localizes to the dominant (usually left) angular gyrus in the inferior parietal lobule. Austrian neurologist Josef Gerstmann described the constellation in the 1920s-30s. Though its status as a unified 'syndrome' has been debated, the four signs together remain a classic localizing clue to dominant parietal pathology.
2018-182: Dextromethorphan, the common cough suppressant, becomes a dissociative hallucinogen at high recreational doses because it acts as an NMDA-receptor antagonist much like PCP and ketamine, producing the floating, 'walking on air' sensation along with tachycardia, agitation, and paranoia. Abuse is especially common among teens due to its over-the-counter availability, and high doses can also produce serotonergic effects and dangerous interactions with MAOIs.
2018-183: The term "double agent" entered medical ethics through Robert Jay Lifton and others writing about physicians whose loyalty is split between the patient and a third party such as an employer, court, or the military. In forensic and fitness-for-duty evaluations there is no traditional treatment relationship, so the ethical safeguard is transparency: explicitly warning the evaluee at the outset who the report goes to and what is not confidential. This disclosure, sometimes called the forensic warning, is the analog of informed consent in non-treatment settings.
2018-184: Classical conditioning was discovered by Ivan Pavlov around 1900 while studying dog salivation, earning him the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. A neutral cue (the crack-house) repeatedly paired with the drug becomes a conditioned stimulus that elicits a conditioned response of craving. This cue-reactivity model underlies cue-exposure therapy and explains why people in recovery are urged to avoid "people, places, and things" tied to past use.
2018-185: The subiculum takes its name from the Latin for "support" or "little prop," reflecting its position as a transitional zone underlying the hippocampus proper. It is the principal output structure of the hippocampal formation, relaying processed signals from CA1 onward to the entorhinal cortex and beyond. It is notable in epilepsy research, as the subiculum can generate interictal activity, and it sits within the classic trisynaptic circuit central to memory.
2018-186: Obstructive sleep apnea was described in the modern era after researchers in the 1960s and 1970s linked repetitive upper-airway collapse to daytime hypersomnolence; the term "Pickwickian syndrome," borrowed from the fat, perpetually drowsy boy Joe in Dickens's The Pickwick Papers, was an early label for the obesity-hypoventilation variant. Morning headaches reflect overnight CO2 retention, and the definitive diagnostic test, polysomnography, quantifies apnea-hypopnea events. Nasal CPAP, introduced by Colin Sullivan in 1981, remains the cornerstone treatment.
2018-187: Narcissistic personality disorder draws its name from Narcissus, the youth of Greek myth who fell in love with his own reflection. Havelock Ellis used "narcissism" clinically in 1898, and Freud elaborated it in his 1914 paper On Narcissism. The rigid devaluation of others' viewpoints and inability to tolerate alternative perspectives reflect the fragile, grandiose self-structure later detailed by Kohut and Kernberg, and NPD formally entered the DSM in 1980 with DSM-III.
2018-188: This taps source memory, the recollection of where or how information was acquired, which declines disproportionately with normal aging while content memory and well-rehearsed procedural skills are preserved. Source-monitoring research was framed prominently by Marcia Johnson and colleagues in the 1980s and 1990s, linking such judgments to prefrontal function. The dissociation explains why an elderly person may recall a fact perfectly yet forget whether they read it or saw it on television.
2018-189: Event-related potentials are tiny, time-locked EEG voltage changes averaged over many trials; the landmark P300 wave was reported by Sutton and colleagues in 1965. In suspected conversion (functional neurological) disorder, ERPs can demonstrate intact sensory pathways, for example a preserved cortical response to a stimulus the patient reports not perceiving, providing objective evidence that the deficit is not due to a lesion in the conducting pathway. This makes ERPs a useful confirmatory adjunct.
2018-19: Anti-Yo (anti-Purkinje cell antibody 1, PCA-1) is the prototypical antibody of paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, named after the index patient. Its presence is a red flag for an underlying gynecologic or breast malignancy, so the priority is hunting the hidden tumor with body imaging rather than further brain studies. The neurologic syndrome often precedes the cancer's discovery, making the antibody a sentinel that prompts urgent oncologic evaluation.
2018-190: Epigenetic drift describes the progressive divergence of DNA methylation patterns with age, vividly demonstrated in studies of identical twins who become epigenetically more different over their lifetimes. Because late-onset Alzheimer disease is driven largely by aging and environment rather than the deterministic gene mutations behind early-onset familial cases, accumulating epigenetic changes are a plausible contributor. This positions the methylome alongside the well-known APOE risk allele in sporadic, age-related Alzheimer pathology.
2018-191: The least-restrictive-alternative principle holds that clinicians should use the mildest effective intervention before escalating to seclusion or restraint, a standard reinforced by decades of regulatory reform including CMS and Joint Commission restraint rules. Offering a genuine choice such as a quiet room or voluntary medication respects autonomy, can de-escalate agitation, and preserves the therapeutic alliance, which is especially important in borderline pathology where coercion often intensifies the crisis.
2018-192: Nonmaleficence, the duty to "first, do no harm," is encapsulated in the Latin maxim primum non nocere and traces to the Hippocratic tradition. Codified as one of the four principles by Beauchamp and Childress in their influential 1979 Principles of Biomedical Ethics, it obliges clinicians to seek consultation and avoid practicing beyond their competence. Asking a supervisor when treatment stalls protects the patient from the harm of uninformed or stubborn care.
2018-193: Linezolid is an oxazolidinone antibiotic that doubles as a reversible, non-selective monoamine oxidase inhibitor, so pairing it with an SSRI like fluoxetine risks excess synaptic serotonin and serotonin syndrome. The FDA issued specific warnings about this interaction in 2011. Serotonin syndrome itself was characterized by Harvey Sternbach, whose 1991 criteria were later refined into the more sensitive Hunter criteria emphasizing clonus, hyperthermia, and autonomic instability.
2018-194: Longitudinal follow-up studies of childhood ADHD consistently show that overt motor hyperactivity attenuates most with maturation, often shifting to subjective inner restlessness, while inattention and executive difficulties tend to persist into adolescence and adulthood. This pattern, documented in cohorts such as those followed by Russell Barkley and in the landmark MTA study begun in the 1990s, underlies the adult ADHD presentation that is dominated by inattentive rather than hyperactive symptoms.
2018-195: The suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus is the body's master circadian clock, named for its position just above the optic chiasm, which lets it receive light input directly via the retinohypothalamic tract. Its pacemaker role was established by lesion and transplant experiments in rodents in the 1970s and 1980s. Melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells, discovered around 2002, are the photoreceptors that entrain it to the day-night cycle and regulate melatonin release.
2018-196: Genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder is a DSM-5 (2013) diagnosis that merged the older categories of vaginismus and dyspareunia, reflecting evidence that the involuntary pelvic-floor muscle spasm and the pain/fear of penetration overlap heavily and are hard to separate clinically. The word vaginismus dates to the 19th century. A normal gynecologic exam pointing toward a psychophysiologic, anxiety-mediated mechanism is characteristic, and treatment classically pairs graded dilation with anxiety reduction.
2018-197: Poverty of speech, or alogia, denotes a marked reduction in the amount of spontaneous speech, a hallmark negative symptom catalogued by Nancy Andreasen, whose Scale for the Assessment of Negative Symptoms (SANS) in the early 1980s operationalized such deficits. The term alogia derives from Greek for "without speech." It must be distinguished from poverty of content, in which speech is normal in quantity but conveys little meaning.
2018-198: HIPAA, enacted in 1996 with its Privacy Rule taking effect in 2003, generally bars sharing protected health information without authorization, but it explicitly permits disclosure to family when, in the provider's professional judgment, a patient lacks decision-making capacity and the disclosure is in the patient's best interest. A floridly psychotic patient with Capgras-type delusions about his parents may meet this exception, allowing clinicians to share information despite the stated objection.
2018-199: The efficacy-versus-effectiveness distinction is central to evidence-based medicine: efficacy trials test an intervention under ideal, tightly controlled conditions, while effectiveness (or pragmatic) trials measure how it performs in routine, real-world practice with heterogeneous patients. Landmark NIMH effectiveness trials such as CATIE for schizophrenia and STAR*D for depression in the 2000s embodied this approach, often using broad enrollment and real-world endpoints like all-cause treatment discontinuation.
2018-2: Periodic limb movement disorder features repetitive, stereotyped limb jerks during sleep that fragment sleep without the patient's awareness, detected on polysomnography. It is closely related to restless legs syndrome (the waking counterpart), historically called nocturnal myoclonus. Karl-Axel Ekbom described restless legs in the 1940s, and the periodic limb movements were later quantified by sleep-laboratory recordings.
2018-20: When a child with ADHD fails one stimulant class, guidelines recommend switching to the other class before abandoning stimulants. Methylphenidate primarily blocks reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine, while amphetamines like dextroamphetamine additionally drive presynaptic release. Because roughly a quarter of children respond to one class but not the other, a non-responder to methylphenidate should next try an amphetamine, reserving non-stimulants like atomoxetine or alpha-2 agonists for later.
2018-200: CATIE, the NIMH-funded Clinical Antipsychotic Trials of Intervention Effectiveness, published its first-phase results in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2005. Using all-cause discontinuation as a pragmatic measure of effectiveness, olanzapine had the longest time to discontinuation, though at the cost of substantial metabolic weight gain. Strikingly, the older typical agent perphenazine performed comparably to several second-generation drugs, challenging assumptions that newer antipsychotics were uniformly superior.
2018-201: Myelination of the central nervous system proceeds in a predictable caudal-to-rostral, sensory-before-motor sequence first mapped systematically by Paul Flechsig over a century ago. The corticospinal (pyramidal) tracts complete myelination relatively early, by roughly age three, which parallels the maturation of voluntary motor control and refined gait in toddlers, whereas association and prefrontal regions continue myelinating well into the third decade.
2018-202: DSM-5 deliberately distinguishes gender dysphoria, which requires clinically significant distress or impairment, from simple gender-nonconforming behavior, which is a normal variant and not a disorder. This reframing in 2013 replaced DSM-IV's stigmatizing "gender identity disorder," shifting the diagnostic focus from identity itself to the suffering that may accompany it. A child who is happy and functioning well, with no distress, by definition does not have a psychiatric diagnosis.
2018-203: Apathy, a primary loss of motivation distinct from the sadness and self-deprecation of depression, is one of the most common neuropsychiatric features of Parkinson disease, tied to dysfunction in dopaminergic frontal-subcortical (especially ventral striatal) circuits. The concept was operationalized by Robert Marin in 1991, who argued apathy is a syndrome in its own right. Its dissociation from low mood is clinically crucial because antidepressants often fail to relieve it.
2018-204: Cigarette smoke induces the hepatic enzyme CYP1A2, the main pathway metabolizing clozapine, so heavy smoking lowers clozapine blood levels and can precipitate relapse even with perfect adherence. The culprits are polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in the smoke, not nicotine itself. Conversely, abrupt smoking cessation, such as during a non-smoking hospitalization, can raise clozapine levels into toxic range, a well-documented and clinically important pharmacokinetic interaction.
2018-205: The Study of Women's Health Across the Nation (SWAN), a multisite longitudinal cohort launched in the 1990s to track the menopausal transition, found that sleep problems distinguished women with persistent or recurrent depressive symptoms from those with a single episode. The finding reinforced the bidirectional link between disturbed sleep and chronic depression, suggesting sleep disruption is both a risk marker and a possible perpetuating factor during midlife in women.
2018-206: Several personality disorders, especially the impulsive cluster B types like borderline and antisocial, show a decline in prevalence and symptom intensity in later life, a phenomenon often called "maturing out" or burnout. This parallels the broader personality-maturation findings of researchers like Robert McCrae and Paul Costa showing that traits such as impulsivity and novelty-seeking soften with age while conscientiousness and agreeableness rise.
2018-207: Synaptic plasticity, the strengthening and weakening of connections between neurons, is the cellular basis of learning and memory, foreshadowed by Donald Hebb's 1949 postulate often paraphrased as "neurons that fire together wire together." Its physiological embodiment, long-term potentiation, was discovered by Bliss and Lomo in the rabbit hippocampus in 1973. Eric Kandel won the 2000 Nobel Prize for elucidating the molecular machinery of synaptic change underlying memory.
2018-208: DNA methylation was long studied only in the nucleus, but researchers have identified methylation machinery, including a mitochondrial form of DNMT1, acting on mitochondrial DNA itself, giving rise to the field of mitoepigenetics. Because mitochondria have their own small circular genome inherited maternally, epigenetic regulation within these organelles offers a novel layer of control over energy metabolism relevant to aging and neuropsychiatric disease.
2018-209: The vignette describes psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (functional/dissociative seizures): preserved awareness, the ability to suppress movements, and prolonged duration argue against true epilepsy. Prognosis is worse with insidious onset and long symptom duration before diagnosis, whereas abrupt onset, a clear precipitating stressor, higher intelligence, and prompt treatment predict better outcomes. Video-EEG remains the gold standard for distinguishing these events from epileptic seizures.
2018-21: The refractory period, the recovery interval after orgasm before another erection is possible, was charted by Masters and Johnson in their landmark 'Human Sexual Response' (1966), which divided the cycle into excitement, plateau, orgasm, and resolution. Aging predictably lengthens this refractory period in men, sometimes to many hours or days, even as libido and the capacity for satisfying sexuality often persist into late life.
2018-210: Bright light therapy works by phase-shifting the circadian clock, and the direction of the shift depends on timing per the light phase-response curve. Light in the morning advances the clock (earlier sleep), while light in the evening delays it (later sleep onset and waking). Pioneered for seasonal affective disorder by Norman Rosenthal and colleagues at the NIMH in the early 1980s, properly timed morning exposure is essential to avoid the delayed pattern described here.
2018-211: Levetiracetam is prized for its clean pharmacokinetics: it is largely renally excreted, minimally protein-bound, and does not meaningfully induce or inhibit hepatic cytochrome enzymes, so it is essentially free of interactions with other antiepileptics. Developed from the nootropic piracetam and FDA-approved in 1999, it acts through the novel synaptic vesicle protein SV2A, a mechanism unlike any earlier anticonvulsant.
2018-212: Boundary violations, distinguished from more benign boundary crossings by their potential to exploit or harm the patient, were extensively framed in psychiatry by Glen Gabbard and Thomas Gutheil in the 1990s. They emphasized that lapses often begin subtly along a "slippery slope," and that meeting a patient outside the office in a social venue such as a coffee bar erodes the professional frame and can presage more serious transgressions.
2018-213: The PHQ-9 maps directly onto the nine DSM criteria for major depressive disorder, with each item scored 0-3 for a maximum of 27. It was developed in the late 1990s by Robert Spitzer, Janet Williams, and Kurt Kroenke as part of the PRIME-MD project, funded by Pfizer. Its simplicity and free availability made it the workhorse depression-severity measure in primary care, and a score of 10 or more is the classic cutoff for clinically significant depression.
2018-214: Newborns lack a consolidated day-night rhythm because the suprachiasmatic nucleus and melatonin secretion are still maturing; sleep is distributed across the 24-hour day. By roughly the third to sixth month, entrainment to the light-dark cycle and to maternal cues produces an adult-like circadian pattern with nighttime sleep consolidation. This emergence of nocturnal melatonin secretion around the second to third month is what underlies the familiar milestone of babies finally sleeping through the night.
2018-215: Atomoxetine (Strattera), approved by the FDA in 2002, was the first nonstimulant approved for ADHD and works as a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor. In 2005 the FDA added a black box warning after pooled pediatric trials showed a small increased risk of suicidal ideation, echoing the SSRI antidepressant warning of the prior year. Because it is noradrenergic rather than dopaminergic and carries no abuse potential, it is unscheduled, unlike the stimulant options.
2018-216: Adjustment disorder traces to the older psychiatric notion of a 'reactive' or 'situational' disturbance and was formalized in DSM-III in 1980. It is defined by emotional or behavioral symptoms arising within three months of an identifiable stressor that are out of proportion or impairing, yet fall short of another disorder's threshold. Sometimes called the diagnosis of 'normal people facing abnormal circumstances,' it is one of the most common diagnoses on consultation-liaison and medical services.
2018-217: Longitudinal developmental research has repeatedly found that internalizing traits such as anxiety and behavioral inhibition delay sexual debut in adolescent boys, while externalizing traits, early substance use, and aggression accelerate it. The protective effect is generally read through avoidance and social caution: anxious boys are less likely to pursue or be pursued into early risk-taking situations. This contrasts with the consistent finding that conduct problems and impulsivity predict earlier first intercourse.
2018-218: The posterior cerebral arteries arise from the basilar artery and supply the occipital lobes and medial temporal structures, so PCA strokes classically produce contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing. Diffusion-weighted MRI, which became clinically widespread in the late 1990s, detects the cytotoxic edema of acute infarction within minutes by showing restricted water diffusion, making it the most sensitive sequence for identifying a hyperacute stroke's vascular territory.
2018-219: This describes body dysmorphic disorder, a preoccupation with imagined or slight defects in appearance. The condition was first detailed by Italian physician Enrico Morselli in 1891 under the term 'dysmorphophobia,' from the Greek 'dysmorphia,' meaning ugliness. DSM-5 moved it into the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders chapter, reflecting its phenomenologic kinship with OCD. SSRIs such as fluoxetine, typically at higher doses, are the pharmacologic mainstay, mirroring OCD treatment.
2018-22: Group psychotherapy is often described as moving through developmental phases. In models drawing on the work of theorists like the MacKenzie framework, the mature working stage, sometimes called the working group, is marked by cohesion, trust, and genuine intimacy among members, who can now risk honest feedback and self-disclosure. This contrasts with earlier phases of engagement and conflict and the eventual termination phase.
2018-220: Social anxiety disorder, long called social phobia, is marked by intense fear of scrutiny and humiliation in performance or interpersonal situations. It entered the DSM as a distinct diagnosis in DSM-III in 1980, partly through the work of Michael Liebowitz, whose Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale remains a standard measure. Often tracing to childhood behavioral inhibition, it is among the most common anxiety disorders and responds to SSRIs and cognitive-behavioral therapy.
2018-221: Broca's aphasia is named for French physician Paul Broca, who in 1861 described a patient nicknamed 'Tan'—the only syllable the man could utter—and on autopsy localized the lesion to the left posterior inferior frontal gyrus. The hallmark is nonfluent, effortful, agrammatic speech with relatively preserved comprehension but impaired repetition. Broca's report was a landmark establishing cerebral localization of language and the dominance of the left hemisphere.
2018-222: Erotic transference and the therapist's reciprocal countertransference were central preoccupations of Freud, who in his 1915 paper 'Observations on Transference-Love' warned analysts not to gratify or dismiss the patient's love but to treat it as analytic material. The modern professional-ethics answer is supervision or consultation: seeking an outside colleague's perspective protects the patient, preserves the frame, and is the recognized first step when a clinician notices boundary-threatening feelings.
2018-223: In a crossover design each subject receives both the intervention and control in sequence, serving as their own control to reduce between-subject variance. The principal threat is the carryover or residual effect, where the first treatment's influence lingers into the second period and contaminates results. Researchers guard against this with a 'washout' period between phases, long enough for the drug or its biological effect to clear before the crossover begins.
2018-224: This describes the lateral orbitofrontal cortico-striato-thalamic loop, one of the five parallel frontal-subcortical circuits delineated by Alexander, DeLong, and Strick in their influential 1986 work. The lateral orbitofrontal circuit is tied to response inhibition and behavioral regulation; its disruption produces disinhibition, impulsivity, and personality change. The classic clinical illustration is Phineas Gage, whose orbitofrontal injury famously transformed his social conduct.
2018-225: Schizotypal personality disorder sits within the genetic 'schizophrenia spectrum,' and relatives of people with schizophrenia show elevated rates of it, as demonstrated in the Danish adoption studies of Seymour Kety, David Rosenthal, and colleagues in the 1960s-70s. The term 'schizotype,' a contraction of 'schizophrenic phenotype,' was coined by Sandor Rado. DSM-III placed it among personality disorders, but its biological link to psychosis remains well established.
2018-226: The Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale was developed by John Overall and Donald Gorham in 1962 and is a clinician-administered instrument, scored by an interviewer rating items such as hostility, suspiciousness, and conceptual disorganization. It became a foundational outcome measure in antipsychotic trials. This contrasts with the SCL-90, MMPI, and Millon inventories, which are patient self-report measures completed without a clinician's observational rating.
2018-227: Pain control is consistently the dominant fear among dying patients and a defining element of a 'bad death,' a concern that catalyzed the modern hospice and palliative care movements. Cicely Saunders, who founded St. Christopher's Hospice in London in 1967, coined the concept of 'total pain'—physical, emotional, social, and spiritual—and championed the principle that no one should die in unrelieved agony, reframing aggressive symptom control as a medical and ethical duty.
2018-228: Depression is the most common neuropsychiatric symptom in mild neurocognitive disorder (mild cognitive impairment) and frequently precedes or accompanies the earliest cognitive decline. The construct of MCI as a transitional state between normal aging and dementia was popularized by Ronald Petersen and colleagues at Mayo Clinic in the 1990s. Late-life depression is now recognized as both a risk factor for and an early manifestation of neurodegenerative disease.
2018-229: Core body temperature follows a robust circadian rhythm driven by the suprachiasmatic nucleus, reaching its nadir in the early morning hours, roughly two hours before habitual waking, precisely when melatonin peaks and sleepiness is greatest. This inverse coupling of falling temperature and rising melatonin is central to Alexander Borbely's two-process model of sleep regulation and explains why the body's thermal minimum aligns with maximal drowsiness.
2018-23: Frontotemporal dementia, historically called Pick's disease after Arnold Pick described it in 1892, classically strikes before age 65 with personality change, disinhibition, loss of empathy, and behavioral compulsions while memory stays relatively spared early on, a profile that distinguishes it from Alzheimer's. Pathology shows tau or TDP-43 inclusions in frontal and temporal lobes. The behavioral variant's striking social and language deficits often get mistaken for primary psychiatric illness.
2018-230: This scenario fails because coercion vitiates informed consent: a 'voluntary' admission obtained through threat is not truly voluntary. Informed consent doctrine in American medicine crystallized in cases like Canterbury v. Spence (1972), which established that consent must be knowing and free of duress. Genuinely voluntary status also confers patient rights regarding discharge, so a threat-driven 'choice' between voluntary and involuntary admission is legally and ethically hollow.
2018-231: Intellectual disability requires deficits in both intellectual functioning and adaptive behavior—a two-pronged definition emphasized since DSM-5 deemphasized IQ alone. The Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales, first published by Sara Sparrow and colleagues in 1984 and descended from Edgar Doll's 1930s Vineland Social Maturity Scale, assess conceptual, social, and practical skills, supplying the adaptive-functioning piece that an IQ test cannot provide.
2018-232: The candidate gene approach tests pre-selected genes hypothesized from biology, but its low prior probability of any single gene being truly causal, combined with small samples and multiple comparisons, yielded a notorious epidemic of false positives in psychiatric genetics during the 1990s and 2000s. Most candidate gene findings failed to replicate, prompting the field's shift to hypothesis-free, genome-wide association studies with stringent significance thresholds.
2018-233: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis was first characterized by Josep Dalmau and colleagues in 2007, who linked the syndrome to antibodies against the NR1 subunit of the receptor. In young women it is strongly associated with ovarian teratomas, which express neural tissue that triggers the autoimmune response, so tumor removal plus immunotherapy is curative. The EEG finding of 'extreme delta brush' is a distinctive, almost pathognomonic marker described in this disorder.
2018-234: A physician-patient relationship—and the duty of care it imposes—forms when the doctor undertakes to diagnose or treat. Curbside referrals or general information typically do not create it, but giving specific, individualized treatment advice, such as endorsing a medication dose change, does. This distinction underlies countless malpractice rulings and is why physicians are cautioned that 'informal' clinical advice to friends can carry the full weight of a treatment relationship.
2018-235: Power analysis estimates the sample size needed to detect an effect of a given magnitude, where statistical power is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis, conventionally targeted at 0.80. The framework grew from Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson's hypothesis-testing theory, and Jacob Cohen's 1969 handbook on power analysis for the behavioral sciences made it standard practice, popularizing the now-ubiquitous effect-size conventions of small, medium, and large.
2018-236: The arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus is the principal integrator of energy-balance signals, sitting near the median eminence where the blood-brain barrier is permeable so it can sense circulating leptin, insulin, ghrelin, and nutrients. It contains the opposing orexigenic AgRP/NPY neurons and anorexigenic POMC neurons. Leptin's discovery in 1994 by Jeffrey Friedman's lab illuminated how peripheral fat stores signal this hub to regulate appetite.
2018-237: In supportive psychotherapy, unlike psychodynamic work, a positive transference is generally left uninterpreted and instead harnessed to bolster the therapeutic alliance and the patient's functioning. This approach was systematized by clinicians such as Arnold Winston and Richard Rosenthal, who framed supportive therapy as deliberately fostering a benign, ego-supportive relationship rather than excavating its unconscious roots, making it well suited to patients with fragile ego strength.
2018-238: SSRIs such as sertraline can cause hyponatremia through the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, especially in older adults, and the resulting low sodium produces a waxing-and-waning delirium with impaired alertness and memory. Checking serum electrolytes is the key first step. SSRI-induced SIADH is a well-documented adverse effect that disproportionately affects the elderly, sometimes within the first weeks of treatment.
2018-239: Aging fragments sleep: older adults show more frequent nighttime awakenings, reduced slow-wave (deep) sleep, advanced sleep phase, and a flattened circadian amplitude. These changes track with age-related neuronal loss in circadian and sleep-regulating centers, including the suprachiasmatic nucleus. The increased arousals and lighter sleep architecture, rather than a reduced biological need for sleep, largely explain the common complaint of poor sleep quality in later life.
2018-24: Heart rate variability, the beat-to-beat fluctuation in heart rate, is a prized biofeedback marker because it reflects the dynamic balance between sympathetic and parasympathetic input, largely via vagal tone. High HRV signals a flexible, well-regulated autonomic system. HRV biofeedback teaches patients to breathe at their resonance frequency (around six breaths per minute) to amplify this variability and dial down stress arousal.
2018-240: The radial nerve winds around the spiral groove of the humerus, where prolonged compression—classically by draping the arm over a chair or bench while intoxicated—causes 'Saturday night palsy.' The result is wrist drop with weak finger and wrist extension but preserved grip, since the flexors are median- and ulnar-supplied. The colorful name reflects its association with passing out drunk against a hard surface.
2018-241: Epigenetics refers to heritable changes in gene expression not encoded in the DNA sequence itself, mediated by mechanisms such as DNA methylation and histone modification. The term was coined by developmental biologist Conrad Waddington in the 1940s, who envisioned an 'epigenetic landscape' channeling cell fate. Its psychiatric relevance exploded after studies, such as work on maternal care in rats, showed early experience can durably alter gene expression.
2018-242: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder requires symptoms confined to the final week of the luteal phase that remit shortly after menses onset and are minimal in the follicular phase—the temporal pattern is the defining feature. After decades in the appendix as 'late luteal phase dysphoric disorder,' PMDD became a full diagnosis in DSM-5 in 2013, a move that drew debate over medicalizing menstruation but reflected robust evidence of a discrete, treatable condition.
2018-243: Erik Erikson, a German-born analyst trained by Anna Freud, extended Freud's psychosexual model into eight lifelong psychosocial stages in his 1950 book Childhood and Society, each framed as a developmental crisis (trust vs. mistrust, identity vs. role confusion, and so on). Erikson coined the phrase 'identity crisis,' and notably never earned a formal college degree yet later taught at Harvard.
2018-244: Incidence captures new cases arising over a period, distinguishing it from prevalence, which counts all existing cases at a point. A classic teaching image is the 'bathtub': incidence is the water flowing in from the faucet (new cases), while prevalence is the standing water level. Incidence is the key measure when studying causation and risk over time.
2018-245: Jean Piaget's concrete operational stage (roughly ages 7 to 11) is when children master conservation, the understanding that quantity, mass, and volume persist despite changes in appearance. Piaget famously demonstrated this by pouring water between tall and wide glasses; younger preoperational children insist the taller glass holds more. The Swiss psychologist began studying children's reasoning after scoring intelligence tests and noticing patterns in their wrong answers.
2018-246: Glucocorticoid receptors belong to the nuclear receptor superfamily: lipophilic steroids cross the cell membrane, bind cytoplasmic receptors, and the complex translocates to the nucleus to act as a transcription factor. This is why steroid effects are comparatively slow, requiring gene transcription rather than the millisecond responses of ion channels. Elwood Jensen's identification of the estrogen receptor in the 1960s opened this entire receptor field.
2018-247: Buspirone, a 5-HT1A partial agonist marketed as BuSpar in the 1980s, is prized for anxiety in pulmonary patients because, unlike benzodiazepines, it lacks respiratory depression and sedation. Its azapirone structure was an accidental discovery while researchers sought antipsychotics. The tradeoff is a slow onset of weeks, making it useless for acute panic but safe for chronic generalized anxiety.
2018-248: The Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act of 2008 built on the weaker 1996 parity law and required that insurers offering mental health and substance use benefits make their financial requirements and treatment limits no more restrictive than for medical and surgical care. Its passage was championed by Senators Pete Domenici and the late Paul Wellstone, both personally touched by mental illness in their families.
2018-249: Theory of mind, the grasp that others hold beliefs different from one's own, typically consolidates around age four, the point at which children reliably pass false-belief tasks. The classic 'Sally-Anne' test was devised by Baron-Cohen, Leslie, and Frith in 1985 to probe this capacity in autism. The phrase 'theory of mind' itself was coined by primatologists Premack and Woodruff in a 1978 chimpanzee study.
2018-25: Symbolic play, in which one object stands in for another, a wooden block becomes a train, emerges in the second year and signals the dawning capacity for mental representation. Jean Piaget saw such pretend play as a hallmark of the transition into the preoperational stage, evidence the toddler can hold an idea apart from the concrete object. It is also closely tied to early language, since both rest on symbol use.
2018-250: Rett syndrome, caused by mutations in the X-linked MECP2 gene, was described by Austrian pediatrician Andreas Rett in 1966 after he noticed two girls in his waiting room making identical hand-wringing movements. The characteristic regression with stereotyped hand movements almost exclusively affects girls, since affected males typically do not survive. Huda Zoghbi's lab identified MECP2 as the cause in 1999.
2018-251: Lithium clearance rises sharply during pregnancy as glomerular filtration and plasma volume expand, then plummets back toward baseline immediately after delivery. If the gestational dose is not reduced postpartum, levels can climb into toxic range within days, compounded by fluid shifts and blood loss. This makes close serum monitoring around delivery essential. Lithium was the first mood stabilizer, introduced by John Cade in 1949.
2018-252: Dissociative amnesia is distinguished by selective, often retrograde memory loss confined to specific traumatic or stressful episodes, with intact procedural memory and learning ability, unlike the global, anterograde-predominant deficits of organic amnesia. The dramatic subtype, dissociative fugue, involves unexpected travel and identity confusion. The concept traces to Pierre Janet and Freud's late-19th-century work on traumatic memory and 'splitting' of consciousness.
2018-253: Schwann cells myelinate the peripheral nervous system, each wrapping a single axon segment, whereas oligodendrocytes serve the CNS and can myelinate many axons at once. They are named for Theodor Schwann, the 19th-century German physiologist who, with Matthias Schleiden, formulated cell theory and also coined the term 'metabolism.' Schwann cells are the source of the benign tumors called schwannomas, such as acoustic neuromas.
2018-254: Corticosteroids characteristically amplify physiological tremor, the fine, fast, 8-to-12-Hz oscillation everyone has, alongside beta-agonists, lithium, valproate, caffeine, and thyroid hormone. The mechanism is thought to involve peripheral beta-adrenergic sensitization of muscle spindles, which is why beta-blockers like propranolol suppress enhanced physiological and essential tremor. Distinguishing this from intention or resting tremor is a frequent clinical task.
2018-255: Core gender identity, the inner sense of being male or female, is generally established by about age three, a milestone emphasized by John Money and later developmental researchers. Money's controversial work, including the tragic David Reimer case, shaped and ultimately challenged mid-century assumptions about gender malleability. Gender identity is distinguished from gender role and sexual orientation, which develop along separate timelines.
2018-256: Face processing is anchored in the fusiform face area on the ventral occipitotemporal surface, identified by Nancy Kanwisher's group using fMRI in 1997. Damage here produces prosopagnosia, the inability to recognize faces, famously described by Oliver Sacks in 'The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat,' a condition Sacks himself had. The region's selectivity for faces remains a touchstone debate in cognitive neuroscience.
2018-257: The chi-square test, devised by Karl Pearson in 1900, evaluates whether observed frequencies across categories differ from expected, making it the standard tool for two dichotomous (categorical) variables arranged in a contingency table. Pearson, a founder of modern statistics and the Biometrika journal, also gave us the correlation coefficient. The Greek letter chi gives the test both its name and its symbol.
2018-258: Acute angle-closure glaucoma is the ocular emergency hiding behind 'thunderclap' headache with a red, painful eye, mid-dilated fixed pupil, and blurred vision; it is confirmed by tonometry showing markedly elevated intraocular pressure. Untreated, the pressure spike can destroy the optic nerve within hours. The drainage angle closes when the iris blocks the trabecular meshwork, often precipitated by dim light or anticholinergic drugs.
2018-259: Across resilience research, the single most robust protective factor for children facing adversity is a warm, competent relationship with a caregiver. Developmental psychologist Ann Masten captured this in her phrase 'ordinary magic,' arguing resilience arises not from rare gifts but from basic, well-functioning human protective systems, chief among them good parenting and secure attachment.
2018-26: Depression is strikingly common in multiple sclerosis, affecting roughly half of patients over a lifetime, far above the rate in other chronic illnesses, suggesting the disease process itself, not just the psychological burden, drives it. Research links greater depression risk to lesion burden, particularly total lesion volume and lesions in regions like the frontal and temporal lobes, supporting an organic, demyelination-related contribution rather than purely reactive sadness.
2018-260: PACAP (pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide), isolated by Akira Arimura's group in 1989 from ovine hypothalamus, is a potent neurotrophic and anti-apoptotic peptide acting through cAMP-coupled receptors to protect neurons from injury. Beyond neuroprotection, PACAP has drawn intense interest as a migraine trigger, since infusing it provokes attacks, making its receptor a target for new headache therapeutics.
2018-261: The Conners Continuous Performance Test measures sustained attention and impulsivity by having the examinee respond to frequent targets while inhibiting responses to rare non-targets, generating metrics like omission and commission errors. Continuous performance paradigms date to Rosvold and colleagues in 1956. The test is widely used in ADHD assessment, though it supplements rather than replaces clinical diagnosis.
2018-262: Persuasion grounded in social psychology works best when a new behavior is framed as consistent with the audience's existing values and group identity rather than by piling on facts. Confronting people with corrective data can trigger the 'backfire effect,' hardening original beliefs. This value-congruence and self-affirmation approach draws on Festinger's cognitive dissonance theory and Claude Steele's work on self-affirmation.
2018-263: Decentration, a Piagetian concept, is the ability to consider multiple aspects of a situation at once rather than fixating on a single, self-referential dimension. The young child's egocentric belief that he caused his parents' divorce reflects centration; recognizing external causes signals decentration, a hallmark of the concrete operational stage. The same cognitive shift underlies success on conservation tasks.
2018-264: The nucleus accumbens, part of the ventral striatum, is the central hub of the mesolimbic dopamine reward pathway and is most consistently tied to alcohol's rewarding effects. James Olds and Peter Milner's 1954 intracranial self-stimulation experiments in rats first localized brain 'pleasure centers' to this circuitry, launching the modern neuroscience of reward and addiction.
2018-265: Akathisia, the agonizing inner restlessness and inability to sit still, is most strongly precipitated by rapid dose escalation and high-potency dopamine blockers. The term was coined in 1901 by Czech neuropsychiatrist Ladislav Haskovec, from Greek meaning 'inability to sit.' It is notoriously underrecognized and has been linked to distress and suicidality, making slow titration the key preventive strategy.
