With a guarded or mandated patient, defining the frame reduces defensiveness and conveys respect for autonomy, contrasting sharply with coercive or confrontational openings that tend to harden resistance.
2020-199: A case-control study starts by selecting subjects on the basis of outcome—cases who already have the disease and controls who do not—then looks backward at exposures, making it efficient for rare diseases. The design's power was famously shown by Doll and Hill's 1950 case-control study linking smoking to lung cancer, and it yields odds ratios rather than the relative risk obtainable from cohort designs.
2020-2: Erik Erikson's seventh stage, generativity versus stagnation, spans middle adulthood (roughly 40-65) and centers on contributing to and guiding the next generation through parenting, mentoring, and productive work. Erikson, who himself coined the term "identity crisis," laid out his eight psychosocial stages in Childhood and Society (1950). Feeling useful to future generations is the hallmark of successfully resolving this midlife task.
2020-20: Operant conditioning, formalized by B.F. Skinner in the 1930s, explains behavior shaped by its consequences rather than by reflex pairing. Here each purchase produces an immediate mood lift, a positive reinforcement that strengthens the buying behavior. Skinner built on Edward Thorndike's earlier 'law of effect' (1898), which held that rewarded behaviors are stamped in, using his famous operant chamber ('Skinner box').
2020-200: Normalizing prefaces—framing a symptom as common before asking about it—lower the threat in eliciting sensitive or stigmatized material and are particularly useful with suspicious patients. Rapport with paranoid patients also rests on respecting interpersonal distance, avoiding excessive warmth or unbroken eye contact that can feel intrusive, and not directly challenging delusions, principles long emphasized in psychiatric interviewing texts.
2020-201: Social learning theory, advanced by Albert Bandura, holds that gender-typed behavior is acquired through observation, modeling, and reinforcement rather than innate drives or fixed cognitive stages. Bandura's 1961 Bobo doll experiments showed children imitate observed behavior, and applied to psychosexual development the theory attributes a girl's identification with feminine roles to modeling of the same-sex parent.
2020-202: Wait—correcting the framing: a case-control study selects participants by known outcome, whereas the design described here that follows groups defined by exposure forward in time is a cohort study. Cohort studies, exemplified by the Framingham Heart Study begun in 1948, measure incidence and relative risk directly and are the standard for establishing temporal sequence between exposure and disease.
2020-203: The zone of proximal development is Lev Vygotsky's signature concept: the gap between what a child can do alone and what they can achieve with guidance from a more capable other. The Russian psychologist, who died of tuberculosis in 1934 at age 37, argued that learning leads development and is fundamentally social; scaffolding—matching tasks to this zone—remains central to educational and developmental practice.
2020-204: Before puberty, major depressive disorder occurs at roughly equal rates in boys and girls; the well-known female preponderance emerges only in adolescence, around the time of puberty. This shift, observed consistently in epidemiologic studies since the 1990s, is attributed to a mix of hormonal, social, and stress-reactivity changes and is a frequently tested developmental fact in child psychiatry.
2020-205: The American Medical Association's professionalism guidance on social media, issued around 2010-2011, advises physicians to maintain professional boundaries online, use privacy settings, separate personal and professional identities, and document patient-relevant electronic communication in the medical record. The guidance arose as social media's blurring of personal and professional life created novel ethical and confidentiality challenges for clinicians.
2020-206: Association analysis tests whether particular genetic variants occur more often in affected individuals, making it suited to common diseases driven by many common variants of small effect—the common disease, common variant hypothesis. Unlike linkage analysis, which tracks co-inheritance within families and excels at rare high-penetrance mutations, association methods underlie the population-scale hunt for the modest genetic contributions typical of psychiatric disorders.
2020-207: Rett syndrome is the textbook example of an epigenetically mediated disorder: it is caused by mutations in MECP2 on the X chromosome, encoding methyl-CpG-binding protein 2, which reads DNA methylation marks to regulate gene transcription. Described by Andreas Rett in 1966 and brought to wide attention by Hagberg in 1983, it causes regression after normal early development, with the hallmark loss of purposeful hand use and stereotypic hand-wringing.
2020-208: Rett syndrome's link to MECP2, identified by Huda Zoghbi and colleagues in 1999, made it a model for how disrupting the machinery that interprets epigenetic marks—DNA methylation—can devastate brain development. By contrast, the distractor conditions are structural or single-gene defects: Williams (7q11.23 deletion), cri-du-chat (5p deletion), Lesch-Nyhan (HPRT mutation), and Cornelia de Lange (usually NIPBL, a cohesin-pathway gene).
2020-209: Autism shows among the highest monozygotic twin concordance rates of any neurodevelopmental condition, with classic studies and later estimates often cited in the 80-90 percent range when broader phenotypes are counted, far exceeding dizygotic rates. The first systematic autism twin study, by Folstein and Rutter in 1977, overturned the prevailing psychogenic refrigerator-mother theory by demonstrating a strong genetic basis.
2020-21: The orbitofrontal circuit, one of the frontal-subcortical loops mapped by Alexander, DeLong, and Strick in 1986, links orbitofrontal cortex through the caudate, globus pallidus, and thalamus. Damage to this loop classically produces disinhibition, impulsivity, and irritability, the inability to restrain hostile responses. The case of Phineas Gage (1848), whose tamping iron destroyed orbitofrontal tissue, is the historical emblem of this syndrome.
2020-210: The WHO's Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP), launched in 2008, addresses the vast treatment gap in low- and middle-income countries by task-shifting: training non-specialist primary-care and community workers to identify and manage priority mental, neurological, and substance-use conditions. The strategy responds to a severe scarcity of psychiatrists in these settings, where building specialist workforces alone could never meet need.
2020-211: Panic disorder is defined not by a single attack but by recurrent, unexpected panic attacks plus persistent worry about further attacks or maladaptive behavior change. DSM-5 notably separated panic disorder from agoraphobia, which had been linked since DSM-III in 1980. The out-of-the-blue, uncued quality of the attacks is the diagnostic key distinguishing panic disorder from situationally bound fears.
2020-212: The two pillars of a sound rating scale are reliability (consistency of measurement) and validity (whether it measures what it claims to). Validity itself has long been subdivided—content, criterion, and construct validity—a framework crystallized by Cronbach and Meehl in their influential 1955 paper. A scale can be highly reliable yet invalid, like a precise instrument calibrated to the wrong target.
2020-213: Electromyography (EMG) records the electrical potentials generated by muscle fibers, and biofeedback pioneers in the 1960s and 1970s used surface EMG to teach patients to consciously relax tense muscles. The term derives from the Greek 'mys' (muscle) plus 'graphein' (to write). EMG biofeedback became a mainstay for tension headache and chronic pain, distinguishing it from skin-conductance (GSR), thermal, and EEG-based modalities.
2020-214: Beneficence, the duty to act for the patient's good, is the principle invoked to justify paternalism, in which a clinician overrides a patient's preferences for their welfare. The framework of beneficence, nonmaleficence, autonomy, and justice was crystallized by Tom Beauchamp and James Childress in their 1979 'Principles of Biomedical Ethics.' The word 'paternalism' itself evokes a parent acting in a child's best interest.
2020-215: Functional imaging in PTSD classically shows an overactive amygdala paired with hypoactive ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), which normally dampens fear responses. This 'top-down failure' model, advanced by researchers such as Lisa Shin and Roger Pitman in the 1990s and 2000s, frames PTSD as the prefrontal cortex losing its ability to brake the fear circuitry, leaving the amygdala disinhibited.
2020-216: Prosody, the melody and rhythm of speech, is frequently disturbed in autism, producing flat, sing-song, or robotic intonation. The word comes from the Greek 'prosoidia,' a song sung to music. Hans Asperger and Leo Kanner both noted odd vocal quality in their original 1940s descriptions, and impaired prosody remains a hallmark distinguishing autistic speech from the fluent grammar and vocabulary often otherwise intact.
2020-217: Sydenham chorea, the writhing movement disorder following group A streptococcal infection, is a major criterion of acute rheumatic fever. It is named for Thomas Sydenham, the 17th-century 'English Hippocrates,' and was historically called 'St. Vitus' dance.' The chorea reflects autoantibodies cross-reacting with basal ganglia, the same molecular-mimicry mechanism implicated in PANDAS.
2020-218: Implicit (nondeclarative) memory operates without conscious awareness and builds generalized mental models from repeated experience, in contrast to explicit memory's discrete recollection. Daniel Schacter and others popularized the implicit/explicit distinction in the 1980s. In attachment and developmental theory, these implicit schemas, present from infancy, underlie procedural learning and emotional 'gut' expectations that summate across many encounters.
2020-219: An advance health care directive lets a patient document treatment wishes and appoint a surrogate before losing capacity. The modern movement grew from the 1990 Patient Self-Determination Act and landmark cases like Karen Ann Quinlan and Nancy Cruzan, which forced courts to grapple with who decides for the incapacitated. Checking for an existing directive is the appropriate first step before pursuing courts or guardianship.
2020-22: The Collaborative Care Model was developed largely by Wayne Katon and Jürgen Unützer at the University of Washington, validated in trials such as IMPACT (2002) for late-life depression. Its measurement-based, team approach hinges on a care manager who coordinates between the primary care provider and a consulting psychiatrist, tracks outcomes with tools like the PHQ-9, and adjusts treatment to target.
2020-220: In postmenopausal women, declining testosterone, not estrogen, is the key physiologic driver of low sexual desire. Although the ovaries and adrenals make androgens, levels fall roughly by half between a woman's twenties and forties. This insight drove research into transdermal testosterone for hypoactive sexual desire disorder, reframing libido as androgen-dependent in both sexes.
2020-221: Orexin (also called hypocretin) neurons cluster in the lateral hypothalamus and stabilize wakefulness. They were independently discovered in 1998 by two groups, hence the two names, and their loss was soon shown to cause narcolepsy with cataplexy. This discovery transformed sleep medicine and spawned a new drug class, the orexin-receptor antagonists ('-orexants') for insomnia.
2020-222: The U.S. incarceration boom is largely attributed to mandatory minimum sentencing for drug offenses, codified in the Anti-Drug Abuse Act of 1986 amid the 'War on Drugs' and crack-cocaine panic. These laws stripped judicial discretion, and the prison population quadrupled over the following decades, a phenomenon Michelle Alexander later analyzed in 'The New Jim Crow.'
2020-223: Aging sleep is marked by decreased REM and slow-wave (Stage 3/4) sleep, more fragmented arousals, and earlier circadian timing. Nathaniel Kleitman and Eugene Aserinsky discovered REM sleep in 1953 at the University of Chicago; subsequent longitudinal studies mapped its gradual decline across the lifespan, contributing to the lighter, more interrupted sleep typical of late life.
2020-224: The brief, excruciating retro-orbital attacks with autonomic features describe cluster headache, and verapamil is the first-line preventive. Cluster headache earned the nickname 'suicide headache' for its severity and the cyclical 'clustering' that gives it its name. Verapamil, a calcium-channel blocker, became the prophylactic mainstay despite the need for ECG monitoring of its cardiac conduction effects.
2020-225: In the Global Burden of Disease studies, depressive disorders consistently top the list of psychiatric contributors to disability-adjusted life years. The DALY metric, combining years lost to death and disability, was introduced in the original 1990 GBD project led by Christopher Murray and Alan Lopez for the World Bank, and helped reframe depression as a leading global cause of disability.
2020-226: Reliability refers to consistency, including agreement among different raters (inter-rater reliability), and is distinct from validity, which concerns accuracy against truth. Jacob Cohen formalized the kappa statistic in 1960 to quantify rater agreement beyond chance. A classic teaching analogy: reliability is hitting the same spot repeatedly, while validity is hitting the bullseye.
2020-227: Bright light therapy is first-line for seasonal affective disorder, a condition named and described by Norman Rosenthal and colleagues at the NIMH in 1984. Rosenthal, who noticed his own winter mood dips after emigrating from sunny South Africa, pioneered light boxes delivering around 10,000 lux, which suppress melatonin and shift circadian phase to counter the winter pattern.
2020-228: Weakness predominantly affecting the contralateral leg points to an anterior cerebral artery (ACA) territory stroke, since the ACA supplies the medial motor cortex where the leg's homunculus resides. Wilder Penfield's mid-20th-century cortical stimulation mapping established this medial-to-lateral somatotopy, explaining why the leg, tucked in the interhemispheric fissure, is selectively affected.
2020-229: A delusion of reference is the false conviction that neutral events, like a TV broadcast, carry personal meaning aimed at oneself. The milder, non-delusional version is an 'idea of reference.' These concepts were elaborated in classic German descriptive psychopathology and remain core to the phenomenology of psychosis distinguishing them from passivity phenomena like thought insertion or broadcasting.
2020-23: The defining feature of delirium is its fluctuating course, waxing and waning over hours. Lipowski's classic descriptions and the DSM emphasize this hallmark, captured in the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM), developed by Sharon Inouye in 1990, which requires both acute onset/fluctuation and inattention. Lucid speech at one exam and disorganized speech hours later is the signature pattern distinguishing delirium from stable dementia.
2020-230: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus, sitting just above the optic chiasm, is the master circadian pacemaker. Lesion studies in rodents in the 1970s abolished circadian rhythms, pinpointing the SCN. It receives light input via the retinohypothalamic tract and entrains the body to the day-night cycle, work that fed into the 2017 Nobel Prize for circadian 'clock genes.'
2020-231: DHEA, an adrenal steroid, diffuses across cell membranes after synthesis rather than being packaged in secretory vesicles, a feature of all steroid hormones, which are lipophilic. This contrasts with peptide hormones like ACTH, LH, and FSH, which are stored in vesicles and released by exocytosis. DHEA is the most abundant circulating steroid and a precursor to sex hormones.
2020-232: Shenjing shuairuo, literally 'weakness of the nerves' in Chinese, is the cultural concept most directly descended from neurasthenia. Neurasthenia itself was coined by American neurologist George Beard in 1869 to label nervous exhaustion. While Western psychiatry largely folded neurasthenia into depression and anxiety, the diagnosis persisted prominently in Chinese medicine, illustrating how illness categories travel and transform across cultures.
2020-233: In collaborative care, having clear policies for behavioral health emergencies is a key risk-management safeguard for the consulting psychiatrist. The collaborative care model, developed by Wayne Katon and Jürgen Unützel at the University of Washington (notably the IMPACT trial in the early 2000s), embeds psychiatric consultation in primary care, raising novel liability questions around indirect, population-based care.
2020-234: Developmental theory holds that the peer group becomes a significant mediator of aggression by late school age, around 10, when belonging and status among peers intensify, particularly for vulnerable boys. This staging reflects psychosocial frameworks tracing how the locus of social influence shifts from family in early childhood toward peers as children approach adolescence.
2020-235: Carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (CDT) is the most specific lab marker of sustained heavy drinking, rising when chronic alcohol disrupts the glycosylation of transferrin. Developed as a biomarker in the 1970s and 1980s, CDT outperforms GGT and the AST/ALT ratio in specificity, since liver enzymes elevate for many non-alcohol reasons, making CDT valuable for detecting relapse.
2020-236: The defining feature of collaborative care is a psychiatric consultant advising the primary care team, especially on patients not improving, rather than seeing patients directly. This 'stepped,' measurement-based model was validated by the IMPACT trial (Unützer et al., 2002), which showed markedly better depression outcomes in older primary care patients and became the template for integrated behavioral health.
2020-237: Ziprasidone's oral absorption roughly doubles when taken with food, requiring a meal of at least about 500 calories; fasting can cut absorption by half. This unusual food effect stems from the drug's lipophilicity and was a notable counseling point when ziprasidone (Geodon) launched, since erratic dosing on an empty stomach undermines efficacy without altering its favorable metabolic profile.
2020-238: The 'magnetic' gait, with feet seeming glued to the floor, is characteristic of normal pressure hydrocephalus, whose triad is gait disturbance, cognitive decline, and urinary incontinence (memorably 'wet, wacky, wobbly'). Salomón Hakim described the syndrome in 1965, noting that CSF removal could reverse symptoms, the rationale for the high-volume tap test and ventriculoperitoneal shunting.
2020-239: The Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act of 2008 prohibits insurers from imposing harsher limits on behavioral health benefits than on medical-surgical benefits. Building on an earlier 1996 parity law, it was championed in part by Senators Paul Wellstone and Pete Domenici, both touched personally by mental illness, and aimed to end discriminatory caps on psychiatric and addiction coverage.
2020-24: Evidence on involuntary outpatient commitment, notably the New York studies of Kendra's Law (enacted 1999) and the Duke randomized trial in North Carolina, found that court-ordered treatment reduced hospitalization mainly when paired with intensive services. Assertive Community Treatment, the wraparound team model pioneered by Stein and Test in Madison, Wisconsin in the 1970s, supplies that intensity, making it the key ingredient for effectiveness.
2020-240: REM sleep is paradoxically 'active,' featuring increased and variable heart rate, irregular respiration, and brain activity resembling wakefulness, alongside skeletal muscle atonia. Discovered by Aserinsky and Kleitman in 1953 and named 'paradoxical sleep' by Michel Jouvet, REM's autonomic surges explain its association with nocturnal cardiac events and vivid dreaming.
2020-241: Deletion of chromosome 17p11.2 causes Smith-Magenis syndrome, marked by a broad flat face that coarsens over time, brachydactyly, hoarse deep voice, and a striking inverted circadian melatonin rhythm with severe sleep disturbance and self-injurious behavior. It was delineated by Ann Smith and Ellen Magenis in the 1980s and involves loss of the RAI1 gene.
2020-242: CT of the posterior fossa is notoriously degraded by beam-hardening artifact from the dense surrounding skull base, the so-called Hounsfield artifact, named for CT inventor Godfrey Hounsfield, who shared the 1979 Nobel Prize. MRI, lacking bone-related X-ray artifact, far better visualizes the brainstem and cerebellum, making it the preferred modality for posterior fossa pathology.
2020-243: The ventral tegmental area to nucleus accumbens dopamine pathway is the mesolimbic reward circuit, mapped largely from Olds and Milner's 1954 discovery that rats would self-stimulate certain brain regions relentlessly. The VTA was named for its position in the ventral midbrain tegmentum. This dopaminergic 'final common pathway' is now central to how every drug of abuse, and behavioral addictions like gambling, hijack natural reward learning.
2020-244: Vagal nerve stimulation was FDA-approved for refractory epilepsy in 1997 and for treatment-resistant depression in 2005. Because the left vagus carries fibers influencing the larynx and airway, activation classically produces voice alteration, cough, and dyspnea during the stimulation 'on' cycle, along with neck tingling. The hoarseness/shortness-of-breath pattern keying off the stimulation cycle is the hallmark side effect to recognize.
2020-245: Medical malpractice rests on the 'four Ds': Duty, Dereliction (breach), Damages, and Direct causation. Abandonment claims fail if no actual harm (damages) occurred, since negligence without injury is not compensable. The doctrine traces to English common law's requirement of demonstrable harm; in psychiatry, proper termination requires notice, time to find new care, and bridging medication, but the strongest single defense is simply that the patient suffered no appreciable bad outcome.
2020-246: Rationalization, blaming the attending and techs rather than oneself, was catalogued among the ego defenses by Anna Freud in her 1936 work The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defense, building on her father Sigmund's concept. The term itself, offering self-serving but false 'reasons,' was popularized by British psychoanalyst Ernest Jones around 1908. It sits among the neurotic-level defenses in modern hierarchies.
2020-247: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency causes Wernicke encephalopathy, the classic triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia, described by Carl Wernicke in 1881. Bariatric surgery is a now-recognized cause, sometimes producing it within weeks. The teaching mantra is to give thiamine before glucose, since a carbohydrate load in a deficient patient can precipitate or worsen Wernicke's, a lesson learned from refeeding catastrophes.
2020-248: Catatonia was first described by Karl Kahlbaum in 1874 as 'die Katatonie,' the tension insanity. The dramatic responsiveness of catatonia to benzodiazepines like lorazepam, often within minutes (the 'lorazepam challenge'), is a striking clinical pearl; if that fails, ECT is highly effective. DSM-5 reclassified catatonia so it can be specified across mood, psychotic, and medical conditions rather than being tied to schizophrenia.
2020-249: The discovery that adult human brains generate new neurons in the hippocampal dentate gyrus overturned a century-old dogma that we are born with all the neurons we will ever have. Fred Gage and Peter Eriksson's landmark 1998 study used BrdU labeling in cancer patients to show adult human hippocampal neurogenesis, linking it to learning, memory, and the action of antidepressants.
2020-25: Projection, attributing one's own unacceptable impulses to others, is the defense underlying persecutory thinking: inner hostility is disowned and experienced as coming from outside. Freud detailed projection in his analysis of the Schreber case (1911), arguing paranoia arises when forbidden feelings are externalized. It sits among the immature defenses in George Vaillant's hierarchy.
2020-250: Cerebellar Purkinje cells, named for Czech anatomist Jan Evangelista Purkinje who described them in 1837, are the sole output of the cerebellar cortex and are uniformly GABAergic, inhibiting the deep cerebellar nuclei. Their enormous, elaborately branched dendritic trees were drawn famously by Ramon y Cajal. This inhibitory output is the cerebellum's mechanism for fine-tuning movement.
2020-251: Oxytocin, the 'bonding hormone' synthesized in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary, was first isolated and synthesized by Vincent du Vigneaud, earning the 1955 Nobel Prize in Chemistry as the first peptide hormone sequenced. Beyond labor and lactation, intranasal oxytocin studies show it enhances reading of facial emotion and trust, fueling interest in social cognition and autism research.
2020-252: This is the Strange Situation, developed by Mary Ainsworth in the 1960s-70s to operationalize John Bowlby's attachment theory. The securely attached infant protests separation but is readily soothed on reunion, using the caregiver as a 'secure base.' Ainsworth's Baltimore and earlier Uganda observations distinguished secure from avoidant and ambivalent patterns; Mary Main later added the disorganized category.
2020-253: Resilience, the capacity to adapt and recover from adversity, has consistently correlated with spirituality and religious involvement in geriatric research, much of it associated with Harold Koenig and the Duke center on religion, spirituality and health. The construct of resilience itself was crystallized in developmental work by Emmy Werner's decades-long Kauai longitudinal study of at-risk children who thrived.
2020-254: The hyperactive cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) loop, with elevated metabolism in orbitofrontal cortex, caudate, and thalamus, is the signature neuroimaging finding in OCD, demonstrated in PET studies by Lewis Baxter and colleagues in the late 1980s. Strikingly, both SSRIs and behavior therapy normalize this circuit, and the loop is the target of modern deep brain stimulation for refractory OCD.
2020-255: The uncinate fasciculus is a hook-shaped white matter tract, its Latin name meaning 'hooked,' connecting the anterior temporal lobe to the orbitofrontal cortex. It is one of the last tracts to mature, not fully myelinating until the third decade, and abnormalities are implicated in psychopathy, anxiety, and semantic dementia. It links memory and emotional limbic regions to inhibitory frontal control.
2020-256: Task-switching difficulty in healthy aging is increasingly traced to declines in basic attentional resources rather than a global executive collapse, reflecting the broader 'processing speed' and attention theories of cognitive aging associated with researchers like Timothy Salthouse. Limited attentional capacity makes disengaging from one set and reconfiguring for another costlier with age, even when overall executive ability is largely preserved.
2020-257: Quetiapine XR (as Seroquel XR) gained FDA approval in 2009 as adjunctive treatment for major depressive disorder, joining aripiprazole as an early atypical antipsychotic augmentation option. The antidepressant effect is attributed largely to its metabolite norquetiapine, a norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor and 5HT-2C blocker, distinguishing quetiapine's pharmacology from a simple dopamine blocker.
2020-258: The NMDA receptor is the molecular 'coincidence detector' of long-term potentiation, requiring both glutamate binding and postsynaptic depolarization to expel its magnesium block. LTP itself was discovered by Terje Lomo and Tim Bliss in the rabbit hippocampus around 1973, providing the cellular basis for Donald Hebb's 1949 rule that 'cells that fire together wire together.'
2020-259: Mirtazapine, a 'noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant,' blocks 5HT-3 receptors, the same receptor targeted by ondansetron, which explains why it causes less nausea than SSRIs and is sometimes used to stimulate appetite. Its 5HT-3 antagonism plus presynaptic alpha-2 blockade make it pharmacologically distinctive; the drug was developed in the Netherlands by Organon and reached the US market in 1996.
2020-26: Among theories of late-life social shrinkage, socioemotional selectivity theory (Laura Carstensen) holds that older adults actively prune networks toward emotionally meaningful ties. But the question targets an external constraint: physical disability and reduced mobility limit the ability to get out and maintain contacts. This contrasts with the older 'disengagement theory' of Cumming and Henry (1961), which controversially framed withdrawal as mutual and natural.
2020-260: This question turns on justice, the principle of fair distribution of benefits and burdens, one of the four pillars of biomedical ethics articulated by Tom Beauchamp and James Childress in their 1979 Principles of Biomedical Ethics. The 'cognitive enhancement for all' argument is fundamentally about equitable access, making it a justice claim rather than one of autonomy or beneficence.
2020-261: The habenula, Latin for 'little rein,' sits in the epithalamus and links the limbic system to midbrain monoamine nuclei. The lateral habenula has drawn intense interest as the brain's 'disappointment' or anti-reward center, firing when expected rewards fail to appear and suppressing dopamine neurons; its hyperactivity is now a candidate mechanism in depression and a deep brain stimulation target.
2020-262: DNA methylation, the addition of methyl groups to cytosine bases that typically silences genes without altering the underlying sequence, is the prototypical epigenetic mechanism. The term 'epigenetics' was coined by Conrad Waddington in the 1940s. In psychiatry, Michael Meaney's rat maternal-care studies showed that nurturing behavior alters methylation of the glucocorticoid receptor gene, embedding early experience into the genome.
2020-263: Limit setting maps onto Erik Erikson's second stage, autonomy versus shame and doubt (roughly ages one to three), when the toddler's drive for independence demands that parents establish boundaries. Margaret Mahler's separation-individuation framework similarly highlights the toddler 'practicing' and 'rapprochement' subphases, where the child tests limits while still needing a secure base.
2020-264: Nonfluent (Broca's) aphasia, described by Paul Broca in 1861 after his patient 'Tan' who could utter only that syllable, spares comprehension while impairing speech production and repetition. Broca localized it to the left inferior frontal gyrus, launching modern lesion-based neurology. The patient can follow simple commands like 'close your eyes' but speaks haltingly and cannot repeat well.
2020-265: The central nucleus of the amygdala is the output hub orchestrating fear's autonomic and behavioral expression, projecting to the hypothalamus and brainstem to produce freezing, blood pressure changes, and startle. Joseph LeDoux's rat fear-conditioning work in the 1980s-90s mapped this 'low road' circuit, showing sensory input reaching the amygdala can bypass the cortex for rapid threat response.
2020-266: Universality (here called universalization) is one of Irvin Yalom's eleven therapeutic factors of group psychotherapy, codified in his 1970 classic The Theory and Practice of Group Psychotherapy. It names the relief members feel on realizing 'I am not alone,' that others share the same fears and struggles, dissolving the isolating sense that one's problems are uniquely shameful.
2020-267: The Joint Commission, founded in 1951 as the Joint Commission on Accreditation of Hospitals, accredits and surveys US hospitals roughly every three years and sets care standards. It introduced the National Patient Safety Goals and the 'sentinel event' reporting system, becoming a driving force in the patient-safety movement spurred by the Institute of Medicine's 1999 report To Err Is Human.
2020-268: In somatic symptom disorder, persistence and poorer outcomes track with markers of disadvantage, including lower educational attainment, consistent with the long-standing observation that somatization is more entrenched where health literacy and resources are limited. DSM-5 reframed the old somatoform disorders in 2013 around excessive thoughts, feelings, and behaviors about symptoms rather than whether symptoms are 'medically unexplained.'
2020-269: Anandamide, the first endocannabinoid identified (by Raphael Mechoulam's group in 1992), is the brain's own ligand for the CB-1 receptor, the same receptor THC activates. Its name comes from the Sanskrit 'ananda,' meaning bliss or joy. CB-1, cloned in 1990, is among the most abundant G-protein-coupled receptors in the brain and mediates cannabis's psychoactive effects.
2020-27: The Transtheoretical (Stages of Change) Model was developed by James Prochaska and Carlo DiClemente in the late 1970s and early 1980s while studying how smokers quit. Preparation is the stage where a person intends to act soon and begins concrete steps, like gathering cessation resources, even before fully stopping. The model's stages range from precontemplation through maintenance.
2020-270: Tertiary prevention aims to reduce disability and restore function in those already established with disease, exactly what vocational rehabilitation does for schizophrenia. The primary/secondary/tertiary framework was popularized by Hugh Leavell and E. Gurney Clark in the 1950s; primary prevents onset, secondary catches disease early via screening, and tertiary limits the long-term impact of chronic illness.
2020-271: DSM-5's 2013 somatic symptom disorder deliberately broke from earlier somatoform diagnoses by no longer requiring that symptoms be 'medically unexplained'; instead the diagnosis hinges on disproportionate and persistent thoughts, anxiety, and behaviors devoted to the symptoms. This shift, championed in the criteria revision, lets patients with genuine medical illness still qualify when their psychological response is excessive.
2020-272: Postpartum psychosis, a psychiatric emergency emerging within days to weeks of delivery, is most strongly linked to bipolar disorder rather than schizophrenia, and a first episode often heralds an underlying bipolar diathesis. Historically termed 'puerperal insanity' in the 19th century by figures like Louis-Victor Marce, after whom the international perinatal psychiatry society is named, it carries elevated risks of suicide and infanticide.
2020-273: Expressed emotion (EE) emerged from British social psychiatry in the 1960s and 1970s, with George Brown and Julian Leff developing the Camberwell Family Interview to quantify a household's criticism, hostility, and emotional over-involvement. Their landmark finding was that schizophrenia patients returning to high-EE homes relapsed far more often than those in low-EE environments. The concept later proved predictive in mood disorders and eating disorders too, and it became a foundational rationale for family psychoeducation.
2020-274: Confidence intervals were pioneered by the Polish-American statistician Jerzy Neyman in the 1930s as part of his frequentist framework for statistical inference. A 95% CI does not mean a 95% probability the true value lies inside it; rather, 95% of such intervals computed from repeated samples would capture the true parameter. Their advantage over a bare p-value is conveying both effect magnitude and precision, which is why journals increasingly require them.
2020-275: Melatonin biosynthesis runs serotonin to N-acetylserotonin to melatonin, with the rate-limiting acetylation step occurring in the pineal gland under cover of darkness. Melatonin itself was isolated in 1958 by dermatologist Aaron Lerner, who named it for its ability to lighten frog skin (melanophore-contracting). The whole pathway begins with dietary tryptophan, making tryptophan to serotonin to melatonin a tidy chain to memorize.
2020-276: The frontal operculum overlies the insula and contains cortical representation for taste, salivation, and oropharyngeal motor function, so seizures there classically produce hypersalivation, chewing, and choking sensations. The term operculum is Latin for little lid, reflecting how these frontal, parietal, and temporal folds cover the buried insular cortex. Hughlings Jackson's nineteenth-century work on focal seizures established that symptom localization mirrors the cortical area discharging.
2020-277: Donald Winnicott, a British pediatrician-turned-analyst, coined good-enough mother (later good-enough parent) in the 1950s, arguing that perfect attunement is neither possible nor desirable. The caregiver's gradual, manageable failures let the infant tolerate frustration and discover its own separate self and drives. Winnicott also gave us the transitional object and the holding environment, all from his decades of observing mothers and babies in clinical practice.
2020-278: Family and twin studies consistently show that relatives of bipolar probands carry elevated risk not only for bipolar disorder but, even more commonly, for unipolar major depression, reflecting a shared genetic liability across the mood-disorder spectrum. This overlap is one reason clinicians scrutinize family history when a depressed patient may actually have an undiagnosed bipolar diathesis, since antidepressant monotherapy can risk a switch.
2020-279: Dialectical behavior therapy was created by Marsha Linehan in the late 1980s and 1990s for chronically suicidal patients with borderline personality disorder, blending behaviorism with Zen-inspired acceptance. Because emotion dysregulation underlies binge eating and bulimia, adapted DBT models targeting these behaviors have accumulated supportive evidence. Linehan later disclosed her own youthful psychiatric hospitalization, lending the therapy a striking lived-experience origin story.
2020-28: This is anticholinergic toxicity, classically remembered by the mnemonic 'hot as a hare, dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter.' Benztropine, an antimuscarinic given for drug-induced parkinsonism, can tip elderly patients into delirium with fever, dry mucosa, tachycardia, mydriasis, and hallucinations. The toxidrome reflects blockade of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors.
2020-280: The findings describe vestibular nystagmus: a slow drift away from a target with corrective fast saccades, suppressed by visual fixation, pointing to peripheral labyrinthine dysfunction. The word labyrinth dates to ancient anatomists who likened the inner ear's winding canals to the mythical Cretan maze. A key teaching pearl is that peripheral (labyrinthine) nystagmus is suppressed by fixation, whereas central nystagmus typically is not.
2020-281: Melanie Klein, working in 1920s Britain, founded object relations theory through her pioneering play technique with very young children, positing the paranoid-schizoid and depressive positions and inner part-objects. Her ideas sparked the famous Controversial Discussions with Anna Freud's camp at the British Psychoanalytical Society during World War II. Klein's emphasis on early internalized relationships influenced Fairbairn, Winnicott, and later attachment theory.
2020-282: Schizotypal personality disorder traces to Danish-American research on the Copenhagen adoption studies of schizophrenia, where Seymour Kety and colleagues noted milder schizophrenia-spectrum traits in biological relatives. The diagnosis entered DSM-III in 1980, capturing odd beliefs, magical thinking, and social aloofness short of psychosis. In ICD it is even classified within the schizophrenia spectrum rather than as a personality disorder, underscoring its genetic kinship to schizophrenia.
2020-283: GnRH-secreting neurons cluster in the infundibular (arcuate) nucleus of the hypothalamus, and puberty hinges on the reawakening of their pulsatile firing. A milestone was the discovery that kisspeptin and its receptor (KISS1/GPR54) gate this pulse generator; loss-of-function mutations cause hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Florence Comite and Ernst Knobil's primate work earlier showed that only pulsatile, not continuous, GnRH sustains gonadotropin release.
2020-284: This applies Winnicott's transitional object concept to pharmacotherapy: like a child's security blanket, the pill can symbolically preserve the patient's bond with the prescriber between appointments. The transitional object occupies an intermediate space between self and other, soothing separation. Clinicians invoke this to explain why some patients resist tapering an inert or minimally helpful medication, since stopping it feels like losing the relationship itself.
2020-285: Gender dysphoria replaced gender identity disorder in DSM-5 in 2013, a deliberate shift to locate the disorder in the distress, not in the gender identity itself, reducing stigma. The word dysphoria comes from Greek for hard to bear, the opposite of euphoria. This reframing paralleled the earlier depathologizing of homosexuality, removed from the DSM in 1973.
2020-286: The classic triple screen for Down syndrome combines maternal serum AFP, unconjugated estriol, and human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG); in trisomy 21 hCG is elevated while AFP and estriol are low. Adding inhibin A makes it the quad screen. These prenatal screens, refined through the 1980s and 1990s, allowed risk stratification before invasive amniocentesis and are now often supplanted by cell-free DNA testing.
2020-287: Research on intimate partner violence repeatedly identifies a perpetrator's own history of childhood abuse or witnessing parental violence as a leading correlate, consistent with social learning theory and the intergenerational transmission of violence. Lenore Walker's 1979 work on the cycle of violence helped frame the field. Notably, mental illness and intoxication are weaker predictors than this developmental exposure.
2020-288: Genomic imprinting describes parent-of-origin-specific gene silencing via epigenetic marks like DNA methylation, so a gene's expression depends on whether it came from mother or father. The dramatic clinical proof is that deletion of the same chromosome 15q region causes Prader-Willi syndrome when paternal but Angelman syndrome when maternal. The phenomenon was elucidated in the 1980s through mouse pronuclear transplantation experiments by Surani and by Solter.
2020-289: Intellectual disability is the single most common comorbidity of autism spectrum disorder, co-occurring in a substantial proportion of cases, though rates fall as broader, milder presentations are recognized. The pairing dates to Leo Kanner's original 1943 description of early infantile autism, when many of his cases showed cognitive impairment. Epilepsy and anxiety are also frequent, but intellectual disability remains the most strongly associated.
2020-29: Fetishistic disorder centers on sexual arousal to nonliving objects or specific non-genital body parts, behavior typically conducted privately and consensually, so it rarely brings legal trouble. The term derives from the Portuguese 'feitiço' (charm or sorcery) and was introduced into sexology by Alfred Binet in 1887. It contrasts with the inherently non-consensual paraphilias like exhibitionism and voyeurism that involve unsuspecting others.
2020-290: Histaminergic neurons in the brain are confined to the tuberomammillary nucleus of the posterior hypothalamus, from which they project widely to promote wakefulness and arousal. This explains why antihistamines that cross the blood-brain barrier cause sedation. The system was mapped in the 1980s using immunohistochemistry for histidine decarboxylase, the synthesizing enzyme, and it is a key target of the wake-promoting and orexin-related circuitry.
2020-291: Rapid return of alertness and orientation immediately after an episode favors psychogenic nonepileptic seizures, since true generalized tonic-clonic seizures are followed by a postictal confusional state. PNES, historically tied to the concept of hysteria and conversion, are now best confirmed by video-EEG monitoring showing no ictal epileptiform discharge. Features like prolonged duration, asynchronous movements, and preserved awareness also point toward the psychogenic diagnosis.
2020-292: Supportive psychotherapy, long dismissed as second-rate, was formalized as a legitimate evidence-informed modality whose explicit aim is bolstering self-esteem, ego function, and adaptive coping rather than fostering insight or transference interpretation. Its techniques grew out of psychodynamic theory, and figures like Arnold Winston helped codify it. It is the default modality for lower-functioning or acutely stressed patients who would be overwhelmed by uncovering work.
2020-293: Modern restraint practice descends from Philippe Pinel's symbolic unchaining of asylum patients in 1790s Paris and is now governed by strict CMS and Joint Commission rules: restraint is permissible only for imminent danger to self or others when less restrictive measures fail. Verbal threats or disruptive but nonviolent behavior do not qualify; active physical assault does. The doctrine of least restrictive intervention anchors this standard.
2020-294: Studies such as the Harvard Study of Moods and Cycles and the SWAN cohort suggest that it is the volatility, the rate and magnitude of estradiol fluctuation during perimenopause, rather than absolute low estrogen, that tracks with depressive episodes. This helps explain why perimenopause, with its erratic hormonal swings, carries higher depression risk than the more stable postmenopausal period.
2020-295: Transient global amnesia is a striking, self-limited syndrome of abrupt anterograde amnesia with repetitive questioning, intact identity, and no other neurologic deficit, resolving within about 24 hours. Named and characterized by Fisher and Adams in the 1950s and 1960s, it often follows physical exertion, emotional stress, or immersion in cold water. Diffusion MRI may show transient hippocampal lesions, and the prognosis is excellent.
2020-296: Fragile X syndrome, the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability, results from a CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome; over roughly 200 repeats silences the gene. The fragile site was visualized cytogenetically in the 1960s-70s as a constriction on the X, and FMR1 was cloned in 1991. It demonstrates anticipation, with repeats expanding across generations.
2020-297: In Pavlov's classical conditioning framework, the explosions are the unconditioned stimulus that innately triggers the fear response, while the shrill noise becomes the conditioned stimulus. Ivan Pavlov stumbled onto the paradigm around 1900 while studying salivation in dogs, winning the 1904 Nobel Prize for digestive physiology. The same model underlies the modern conditioning theory of PTSD and exposure-based treatments.
2020-298: STAR*D, launched in 2001 and led by A. John Rush, was the largest prospective trial of real-world depression treatment. To mimic clinical practice it used equipoise-stratified randomization letting patients exclude switch or augment options they found unacceptable, broadening generalizability. Its sobering bottom line was that cumulative remission required multiple treatment steps and roughly a third never remitted, reshaping expectations about antidepressant outcomes.
2020-299: Diffuse slowing of background rhythms, with increased theta and delta activity, is the EEG hallmark of metabolic or toxic encephalopathy and delirium, often correlating with severity. This generalized slowing distinguishes delirium from primary psychiatric disorders, which usually show a normal EEG. Engel and Romano demonstrated in the 1940s that delirium reflects diffuse cerebral insufficiency mirrored by EEG slowing, a foundational observation.
2020-3: Taste is unusual among the senses for having its primary cortex tucked deep inside the brain rather than on the surface. The anterior insula (with the adjacent frontal operculum) is the gustatory cortex, while the orbitofrontal cortex serves as a secondary, integrative taste area where flavor, smell, and reward converge. The insula was named by Johann Christian Reil around 1809 ('island of Reil'), reflecting how it sits hidden beneath the overlying opercula.
2020-30: Borderline personality disorder is marked by rapid mood shifts, impulsivity (spending, binge eating), and the splitting captured in early idealization ('the only one who listens'). The diagnosis entered DSM-III in 1980; the term traces to Adolf Stern (1938), who described patients on the 'borderline' between neurosis and psychosis. Marsha Linehan later developed dialectical behavior therapy specifically for it.
2020-300: Normal aging brings sleep fragmentation: more frequent and longer nocturnal awakenings, reduced slow-wave (deep) sleep, advanced sleep phase, and poorer subjective quality. Slow-wave sleep declines steadily from young adulthood, so increased awakenings is the change that increases. These architectural shifts, documented by polysomnography, partly explain the high prevalence of insomnia complaints among older adults.
2020-301: Duloxetine, gabapentin, and venlafaxine all outperform placebo for painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy independent of any antidepressant effect, acting through descending noradrenergic/serotonergic modulation (the SNRIs) or calcium-channel alpha-2-delta binding (gabapentin). Duloxetine and pregabalin hold FDA approval for this indication. The analgesic-at-lower-doses, mood-at-higher-doses distinction for SNRIs is a useful clinical pearl.
2020-31: Basilar migraine, described by Edwin Bickerstaff in the 1960s and once called basilar artery or Bickerstaff migraine, produces aura referable to the brainstem and occipital lobes: bilateral visual disturbance, vertigo, dysarthria, and perioral or limb paresthesias, followed by occipital headache. Now termed migraine with brainstem aura, it reflects spreading neuronal dysfunction rather than true vascular ischemia.
2020-32: This is optic neuritis: painful monocular vision loss, dyschromatopsia (faded colors), and a relative afferent pupillary defect, often the first manifestation of multiple sclerosis. The Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial, launched in the late 1980s, established its strong link to later MS and showed that oral prednisone alone was inappropriate. The afferent defect is also called a Marcus Gunn pupil.
2020-33: The principle that decision-making capacity must be assessed for a specific decision—rather than presumed absent because of a diagnosis like dementia—is rooted in the bioethics movement that followed cases like Karen Ann Quinlan and the 1982 President's Commission report. Capacity is task-specific and can fluctuate; the widely taught framework by Appelbaum and Grisso breaks it into four abilities: understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and communicating a choice. A diagnosis alone never settles the question.
2020-34: Dysdiadochokinesia comes from Greek roots meaning difficulty (dys) with successive (diadochos) movement (kinesis), describing impaired rapid alternating movements. It is a classic sign of cerebellar dysfunction, the cerebellum being responsible for the timing and coordination of agonist-antagonist muscle switching. The tongue-twisting term is itself a memorable bedside hook, and the rapid alternating palm-flip test is a staple of every neurological screening exam.
2020-35: This is the excitotoxicity hypothesis, a term coined by John Olney in the 1970s after he observed neurons dying when exposed to glutamate. Overactivation of NMDA receptors floods the cell with calcium, triggering mitochondrial dysfunction, caspase-mediated apoptosis, and necrosis. The concept underlies the rationale for memantine, an NMDA antagonist used in Alzheimer disease, and informs theories of stroke and neurodegenerative injury.
2020-36: Illness anxiety disorder debuted in DSM-5 (2013), splitting off from the older diagnosis of hypochondriasis—a term derived from the ancient belief that the hypochondrium, the region below the ribs, harbored melancholic vapors. The DSM-5 reform divided former hypochondriacs: those with prominent somatic symptoms became somatic symptom disorder, while those preoccupied with having a disease despite minimal or no symptoms became illness anxiety disorder. Care-avoidant and care-seeking subtypes are recognized.
2020-37: Projection—attributing one's own unacceptable feelings to another person—was articulated by Sigmund Freud and elaborated within his daughter Anna Freud's 1936 catalogue of ego defense mechanisms. It is considered an immature or primitive defense and forms the conceptual ancestor of projective identification described by Melanie Klein. A handy mnemonic: the patient who is angry insists it is the therapist who hates.
2020-38: Reactive attachment disorder grew out of mid-twentieth-century observations of institutionalized and neglected children, drawing on John Bowlby's attachment theory and René Spitz's studies of 'hospitalism' and anaclitic depression. DSM-5 split the older construct into two disorders: RAD, marked by emotionally withdrawn, inhibited behavior toward caregivers, and disinhibited social engagement disorder, marked by indiscriminate over-friendliness. Both require a history of pathogenic care.
2020-39: Fragile X syndrome is named for the constricted, fragile-appearing site on the long arm of the X chromosome (Xq27.3), first observed cytogenetically. It is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and results from a CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion silencing the FMR1 gene, identified in 1991. Classic features include macrocephaly, large ears, macroorchidism after puberty, autism, and—the boards' favorite hook—the maternal-line inheritance pattern.
2020-4: Construct validity asks whether a test truly measures the abstract theoretical 'construct' it claims to, like intelligence or depression. The term was crystallized in a landmark 1955 paper by Lee Cronbach and Paul Meehl, who introduced the nomological network, the web of theoretical relationships a construct should have with other variables. It remains the overarching concept under which other validity types are now often subsumed.
2020-40: REM sleep behavior disorder, in which the normal muscle atonia of dreaming sleep is lost so patients physically act out dreams, was first formally described by Carlos Schenck and Mark Mahowald in 1986. It is now recognized as one of the strongest prodromal markers of synucleinopathies; a majority of patients eventually develop Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia, often years to decades later.
2020-41: Physician suicide is a long-documented occupational hazard, and among specialties psychiatrists have repeatedly shown elevated rates—sometimes attributed to ready access to lethal means, self-selection of those with personal or family psychiatric history, and patient suicide exposure. The disturbing gender finding from older literature is that female physicians' suicide rates approach those of male physicians, far exceeding rates in the general female population.
2020-42: This is Capgras syndrome, the delusion that a familiar person has been replaced by an identical impostor, first described by French psychiatrist Joseph Capgras in 1923 (he called it 'l'illusion des sosies,' the illusion of doubles). Modern cognitive neuroscience attributes it to a disconnection between face recognition and the emotional/autonomic response—a failure of predictive emotional confirmation, so the face looks right but feels wrong.
2020-43: The periaqueductal gray, the gray matter surrounding the cerebral aqueduct in the midbrain, is a hub of the descending pain-modulation system mapped through landmark stimulation studies by Reynolds in 1969, who produced analgesia in rats by electrically stimulating it. Rich in opioid receptors and connected to the amygdala, it integrates emotional and pain signals and drives the fight-or-flight and defensive behaviors.
2020-44: The bidirectional link between epilepsy and depression dates back to Hippocrates, who reportedly noted that melancholics and epileptics were prone to each other's condition. Depression is the most frequent psychiatric comorbidity in epilepsy and may share underlying neurobiology rather than being merely a reaction to seizures; importantly, it often predicts poorer seizure control and quality of life.
2020-45: Eligibility for special education in the United States flows from the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), originally passed in 1975 as the Education for All Handicapped Children Act. The two-pronged standard requires both a qualifying disability—intellectual disability is one of IDEA's listed categories—AND a demonstrated adverse effect on educational performance, which is why inadequate academic progress is the decisive element.
2020-46: Resilience as a predictor of successful aging draws on the 'successful aging' framework popularized by Rowe and Kahn in the 1980s–90s and on longitudinal work such as George Vaillant's Study of Adult Development. Resilience—the capacity to adapt to adversity and recover from setbacks—consistently correlates with better physical and psychological outcomes in late life, sometimes outweighing the absence of disease itself.
2020-47: SSRIs and SNRIs became first-line for generalized anxiety disorder as the field deliberately moved away from benzodiazepines because of dependence, tolerance, and especially the danger of combining them with alcohol. The serotonergic agents avoid those liabilities and treat comorbid depression. Venlafaxine and duloxetine carry specific FDA approvals for GAD, cementing the SNRI/SSRI class as the preferred starting point.
2020-48: Huntington disease, described by American physician George Huntington in his 1872 essay 'On Chorea,' is a CAG-repeat expansion disorder of the huntingtin gene on chromosome 4, identified in 1993. The hallmark imaging finding is atrophy of the caudate nucleus, producing the boxcar-shaped enlargement of the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles. Chorea derives from the Greek for 'dance.'
2020-49: The mesolimbic dopamine pathway—projecting from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens—is the brain's reward circuit and the common final pathway for virtually all drugs of abuse. Its central role was cemented by James Olds and Peter Milner's 1954 discovery of intracranial self-stimulation, in which rats pressed levers to electrically stimulate this region to the exclusion of food.
2020-5: Metformin, a biguanide derived from French lilac (Galega officinalis), has become the best-evidenced agent for antipsychotic-induced weight gain and metabolic disturbance. Multiple randomized trials and meta-analyses, including studies in patients on olanzapine and clozapine, show modest but reliable reductions in weight and improvements in insulin sensitivity. Its repurposing for psychiatric metabolic side effects reflects its strong safety record and low cost.
2020-50: Vagus nerve stimulation, originally FDA-approved for refractory epilepsy in 1997, received approval in 2005 as an adjunctive treatment for chronic or recurrent treatment-resistant major depression after patients with epilepsy were noted to have mood improvement. The implanted device stimulates the left vagus nerve; afferent fibers modulate limbic and brainstem circuits, though its antidepressant onset is famously slow, often taking months.
2020-51: The forensic psychiatric evaluation differs fundamentally from clinical care because the evaluee is not the psychiatrist's patient and there is no treatment relationship—and crucially, the usual confidentiality does not apply. Forensic psychiatry's guiding ethical pillars, articulated by Paul Appelbaum, are 'truth-telling' and 'respect for persons'; the examiner must warn the evaluee at the outset that disclosures will be reported, not kept private.
2020-52: This is alexia without agraphia (pure word blindness), classically described by the French neurologist Joseph Jules Dejerine in 1892. A left posterior cerebral artery stroke damages the left occipital cortex and the splenium of the corpus callosum, disconnecting intact right-hemisphere visual input from the left-hemisphere language areas—so the patient can write and speak but cannot read what was written, even their own words.
2020-53: This describes a positive Romberg sign, named for the nineteenth-century German neurologist Moritz Heinrich Romberg, who described it in patients with tabes dorsalis from syphilis. Loss of balance only when the eyes close indicates impaired proprioception from dorsal (posterior) column dysfunction, since the patient can no longer use vision to compensate. A cerebellar patient, by contrast, sways with eyes open or closed.
2020-54: Resident duty-hour limits trace to the 1984 death of Libby Zion in New York, whose case was blamed partly on overtired, unsupervised residents, prompting the 1989 Bell Commission rules and the ACGME's national 80-hour week cap in 2003. High-quality studies of these reforms have generally found improved resident alertness and cognitive performance without the feared harms to patient mortality or education.
2020-55: Major depressive disorder is the most common comorbidity of OCD, a relationship recognized since OCD's earliest descriptions—indeed, depressive symptoms so often accompany obsessions that clinicians debate which is primary. The secondary nature of much OCD-related depression (demoralization from the disorder's burden) shaped treatment: SSRIs at high doses target both conditions, and OCD's removal from the anxiety-disorders chapter in DSM-5 reflected its distinct profile.
2020-56: The insula, Latin for 'island,' was named by Johann Christian Reil in the early 1800s and is sometimes still called the island of Reil. Buried deep within the lateral sulcus beneath the overlying opercula of the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes, it is hidden from the brain's surface view. It integrates interoception, taste, autonomic function, and emotional awareness, including disgust.
2020-57: ECT for depression in pregnancy is considered relatively safe and is favored when rapid response is imperative—above all for active suicidality with a plan—because it avoids the fetal exposure concerns of ongoing pharmacotherapy and works faster than waiting for medication. ECT, introduced by Cerletti and Bini in 1938, remains the most effective acute treatment for severe depression, and acute suicide risk is a classic indication.
2020-58: The link between disadvantaged neighborhoods and adolescent high-risk behavior is a cornerstone of social-ecological and 'collective efficacy' research, notably the work of Robert Sampson and colleagues on Chicago neighborhoods in the 1990s. Beyond individual and family factors, the surrounding environment—concentrated poverty, limited supervision, exposure to violence—independently predicts risk-taking, illustrating that context shapes development as powerfully as parenting.
2020-59: Harm reduction emerged from public health responses to the HIV epidemic in the 1980s, when needle-exchange programs sought to reduce disease transmission without requiring abstinence. Distributing naloxone—an opioid antagonist patented in the 1960s and marketed as Narcan—to communities with high opioid use exemplifies the philosophy: meeting people where they are and reducing the dangers of drug use rather than demanding cessation first.
2020-6: The federal mandate flows chiefly from the Education for All Handicapped Children Act of 1975, later reauthorized as the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA). It guarantees a 'free appropriate public education' (FAPE) in the least restrictive environment, enforced through the federally required Individualized Education Program (IEP). The landmark 1954 Brown v. Board ruling helped establish education as a right that government cannot deny on arbitrary grounds.
2020-60: The ventral tegmental area, in the midbrain, houses the dopaminergic cell bodies whose axons form the mesolimbic 'reward pathway' projecting to the nucleus accumbens. Its central role in motivation and addiction was illuminated by the self-stimulation experiments of Olds and Milner in the 1950s and by Arvid Carlsson's foundational work establishing dopamine as a neurotransmitter, for which he shared the 2000 Nobel Prize.
2020-61: The distinction between semantic memory (general facts and knowledge, like 'Paris is the capital of France') and episodic memory (personally experienced events) was introduced by Estonian-Canadian psychologist Endel Tulving in 1972. Both are forms of explicit, declarative memory. Tulving's taxonomy reshaped memory science, and the dissociation is dramatically illustrated by amnesic patients who lose episodic recall while retaining intact factual knowledge.
2020-62: General systems theory was developed by biologist Ludwig von Bertalanffy in the mid-twentieth century and imported into family therapy by pioneers like Murray Bowen and the Palo Alto group. Its core insight is wholeness: a family is an interconnected system in which a change in any one member reverberates through the whole, so the family—not the individual—becomes the unit of treatment.
2020-63: Legal competency (capacity in a strict legal sense) is fundamentally a judicial determination, not a medical one. While clinicians supply expert testimony, only a court can adjudicate a person incompetent and appoint a guardian or conservator. This reflects the longstanding common-law principle that adults are presumed competent and may be stripped of decision-making rights only through due process, an idea rooted in English parens patriae doctrine over the 'lunatics and idiots' of the Crown.
2020-64: Ketamine's rapid antidepressant effect, popularized after a small 2000 Berman trial and a 2006 Zarate study at the NIMH, is classically attributed to its action as an NMDA receptor antagonist, triggering a downstream glutamate surge and synaptogenesis via AMPA and mTOR signaling. Ketamine was synthesized by Calvin Stevens in 1962 as a safer alternative to phencyclidine; the FDA approved its S-enantiomer esketamine (Spravato) for treatment-resistant depression in 2019.
2020-65: Next-generation (massively parallel) sequencing begins with fragmenting genomic DNA into small pieces before adapters are ligated and clusters generated on a flow cell. This contrasts with first-generation Sanger sequencing, the chain-termination method Frederick Sanger devised in 1977 that earned him his second Nobel Prize. The Human Genome Project, completed in 2003, relied on Sanger sequencing; NGS platforms commercialized later that decade slashed sequencing costs by orders of magnitude.
2020-66: Benzodiazepines and other sedative-hypnotics are well known for paradoxical reactions, including disinhibition, agitation, and dissociative-like states, especially in children, the elderly, and those with brain injury. The phenomenon is thought to involve GABAergic disinhibition of behavioral control. The class traces to chlordiazepoxide (Librium), accidentally discovered by Leo Sternbach at Roche and marketed in 1960, followed by diazepam (Valium) in 1963.
2020-67: Number needed to treat is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction. Here event rates are 10% (placebo) versus 5% (lithium), an ARR of 5%, so NNT equals 1/0.05 = 20. The NNT concept was introduced by Laupacis, Sackett, and Roberts in a 1988 New England Journal of Medicine paper as an intuitive way to express treatment effect. Lithium's anti-suicidal signal, distinct from its mood effect, has been replicated across multiple analyses.
2020-68: HIPAA's Privacy and Security Rules, which took effect in the early 2000s following the 1996 act, do not strictly mandate email encryption; rather, providers must apply reasonable safeguards and minimize the protected health information disclosed. The 'minimum necessary' standard is a core HIPAA principle. The act was originally championed for insurance portability, with the privacy provisions added as administrative simplification requirements.
2020-69: In neuropsychological screening for early dementia, language is often assessed first because intact verbal comprehension and expression are prerequisites for validly testing other domains like memory and executive function. The systematic study of language localization dates to Paul Broca's 1861 aphasic patient 'Tan' and Carl Wernicke's 1874 description of receptive aphasia, foundational landmarks linking specific cortical regions to language.
2020-7: Heinz Kohut, founder of self psychology, broke with classical Freudian thinking by reframing narcissism not as pathology to be outgrown but as a normal developmental line. In works like 'The Analysis of the Self' (1971), he argued that healthy grandiosity, mirrored by empathic caregivers, matures into stable self-esteem, ambition, and ideals. Failures of empathic 'mirroring' instead produce narcissistic injury.
2020-70: The diencephalon, one of the embryonic brain vesicles derived from the prosencephalon (forebrain), gives rise to the thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus, and subthalamus. The name comes from Greek for 'interbrain,' reflecting its position between the cerebral hemispheres. This vesicle scheme, with three then five primary brain vesicles, is standard developmental neuroanatomy describing the neural tube's regional differentiation early in gestation.
2020-71: Depersonalization/derealization disorder features persistent detachment from one's self or surroundings, classically described as feeling like an outside observer or living in a dream, with reality testing intact. The term depersonalization was coined by Ludovic Dugas around 1898. DSM-5 merged depersonalization and derealization into a single diagnosis, recognizing them as two faces of the same dissociative experience under acute stress.
2020-72: In boys, ADHD and OCD have been linked to reductions in basal ganglia gray matter, particularly the caudate, consistent with cortico-striatal-thalamo-cortical circuit dysfunction. The basal ganglia's role in habit, motor gating, and inhibition makes striatal abnormalities a recurring theme across these disorders. Imaging cohorts have repeatedly implicated caudate volume reductions in childhood-onset ADHD.
2020-73: Secondary mania, a manic syndrome arising from a medical or neurological cause rather than primary bipolar disorder, was characterized by Krauthammer and Klerman in a 1978 paper. Multiple sclerosis is a classic culprit, with demyelinating lesions, often in temporal or frontal regions, disrupting mood circuits; MS patients also show elevated rates of euphoria and pathological laughing or crying. Steroid treatment can compound the manic picture.
2020-74: Commissural fibers cross the midline to connect homologous regions of the two cerebral hemispheres, the corpus callosum being the largest. The word commissure comes from Latin for 'joining together.' Severing the corpus callosum to treat intractable epilepsy produced the famous 'split-brain' patients studied by Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga, work that won Sperry the 1981 Nobel Prize and revealed hemispheric specialization.
2020-75: This presentation suggests clozapine-induced myocarditis, an idiosyncratic, potentially fatal reaction often emerging within the first weeks of treatment, with eosinophilia, tachycardia, and ECG changes as clues. Troponin and CRP help confirm cardiac injury and guide management. Clozapine, the prototype atypical antipsychotic synthesized in the 1950s-60s, was nearly abandoned after agranulocytosis deaths in 1970s Finland but revived by Kane's landmark 1988 trial for treatment-resistant schizophrenia.
2020-76: Dissociative identity disorder requires recurrent gaps in recall of everyday events, personal information, or trauma beyond ordinary forgetting, alongside two or more distinct identity states. The amnesia criterion is what distinguishes DID from mere role-playing. Formerly called multiple personality disorder, it was renamed in DSM-IV in 1994; its prominence rose dramatically after the 1973 book and film 'Sybil.'
2020-77: Effect size expresses the magnitude of a difference in standardized units, independent of sample size, making it the best way to appreciate clinical meaningfulness. Cohen's d, popularized by Jacob Cohen in his 1969 work on statistical power, divides the mean difference by a pooled standard deviation, with conventional benchmarks of 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, and 0.8 large. It addresses the limitation that a p-value alone says nothing about how big an effect is.
2020-78: When a trainee receives an order they believe is unsafe, the appropriate step is to escalate within the supervisory chain, here consulting the supervising attending, rather than blindly comply or unilaterally override. This reflects modern patient-safety culture emphasizing speaking up and graded assertiveness. Clozapine in particular is titrated slowly to mitigate orthostasis, seizures, and cardiac risk, making dose vigilance clinically warranted.
2020-79: Effectiveness trials test interventions under real-world, naturalistic conditions with broad, representative populations, whereas efficacy trials use tightly controlled settings and restrictive criteria. The distinction was sharpened by the NIMH-funded practical trials of the 2000s such as CATIE for antipsychotics and STAR*D for depression, which deliberately enrolled typical, comorbid patients to learn what works in everyday practice.
2020-8: Modern de-escalation guidance, codified in Project BETA (Best practices in Evaluation and Treatment of Agitation), published by the American Association for Emergency Psychiatry around 2012, emphasizes verbal engagement and validation over coercion. Acknowledging frustration is a core technique: naming and legitimizing the patient's emotion builds rapport and lowers arousal, the opposite of confrontation or shows of force.
2020-80: Self-monitoring with daily diaries or thought records is a cornerstone of CBT psychoeducation, helping patients link situations, thoughts, feelings, and behaviors. The technique descends from Aaron Beck's cognitive therapy developed in the 1960s, with the dysfunctional thought record becoming an iconic tool. For adolescents, mood and activity logs build the metacognitive awareness that later cognitive restructuring depends upon.
2020-81: Tactile agnosia, the inability to recognize objects by touch despite intact primary sensation, is astereognosis and localizes to the posterior parietal association cortex, where somatosensory information is integrated into meaningful percepts. The term agnosia, meaning 'absence of knowledge,' was coined by Sigmund Freud in 1891. The parietal lobe's role in higher-order spatial and tactile processing distinguishes it from the primary sensory strip just anterior.
2020-82: Persistent (chronic) motor or vocal tic disorder requires single or multiple tics, but not both motor and vocal, lasting over a year, which distinguishes it from Tourette disorder, where both motor and vocal tics coexist. Tics characteristically wax and wane, worsen with fatigue or stress, and are briefly suppressible, often preceded by a premonitory urge. Georges Gilles de la Tourette described his eponymous syndrome in 1885 under Charcot.
2020-83: Thermal biofeedback, training patients to raise finger temperature through autonomic relaxation and vasodilation, is an evidence-based behavioral treatment for migraine, and is also used for Raynaud phenomenon. Biofeedback emerged in the late 1960s and 1970s as researchers showed people could voluntarily modify 'involuntary' physiological functions. Hand-warming is thought to reflect reduced sympathetic arousal that aborts the migraine cascade.
2020-84: In a previously healthy child, transient separation anxiety and worry about the surviving parent after a parent's death represent normal, age-typical bereavement rather than pathology. Developmentally, young children grasp death's permanence incompletely and naturally fear further loss. John Bowlby and Mary Ainsworth's attachment research framed how children process separation and grief, with protest and anxiety being expected early responses.
2020-85: N-acetylcysteine, a glutathione precursor with antioxidant and glutamate-modulating properties, has shown promise as an adjunct in schizophrenia, reducing negative symptoms and markers of oxidative stress in trials such as the 2008 Berk study. Long used as an antidote for acetaminophen overdose and a mucolytic, NAC has been investigated across psychiatry for OCD, trichotillomania, and addiction, reflecting interest in oxidative and glutamatergic mechanisms.
2020-86: Alzheimer disease involves loss of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and degeneration of cholinergic neurons, especially in the nucleus basalis of Meynert, underpinning the cholinergic hypothesis of memory decline. This rationale drove development of cholinesterase inhibitors like donepezil. Alois Alzheimer described the hallmark plaques and tangles in 1906 in his patient Auguste Deter; the cholinergic deficit was characterized in the 1970s and 1980s.
2020-87: Derealization is the sense that the external world is unreal, foggy, dreamlike, or muffled, distinct from depersonalization, which targets the self. Ludovic Dugas introduced related terminology around the turn of the twentieth century. These experiences commonly accompany anxiety, panic, trauma, and migraine; reality testing stays intact, which separates them from psychosis. DSM-5 groups both under one dissociative disorder.
2020-88: Lean methodology, derived from the Toyota Production System developed by Taiichi Ohno in postwar Japan, focuses on identifying and eliminating waste (muda) to maximize value in workflow. Adapted to healthcare as 'Lean,' it underpins many quality-improvement programs. The term 'lean production' was popularized by Womack, Jones, and Roos in their 1990 book 'The Machine That Changed the World.'
2020-89: Adult hippocampal neurogenesis arises from neural stem cells in the subgranular zone of the dentate gyrus, which generate new granule neurons throughout life. This was famously demonstrated in humans by Eriksson, Gage, and colleagues in a 1998 study using BrdU labeling in cancer patients, overturning the old dogma that the adult brain grows no new neurons. The subventricular zone is the other recognized neurogenic niche.
2020-9: Anticipatory nausea before chemotherapy is the textbook clinical example of Pavlovian classical conditioning. The neutral hospital setting (conditioned stimulus) becomes paired with the chemotherapy drugs (unconditioned stimulus) that reliably cause nausea, until the environment alone triggers vomiting. Ivan Pavlov discovered the phenomenon around 1900 studying salivating dogs, work that earned him the 1904 Nobel Prize, originally for digestive physiology.
