2021-232: Cognitive behavioral therapy, often combined with relapse-prevention models adapted from addiction work, has the strongest support for paraphilic disorders and sex offenders. Relapse prevention itself was developed by G. Alan Marlatt in the 1980s. CBT targets cognitive distortions, deviant arousal patterns, and victim empathy, frequently alongside antiandrogen pharmacotherapy in higher-risk cases.
2021-233: Conservation, the understanding that quantity stays constant despite changes in shape or arrangement, is the signature achievement of Jean Piaget's concrete operational stage (roughly ages 7 to 11). Piaget's famous demonstration poured water between a tall thin glass and a short wide one; preoperational children insist the amounts differ, while concrete-operational children grasp that nothing was added or removed.
2021-234: The recovery movement reframed the psychiatrist from authoritative expert to collaborative partner who supports a person's self-defined goals. Its foundational text is often traced to William Anthony's 1993 paper declaring recovery 'the guiding vision' of mental health services, and SAMHSA later codified recovery principles emphasizing person-centered, hope-oriented, consumer-driven care.
2021-235: The 5-HT3 receptor is unique among serotonin receptors as a ligand-gated ion channel rather than a G-protein-coupled receptor, and alcohol potentiates its function, contributing to dopamine release and reward. This pharmacology is why the 5-HT3 antagonist ondansetron has been studied for alcohol use disorder, particularly in early-onset drinkers, an interesting crossover from its antiemetic role.
2021-236: A clouded or fluctuating sensorium is the cardinal feature of delirium and strongly flags an underlying medical cause rather than a primary psychiatric disorder. The concept traces to Engel and Romano's classic 1959 description of delirium as a syndrome of cerebral insufficiency reflected in diffuse EEG slowing. Disturbed level of consciousness and attention, not the specific hallucination or mood, is the key discriminator.
2021-237: Sudden irresistible sleep attacks with shortened REM latency point to narcolepsy, and modafinil is the standard wake-promoting first-line agent, FDA-approved for the disorder in 1998. The condition was named by Jean-Baptiste Gélineau in 1880, and its biology was cracked around 1999-2000 with the discovery that loss of hypothalamic orexin (hypocretin) neurons underlies type 1 narcolepsy with cataplexy.
2021-238: Clanging (or clang association) is speech driven by sound rather than meaning, where rhyme and punning dictate word choice, classically seen in mania. Because it reflects disordered associations and form of thought rather than the ideas themselves, it is documented under thought process. The term derives from the German psychiatric concept of 'Klangassoziation' from the Kraepelinian era.
2021-239: The ABPN replaced lifelong certification with time-limited certificates and a Maintenance of Certification program built on four pillars: licensure, lifelong learning/self-assessment CME, an examination component, and improvement in medical practice (PIP). Completing a patient safety activity falls under that practice-improvement pillar, reflecting a broader 21st-century shift across ABMS boards from one-time exams to ongoing competency.
2021-24: The periaqueductal gray, surrounding the cerebral aqueduct in the midbrain, is a hub for defensive responses and descending pain modulation. Its dorsal portion orchestrates active fight-or-flight reactions, while the ventral region mediates passive freezing. Stimulation studies in the 20th century revealed its dual role, and it remains central to fear-circuitry models linking the amygdala to behavioral output.
2021-240: Pramipexole, a non-ergot dopamine agonist, is a first-line treatment for moderate-to-severe restless legs syndrome, reflecting the disorder's dopaminergic basis. A notorious caveat is augmentation, a paradoxical worsening and earlier onset of symptoms with prolonged dopaminergic therapy, which has shifted many guidelines toward alpha-2-delta ligands like gabapentin as preferred long-term agents.
2021-241: Advancing age is overwhelmingly the leading risk factor for dementia, with prevalence roughly doubling every five years after 65. Alois Alzheimer described the disease in 1906 in Auguste Deter, a patient in her early fifties, making her presentation atypically young; the far more common late-onset form tracks closely with aging itself and with the APOE4 allele identified in the early 1990s.
2021-242: Activation procedures in EEG were designed precisely to provoke discharges that resting recordings miss. Hyperventilation (lowering CO2) and intermittent photic stimulation date back to the early decades of clinical EEG in the 1930s-40s, and sleep deprivation famously unmasks epileptiform activity. Visual fixation, by contrast, tends to suppress activity such as occipital rhythms, which is the basis of the Berger maneuver named after Hans Berger, who recorded the first human EEG in 1924.
2021-243: This is frontotemporal dementia, historically called Pick disease after Czech neurologist Arnold Pick, who described focal lobar atrophy in 1892. Alois Alzheimer later identified the silver-staining argentophilic 'Pick bodies,' now known to be composed of tau protein. The behavioral variant, with disinhibition, apathy, and hyperorality echoing Kluver-Bucy features, is one of the leading causes of early-onset dementia. Tau is a microtubule-associated protein central to a family of disorders called tauopathies.
2021-244: BDNF rose to prominence through the neurotrophic hypothesis of depression, popularized by Ronald Duman and colleagues in the late 1990s. The idea reframed depression as a disorder of impaired neuroplasticity: chronic stress and elevated cortisol lower BDNF and shrink hippocampal volume, while antidepressants, ECT, exercise, and even ketamine raise BDNF and promote synaptogenesis. BDNF was first isolated from pig brain by Yves-Alain Barde in 1982, the second neurotrophin discovered after nerve growth factor.
2021-245: The modern prevention framework comes from a landmark 1994 Institute of Medicine report that replaced the old primary/secondary/tertiary scheme (drawn from Gerald Caplan's 1960s work) with universal, selective, and indicated categories. Indicated prevention targets high-risk individuals already showing detectable subclinical signs, like the attenuated psychosis or clinical high-risk state, but who do not yet meet full diagnostic threshold. This tier underlies early-intervention psychosis programs aiming to delay or prevent conversion.
2021-246: Cognitive behavioral therapy for chronic pain grew out of the gate control theory of pain proposed by Ronald Melzack and Patrick Wall in 1965, which established that psychological factors modulate pain perception. Rather than chasing pain elimination, CBT borrows from operant and acceptance models to target functional restoration, reducing catastrophizing and pain-related avoidance. The emphasis on living well despite pain rather than being pain-free is the conceptual heart of modern multidisciplinary pain management.
2021-247: The Babinski sign, an upgoing great toe on plantar stimulation indicating corticospinal tract damage, was described by Joseph Babinski in 1896 and remains the classic upper motor neuron localizer. Upper motor neuron lesions produce a syndrome of spasticity, hyperreflexia, and pathological reflexes because descending inhibition of the spinal reflex arc is lost. The mnemonic contrast is everything-up (tone, reflexes, toes) for upper motor neuron versus everything-down for lower motor neuron.
2021-248: This question turns on informed consent and parental authority in pediatric care. With limited exceptions such as emancipated minors, suspected abuse reporting, or emergencies, a clinician cannot evaluate a minor over parental refusal. Non-intrusive observation in the natural setting and collateral discussion respect both the duty to assess possible suicidality and the legal boundary of consent, a tension formalized in U.S. consent doctrine and reinforced by cases like the 1914 Schloendorff decision establishing self-determination in medical care.
2021-249: Although suicide drives the dramatic loss of life expectancy in schizophrenia (roughly 15-20 years shortened), cardiovascular disease is the leading overall cause of death. The drivers form a perfect storm: metabolic syndrome from second-generation antipsychotics, high smoking rates, sedentary lifestyle, and reduced access to medical care. This excess mortality gap has actually widened in the antipsychotic era, prompting metabolic monitoring guidelines and the integration of physical health into psychiatric practice.
2021-25: Enrichment designs that pre-screen out placebo responders, such as the sequential parallel comparison design developed by Maurizio Fava and colleagues, aim to reduce the inflated placebo response rates that doom many psychiatric trials. By concentrating drug-placebo signal in a less placebo-prone sample, they improve the odds of detecting true treatment effects without simply expanding the sample size.
2021-250: Autonomy, the patient's right to self-determination, is one of the four principles codified by Tom Beauchamp and James Childress in their 1979 Principles of Biomedical Ethics. Its modern legal roots trace to Justice Cardozo's 1914 ruling that every adult of sound mind has a right to decide what is done to their body. When decisional capacity is intact, a competent refusal of a procedure must be honored even when clinicians believe the procedure is beneficial.
2021-251: Lipid monitoring reflects the metabolic burden of second-generation antipsychotics. The 2004 consensus statement from the American Diabetes Association, American Psychiatric Association, and partner organizations established the now-standard metabolic monitoring schedule, including fasting lipids at baseline, at 3 months, and then annually. Risperidone is also notably prolactin-elevating, but routine prolactin testing is reserved for symptomatic patients rather than asymptomatic surveillance.
2021-252: Valproate is a potent neural tube teratogen. Neurulation, the folding of the neural plate into the neural tube, occurs around the third to fourth week of gestation; failure of closure produces spina bifida and anencephaly. Valproate's risk of neural tube defects, recognized after reports in the early 1980s, is dose-dependent and tied to folate antagonism and histone deacetylase inhibition, which is why high-dose periconceptional folate is advised and the drug is avoided in pregnancy.
2021-253: Huntington disease is the textbook CAG trinucleotide repeat disorder, caused by an expansion in the HTT (huntingtin) gene on chromosome 4. The gene was identified in 1993 by the Huntington's Disease Collaborative Research Group after a search anchored by Nancy Wexler's work with a large Venezuelan kindred. Normal alleles carry fewer than about 27 repeats; 40 or more cause disease, and longer repeats explain the anticipation seen across generations.
2021-254: Root cause analysis was adapted to healthcare from aviation and industrial engineering and became standard after the Joint Commission mandated it for sentinel events in 1997. The structured RCA process begins with fact-finding, chronologically reconstructing what happened, before moving to why. Reviewing the clinical record establishes the verified timeline first, the foundation on which interviews, flow diagrams, and risk-reduction strategies are subsequently built. The guiding philosophy is systems thinking over individual blame.
2021-255: Angelman and Prader-Willi syndromes are the classic teaching pair for genomic imprinting, an epigenetic phenomenon where gene expression depends on parental origin. Both arise from the same 15q11-13 region: Angelman from loss of the maternal copy (UBE3A), Prader-Willi from loss of the paternal contribution. 2021-256: Dendritic spines, the tiny protrusions where most excitatory synapses form, were first depicted by Santiago Ramon y Cajal using Golgi staining in the late 19th century. Cajal speculated they might be sites of learning. Modern two-photon imaging confirmed his hunch: spines grow, shrink, and remodel within minutes in response to activity, providing the structural substrate for long-term potentiation and the plasticity underlying memory and experience-dependent rewiring.
2021-257: This reflects developmental psychology of adolescent risk perception. Teenagers heavily discount distant, abstract future harms but respond to immediate, socially salient consequences. 2021-258: Friedreich ataxia is unusual among trinucleotide repeat disorders: it involves a GAA repeat expansion in the FXN (frataxin) gene, it is autosomal recessive (most repeat disorders are dominant), and the expansion sits within an intron rather than a coding region, reducing frataxin and impairing mitochondrial iron handling. 2021-259: FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridization) uses fluorescently labeled DNA probes that bind specific chromosomal regions, developed in the early 1980s. Because it visualizes intact chromosomes, it can reveal balanced structural rearrangements like inversions and translocations that array CGH misses, since balanced rearrangements involve no net gain or loss of genetic material. 2021-26: Group therapy for psychotic disorders deliberately targets concrete social skills rather than insight or deep personality change, which can overwhelm patients with fragile reality testing. This pragmatic, supportive, here-and-now approach echoes social skills training rooted in social learning theory, and contrasts with the interpersonal, process-oriented groups described by Irvin Yalom for higher-functioning patients.
2021-260: Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) became the first FDA-approved medication for binge-eating disorder in 2015, the same year BED entered the DSM-5 as a formal diagnosis rather than a subtype. 2021-261: Epigenetics, a term coined by Conrad Waddington in the 1940s for how genotype produces phenotype, explains why genetically identical twins diverge over a lifetime. DNA methylation and histone modification alter gene expression without changing the underlying sequence, and these marks accumulate divergently with differing environments. 2021-262: Functional (psychogenic) tremor is distinguished by positive clinical signs rather than absence of pathology. The entrainment test and variable, distractible frequency are classic, but increased amplitude with added load (weighting the limb) is a hallmark: organic tremors typically dampen with loading, whereas functional tremors paradoxically worsen. These bedside maneuvers reflect the modern shift toward diagnosing functional neurological disorders by their characteristic positive features.
2021-263: The presumption of competence is a bedrock legal principle: every adult is presumed competent until proven otherwise by clear evidence, and incompetence must be adjudicated, not assumed from a diagnosis. Neither dementia, psychosis, nor developmental disability automatically removes legal competence. The landmark capacity framework draws on Paul Appelbaum and Thomas Grisso's work identifying the four functional abilities: understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and communicating a choice.
2021-264: Rationalization, offering a plausible but false justification to make an unacceptable act palatable, was elaborated within Freudian defense theory and systematized by Anna Freud in her 1936 work The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence. The classic illustration is Aesop's fox dismissing the unreachable grapes as sour, which gave us the phrase 'sour grapes.' It is considered a neurotic-level defense, more mature than denial but still self-deceptive.
2021-265: Oligodendrocytes are the CNS myelinating glia, the central counterpart to Schwann cells in the periphery. 2021-266: Withdrawal from sedative-hypnotics (alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates) is life-threatening because these GABA-enhancing drugs cause physiological dependence whose abrupt removal triggers autonomic instability, delirium tremens, and seizures. 2021-267: A missense mutation swaps one amino acid for another, the term coined within the genetic code framework of the 1960s alongside nonsense and silent mutations. 2021-268: Copy number variants, deletions or duplications of DNA segments, emerged as major autism contributors after genome-wide microarray studies in the late 2000s. This work, advanced by groups including Michael Wigler and the Simons Simplex Collection, reframed autism as highly genetically heterogeneous.
2021-269: The Stroop test, published by John Ridley Stroop in his 1935 doctoral dissertation, demonstrates interference: naming the ink color of an incongruent color word (the word RED printed in blue) is slowed because automatic reading competes with the demanded response. 2021-27: Convulsive therapy began with Ladislas Meduna in 1934 and electrical induction with Cerletti and Bini in 1938, but early ECT caused fractures and dislocations from the unmodified seizure. 2021-270: CRIPA, the Civil Rights of Institutionalized Persons Act of 1980, authorizes the U.S. Department of Justice to investigate and sue when institutionalized people face systemic, egregious rights violations. CRIPA covers prisons, nursing homes, psychiatric hospitals, and facilities for people with developmental disabilities.
2021-271: The maxim that past violence predicts future violence is the most robust finding in violence risk assessment. 2021-272: Ghrelin was discovered in 1999 by Kojima and Kangawa, who identified it as the endogenous ligand for the growth hormone secretagogue receptor. 2021-273: Object constancy is a cornerstone of Margaret Mahler's separation-individuation theory, developed through her observational studies of toddlers in the 1960s and 70s. Mahler famously described psychological birth as occurring well after physical birth, culminating in this milestone.
2021-274: Naltrexone, an opioid receptor antagonist, was FDA-approved for alcohol use disorder in 1994 after trials by Volpicelli and O'Malley showed it reduced relapse and heavy drinking. 2021-275: Dissociative amnesia, once called "psychogenic amnesia," is most strongly linked to chronic, repeated, interpersonal trauma, especially abuse by a caretaker, rather than single-event disasters. The betrayal trauma theory of Jennifer Freyd argues that when a victim depends on the perpetrator, memory blocking becomes adaptive, preserving the attachment needed for survival. 2021-276: Pyromania derives from the Greek "pyr" (fire) plus "mania," and the concept dates to early 19th-century French alienists who described "monomania" of fire-setting. 2021-277: Carbamazepine is a classic, potent inducer of cytochrome P450 enzymes, notably CYP3A4, and it even induces its own metabolism (autoinduction). 2021-278: Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) was newly introduced in DSM-5 (2013), expanding and replacing the old infancy/early-childhood feeding disorder. Unlike anorexia, ARFID involves no body-image disturbance or fear of weight gain; restriction stems from sensory aversion, low interest in eating, or fear of aversive consequences like choking. It can affect any age and was a notable broadening of the feeding and eating disorders chapter.
2021-279: The conditioned stimulus comes from Ivan Pavlov's classical conditioning experiments around 1900, where a neutral bell (the CS) paired with food eventually elicited salivation on its own. This taste-aversion scenario echoes the Garcia effect, John Garcia's 1960s work showing that flavor-illness pairings produce especially rapid, durable learning. The previously neutral apple flavor, now triggering nausea, is the textbook conditioned stimulus.
2021-28: Polygenic risk scores aggregate the tiny effects of thousands of common variants identified through genome-wide association studies, which matured for psychiatry through the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium. They cannot diagnose an individual, but at a group level they show promise for stratifying outcomes, such as predicting prognosis in first-episode psychosis, where higher schizophrenia PRS may track with poorer course.
2021-280: The term astrocyte ("star cell") was coined in the late 19th century by Michael von Lenhossek. 2021-281: The ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO) is the brain's "sleep switch," identified largely through the work of Clifford Saper and colleagues. Saper described this mutually inhibitory "flip-flop switch," explaining the rapid, stable transitions between sleep and wakefulness.
2021-282: In a crossover design each subject receives both treatment and control sequentially, serving as his or her own control, which sharply reduces between-subject variability. A key methodological concern is the carryover effect, addressed by inserting a washout period between phases. The approach became a staple of pharmacology and clinical trials precisely because it boosts statistical power with fewer participants.
2021-283: Large WHO World Mental Health Surveys, led by Ronald Kessler and colleagues, repeatedly found that the single biggest reason people with mental disorders go untreated is low perceived need, the belief that they did not have a problem requiring care, outranking cost or access. This finding reframed the global "treatment gap" as partly an attitudinal and recognition problem, not merely a resource shortage.
2021-284: Supportive psychotherapy is often considered the most widely practiced yet least formally studied therapy. Rooted in psychodynamic tradition but distinguished from it, it deliberately bolsters defenses and self-esteem rather than uncovering the unconscious, using praise, advice, reassurance, and direct problem-solving. Lawrence Rockland and others helped codify its techniques, positioning it on the "supportive" end of the expressive-supportive continuum.
2021-285: Valbenazine (Ingrezza) was the first FDA-approved treatment specifically for tardive dyskinesia, approved in 2017. It descends pharmacologically from tetrabenazine, the older VMAT2 inhibitor long used for Huntington's chorea; deutetrabenazine was also approved for TD that same year.
2021-286: The Hoover sign, described by neurologist Charles Franklin Hoover in 1908, distinguishes functional (non-organic) from organic leg weakness. When a person with genuine paralysis tries to raise the good leg, the weak leg involuntarily presses down via crossed extensor synergy. In functional weakness, that automatic downward pressure on the "paretic" side is present even though voluntary effort seems absent, exposing the inconsistency.
2021-287: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 was the first federal civil-rights law protecting people with disabilities, barring discrimination by recipients of federal funds. Its broad definition of disability lets students who do not qualify for special education under IDEA still receive classroom accommodations through a "504 plan." It is widely regarded as a precursor to the 1990 Americans with Disabilities Act.
2021-288: Professionalism in the digital age is now a formal competency. Bodies like the American Medical Association and Federation of State Medical Boards have issued social-media guidance urging physicians to periodically self-audit their online presence, the so-called "e-professionalism," while maintaining clear patient-provider boundaries. The principle echoes the older idea that physicians should monitor their public reputation, updated for the era of search engines.
2021-289: Permissive parenting comes from Diana Baumrind's influential 1960s typology, which crossed two dimensions, demandingness and responsiveness, to yield parenting styles. Permissive parents are high in warmth but low in control, indulgent and reluctant to enforce limits. Maccoby and Martin later expanded the scheme to four styles by adding the neglectful type, but Baumrind's original framework remains a developmental-psychology cornerstone.
2021-29: Paroxetine's short half-life of about a day, combined with its potent anticholinergic activity and lack of an active metabolite, makes it the SSRI most notorious for discontinuation syndrome—dizziness, flu-like symptoms, and the vivid 'brain zaps.' Fluoxetine sits at the opposite extreme: its long half-life and active metabolite norfluoxetine let it self-taper, sparing patients withdrawal.
2021-290: The Tanner stages of pubertal development were described by British pediatrician James Mourilyan Tanner and colleagues in the 1960s, drawing on the Harpenden longitudinal growth study. The scale remains the standard worldwide tool for staging breast, genital, and pubic-hair development.
2021-291: "Copy-forward" or "cloning" became widespread with electronic health records and quickly drew scrutiny from CMS and the Office of Inspector General for fostering "note bloat" and fraudulent upcoding. Guidance from bodies such as the American Health Information Management Association stresses that any carried-forward data must be reviewed, updated, and clinically pertinent to the current encounter, never copied wholesale to pad documentation or billing.
2021-292: Early genome-wide association studies in psychiatry produced disappointingly null results, a failure later attributed largely to underpowered sample sizes. Because psychiatric disorders are highly polygenic, with thousands of variants of tiny effect, researchers needed enormous samples to detect them. The Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, founded in 2007, pooled tens of thousands of cases and finally began yielding replicable genome-wide-significant hits, vindicating the sample-size explanation.
2021-293: The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) is the canonical seat of working memory, the brief "online" holding and manipulation of information. Patricia Goldman-Rakic's elegant 1980s-90s primate studies showed neurons there firing during the delay period of memory tasks, sustaining a representation without ongoing stimulus. Her work established the cellular basis of working memory and made the DLPFC central to theories of executive function.
2021-294: Motivational interviewing was developed by William Miller and Stephen Rollnick, first described by Miller in 1983 and elaborated in their 1991 book. A core technique is using open-ended questions to elicit "change talk" from the patient rather than lecturing, expressing empathy while letting the person voice their own reasons and obstacles. Asking what the hardest part of quitting is invites reflection and reinforces autonomy.
2021-295: Combined oral contraceptives induce the glucuronidation (UGT) enzymes that clear lamotrigine, so starting an estrogen-containing pill can drop lamotrigine levels by roughly half, risking breakthrough symptoms or seizures, and levels may rebound during the pill-free week. 2021-296: Migraine, especially the more common migraine without aura, tends to improve markedly during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy, with many women becoming headache-free. The improvement is attributed to sustained high, stable estrogen levels, contrasting with the estrogen-withdrawal trigger of menstrual migraine. This pattern often reverses postpartum as hormone levels fall abruptly.
2021-297: Nearly all addictive drugs converge on the mesolimbic dopamine pathway, the projection from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens, sometimes called the mesoaccumbens or brain "reward pathway." James Olds and Peter Milner's 1954 intracranial self-stimulation experiments in rats first revealed these reward circuits. Roy Wise later championed the dopamine hypothesis of reward that unified the neurobiology of addiction.
2021-298: Genomic imprinting, parent-of-origin-specific gene silencing by DNA methylation, was elucidated in the 1980s-90s. It was long dismissed as psychogenic until functional imaging and the 1990 American College of Rheumatology criteria with their 18 tender points legitimized it; the criteria were later revised to emphasize symptom burden over tender-point counts.
2022-10: The NMDA glutamate receptor is central to the "excitotoxicity" hypothesis of neurodegeneration, in which sustained calcium influx triggers neuronal death. This rationale underlies memantine, an uncompetitive NMDA antagonist approved by the FDA in 2003 for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease. Memantine descends from the older compound amantadine; its low-affinity, voltage-dependent blockade lets it dampen pathologic glutamate signaling while sparing normal synaptic transmission.
2022-100: An elevated CSF white blood cell count, or pleocytosis, is the cardinal marker of central nervous system inflammation, whether infectious or autoimmune. Normal CSF contains only a handful of lymphocytes; a lymphocytic predominance suggests viral or chronic processes while neutrophils point to bacterial infection. This simple cell count, alongside glucose and protein, anchors the classic interpretation of the lumbar puncture first popularized after Quincke introduced the procedure in the 1890s.
2022-101: The family trio design (affected child plus both parents) elegantly controls for population stratification by using transmitted versus untransmitted parental alleles, but it founders for late-onset disorders because the parents of an older affected patient are frequently deceased or unavailable. This practical limitation makes trios well suited to childhood and developmental conditions but awkward for diseases like Alzheimer's or late-onset psychiatric illness.
2022-102: Chronic stress and major depression share a pattern of immunosuppression and dysregulation, including reduced lymphocyte responses; decreases in B cells are among the changes reported. The framework grew from psychoneuroimmunology, a field named by Robert Ader after his 1970s conditioned-immunosuppression experiments in rats. Cortisol elevation from HPA-axis activation is the classic mediator suppressing adaptive immune compartments under sustained stress.
2022-103: The macrophage theory of depression and later the cytokine hypothesis, advanced by researchers such as Maes and Smith in the 1990s, hold that pro-inflammatory cytokines like IL-6, TNF-alpha, and CRP are elevated in depression. The observation that interferon-alpha therapy for hepatitis induced depression provided striking human evidence. Cytokines do cross into the brain by several routes, and trials of anti-inflammatory adjuncts grew directly from this neuroimmune model.
2022-104: REM sleep appears strikingly early, detectable in utero, where the fetus spends enormous proportions of time in active (REM) sleep, far more than at any later age. This abundance fuels the ontogenetic hypothesis proposed by Roffwarg, Muzio, and Dement in 1966, which argued that REM provides endogenous stimulation driving brain maturation when external input is scarce. REM proportion then declines steadily across the lifespan.
2022-105: MAOIs can induce a functional pyridoxine (vitamin B6) deficiency, particularly the hydrazine-derived agents like phenelzine, whose hydrazine moiety reacts with and inactivates pyridoxal phosphate. The result can be peripheral neuropathy reversible with B6 supplementation. This echoes the better-known isoniazid, an antitubercular hydrazide that likewise depletes B6 and causes neuropathy, a useful cross-link for remembering the mechanism.
2022-106: Policy-level interventions operate on the structural rules and systems that shape populations, such as what insurance covers, rather than on individual behavior. This sits at the top of the socio-ecological model, popularized in public health by Bronfenbrenner's ecological framework, which nests individual, interpersonal, community, and policy levels. Changing covered benefits alters access for everyone at once, the hallmark of upstream policy action versus downstream individual counseling.
2022-107: Competence as the engine of self-worth in school-aged children maps onto Erik Erikson's fourth psychosocial stage, Industry versus Inferiority, roughly ages six to twelve. Erikson, who actually coined the phrase 'identity crisis,' described this period as one in which mastering skills and feeling capable builds esteem, while repeated failure breeds inferiority. The child's developing sense of competence in school and tasks is the pivotal achievement.
2022-108: Among incarcerated populations, a current psychiatric diagnosis carries the strongest association with self-harm, outweighing demographic and offense-related factors. Prison self-harm research, including large studies by Hawton and colleagues using English prison data, consistently flags active mental illness as the dominant correlate. This underscores why mental health screening at intake is a central suicide-prevention strategy in correctional psychiatry.
2022-109: MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for PTSD was pioneered by Rick Doblin's MAPS organization, whose phase 3 trials reported substantial symptom reduction and drew major regulatory attention in the early 2020s. MDMA, synthesized by Merck in 1912 and later popularized by Alexander Shulgin, is thought to facilitate trauma processing by boosting serotonin and oxytocin while dampening amygdala fear responses, allowing patients to revisit memories with reduced threat.
2022-11: Risk management in sexual-addiction treatment teaches patients to recognize the people, places, moods, and situations that precede acting out, echoing the "identify your triggers" logic of relapse-prevention therapy. That broader relapse-prevention model was developed by psychologist G. Alan Marlatt for addictive behaviors, emphasizing high-risk situations and the abstinence-violation effect. Spotting risk factors precedes the coping skills (urge handling, containment) deployed once a craving arises.
2022-110: Visuomotor milestones follow a predictable sequence on tools like the Denver Developmental Screening Test: toddlers around 18 months can imitate a vertical stroke or scribble line, progressing later to copying circles, crosses, and squares. The mnemonic for shape copying is that a circle comes around age three, a cross around four, and a square around four to five, with the simple line preceding them all in the toddler year.
2022-111: Climbing stairs unassisted is a hallmark gross-motor achievement of the three-year-old on standard developmental scales like the Denver II, while skipping, hopping on one foot, and somersaulting are later, more advanced skills. The classic rule of thumb is that a three-year-old rides a tricycle and alternates feet going up stairs, distinguishing this age from the more rudimentary furniture-cruising of the one-year-old.
2022-112: The benzodiazepine binding site sits at the interface between the alpha and gamma subunits of the pentameric GABA-A receptor, and the gamma subunit (specifically gamma-2) is required for benzodiazepines to potentiate GABA-evoked chloride currents. This subunit architecture explains why benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators that enhance, rather than directly open, the channel, and why receptors lacking gamma are benzodiazepine-insensitive.
2022-113: In an elementary-age child, persistent difficulty with fundamental gross-motor skills like jumping and hopping is more developmentally concerning than weakness in optional, complex skills such as playing an instrument or team sports, which depend heavily on practice and exposure. Failure to master basic locomotor abilities expected years earlier raises flags for developmental coordination disorder or an underlying neurologic problem.
2022-114: For agitation from synthetic cathinones ('bath salts'), benzodiazepines like lorazepam are first-line because the toxidrome is sympathomimetic, and benzodiazepines calm agitation, lower temperature, and reduce seizure risk without the temperature-raising or dystonic liabilities of antipsychotics. Bath salts surged into public awareness around 2010-2012 and were federally scheduled in 2012; their mephedrone-type compounds block monoamine reuptake much like amphetamines yet often evade standard urine screens.
2022-115: Interictal refers to the period between seizures, and on EEG the absence of epileptiform discharges with nonspecific slow, low-voltage activity is consistent with this baseline state, in contrast to the spikes, spike-wave complexes, and bursts seen ictally. Hans Berger recorded the first human EEG in 1924, and the distinction between ictal, interictal, and postictal tracings remains foundational to clinical electroencephalography.
2022-116: The DSM-5 sets a minimum age of 18 for diagnosing voyeuristic disorder, a deliberate safeguard so that the normal sexual curiosity and peeping of adolescence is not pathologized. This age floor distinguishes voyeuristic disorder from the others in the paraphilia chapter and reflects the framers' caution about overdiagnosing developmentally typical behavior in minors.
2022-117: Dorothea Dix, a Boston schoolteacher, launched her crusade after witnessing the brutal conditions of mentally ill people confined in jails and almshouses, famously presenting an 1843 'Memorial' to the Massachusetts legislature documenting people kept in cages and chains. Her lobbying spurred the founding or expansion of dozens of state psychiatric hospitals across the nineteenth century, making her the iconic figure of the asylum-reform movement.
2022-118: In a crossover design each subject serves as their own control, receiving both treatments in sequence separated by a washout period to eliminate carryover effects. This boosts statistical power and controls between-subject variability, but it is unsuitable for conditions that are cured or progress irreversibly. The washout interval is the signature feature distinguishing it from a parallel-group trial where subjects get only one treatment.
2022-119: GABA-B receptors are metabotropic G-protein-coupled receptors, unlike the ionotropic GABA-A. Acting through Gi/Go, they inhibit adenylyl cyclase and, critically, open inwardly rectifying potassium (GIRK) channels, producing slow, long-lasting hyperpolarization, while also inhibiting presynaptic calcium channels. Baclofen is the prototypical GABA-B agonist, and this slow K-channel mechanism contrasts with the fast chloride influx of GABA-A.
2022-12: Antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinemia arises because dopamine, acting at pituitary D2 receptors, is the brain's main brake ("prolactin-inhibiting factor") on prolactin release; blocking D2 disinhibits secretion. Elevated prolactin causes galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and reduced libido. Risperidone and paliperidone are the second-generation agents most notorious for this, whereas aripiprazole, a partial agonist, can actually lower prolactin. Checking the prolactin level directly tests the suspected mechanism.
2022-120: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy, marked by deposition of hyperphosphorylated tau, was described in boxers as 'dementia pugilistica' or punch-drunk syndrome by Harrison Martland in 1928 and was thrust into modern prominence by Bennet Omalu's 2005 report on a deceased NFL player. The tau accumulates in a distinctive pattern around small blood vessels at the depths of cortical sulci, and definitive diagnosis still requires autopsy.
2022-121: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) arose in the mid-2000s after the HapMap project mapped common single-nucleotide polymorphisms across the genome. Unlike older linkage studies that hunted rare, high-penetrance variants in families, GWAS scan hundreds of thousands of common variants across large case-control samples, each typically conferring only a tiny increase in risk. The 2014 Psychiatric Genomics Consortium schizophrenia study, which identified over 100 loci, became a landmark demonstration that schizophrenia is highly polygenic, with risk spread across many small-effect common variants.
2022-122: Electromyography, which records electrical activity of muscle fibers, was developed in the mid-twentieth century and remains the workhorse for distinguishing neurogenic from functional weakness. In motor neuron disease such as ALS, EMG reveals denervation signs like fibrillations, positive sharp waves, and large polyphasic motor units, whereas functional (conversion) weakness shows a normal study. This objective electrophysiologic signature is why EMG is so valued in separating organic lower-motor-neuron pathology from psychogenic presentations.
2022-123: The t-test was devised by William Sealy Gosset, a chemist at the Guinness brewery in Dublin, who published it in 1908 under the pseudonym Student because his employer barred staff from publishing. The paired (dependent) t-test compares two measurements on the same subjects, such as before and after an intervention, controlling for individual baseline differences. Remember the memory hook: same people measured twice equals paired.
2022-124: Setting limits while acknowledging concerns reflects the principle that difficult, demanding patients are often expressing fear and loss of control. The classic framing comes from James Groves's influential 1978 New England Journal of Medicine essay, Taking Care of the Hateful Patient, which categorized dependent clingers, entitled demanders, manipulative help-rejecters, and self-destructive deniers. Groves argued that clinicians must recognize their own countertransference and respond with empathic but firm structure rather than retaliation or capitulation.
2022-125: Clozapine, synthesized in the late 1950s and the first true atypical antipsychotic, earned a unique FDA indication in 2002 for reducing suicidal behavior in schizophrenia. That approval rested largely on the InterSePT trial (International Suicide Prevention Trial), published in 2003 by Meltzer and colleagues, which showed clozapine outperformed olanzapine in preventing suicide attempts. No other antipsychotic carries this anti-suicidal indication, making clozapine the standout answer despite its agranulocytosis monitoring burden.
2022-126: Prader-Willi syndrome was described in 1956 by Swiss endocrinologists Andrea Prader, Alexis Labhart, and Heinrich Willi. It results from loss of paternally expressed genes on chromosome 15q11-13, usually via paternal deletion or maternal uniparental disomy, and is a textbook example of genomic imprinting paired with Angelman syndrome (the maternal counterpart). The hallmark course is neonatal hypotonia and failure to thrive giving way to insatiable hyperphagia and obesity, with hypogonadism and small hands and feet.
2022-127: The odds ratio is the appropriate measure for case-control studies, where investigators start with diseased cases and healthy controls and look backward for exposure, as here with childhood trauma. Because subjects are sampled by outcome rather than followed forward, true incidence cannot be calculated, so relative risk is invalid; the odds ratio approximates it well when disease is rare. This case-control / odds-ratio pairing is one of the most heavily tested epidemiology associations.
2022-128: This is dementia with Lewy bodies, named for Friedrich Lewy, who first described the alpha-synuclein inclusions in 1912 while working in Alois Alzheimer's laboratory. A defining and dangerous feature is severe neuroleptic sensitivity: dopamine-blocking agents, especially high-potency typicals like haloperidol, can provoke profound rigidity, worsening parkinsonism, and life-threatening reactions. The core triad of fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, and spontaneous parkinsonism, plus this antipsychotic sensitivity, distinguishes DLB.
2022-129: A bitemporal hemianopia localizes to the optic chiasm, where the nasal retinal fibers (carrying the temporal visual fields) cross. The classic cause is a pituitary adenoma pressing upward on the chiasm from below. The decussation at the chiasm was understood by anatomists like Isaac Newton, who reasoned about partial crossing of optic fibers to explain binocular vision long before it was confirmed microscopically.
2022-13: Post-vaccination ascending weakness with areflexia and albuminocytologic dissociation points to Guillain-Barre syndrome, an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy. It was described in 1916 by French physicians Georges Guillain, Jean Alexandre Barre, and Andre Strohl. Because demyelination slows peripheral conduction, nerve conduction studies are the confirmatory electrophysiologic test, classically showing prolonged distal latencies and conduction block.
2022-130: Mock-juror research on the insanity defense has repeatedly found that vivid biological evidence, particularly neuroimaging such as brain scans, exerts an outsized persuasive pull on jurors, sometimes dubbed the seductive allure of neuroscience. Studies in the 2000s and 2010s showed that adding brain images or neurobiological language increased perceived credibility of insanity claims, even when the scientific content added little. This bias is a recurring concern in forensic psychiatry testimony.
2022-131: Successful malpractice requires the four Ds: Duty, Dereliction (breach of the standard of care), Damages, and Direct causation. Prescribing multiple benzodiazepines to an elderly patient who then falls and fractures a hip satisfies all four: a clear deviation from standard prescribing in geriatrics directly producing real physical harm. The Beers Criteria, first published by Mark Beers in 1991, specifically flag benzodiazepines as inappropriate in older adults because of fall and fracture risk.
2022-132: Bulimia nervosa is distinguished from binge eating disorder by recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviors such as self-induced vomiting, laxative misuse, fasting, or excessive exercise, which are absent in BED. Binge eating disorder was elevated from an appendix research category to a full DSM-5 diagnosis in 2013. The eating-disorder triad mnemonic emphasizes that purging behavior, not weight, is the dividing line, since both disorders can occur at a normal BMI.
2022-133: Cognitive aging research, including longitudinal work like the Seattle Longitudinal Study begun by K. Warner Schaie in 1956, consistently shows that processing speed is among the earliest and most reliably declining abilities after midlife. This slowing of fluid cognition contrasts with crystallized abilities such as vocabulary and general knowledge, which are well preserved or even improve into later life. Salthouse's processing-speed theory proposed that much age-related cognitive change cascades from this slowing.
2022-134: Myelination in the human brain proceeds in an orderly caudal-to-rostral and central-to-peripheral sequence, beginning before birth in subcortical structures. The cerebellum and brainstem myelinate early, supporting basic motor and reflexive function, while association cortices and the prefrontal regions and corpus callosum continue myelinating well into adolescence and the third decade. This protracted prefrontal maturation underlies the relatively late development of executive control and judgment.
2022-135: Valproic acid carries among the highest teratogenic risks of all anticonvulsants and mood stabilizers, including neural tube defects such as spina bifida (roughly 1-2%) and a dose-dependent reduction in childhood IQ documented by the NEAD study. Because the neural tube closes within the first month, often before pregnancy is recognized, valproate is avoided in women of childbearing potential when alternatives exist. Lithium's Ebstein anomaly risk, by contrast, is far lower than once feared.
2022-136: Deinstitutionalization accelerated after the 1963 Community Mental Health Act signed by President Kennedy and the spread of chlorpromazine, emptying state hospitals from over half a million beds to a small fraction. The promised community services were chronically underfunded, and a major unintended consequence was transinstitutionalization: the migration of people with serious mental illness into jails and prisons. The Penrose hypothesis, framed by Lionel Penrose in 1939, anticipated this inverse relationship between psychiatric beds and prison populations.
2022-137: The American Psychiatric Association's position resists blanket bans tied merely to a diagnosis, recognizing that most people with mental illness are not violent and that stigmatizing categorical prohibitions are both unjust and ineffective. Instead the APA supports restrictions focused on demonstrable elevated risk of violence to self or others. This risk-based stance aligns with extreme-risk protection order or red-flag laws, which target dangerousness rather than psychiatric labels.
2022-138: Number needed to harm is the reciprocal of the absolute risk increase. Here the treatment mortality of 4% minus placebo mortality of 2% gives an absolute risk increase of 2%, or 0.02, and 1 divided by 0.02 equals 50. This calculation underlies the FDA's 2005 black box warning on atypical (and later all) antipsychotics for increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis.
2022-139: Seclusion and restraint, though sometimes necessary for acute safety, are increasingly recognized as potentially traumatizing interventions that can produce or re-activate post-traumatic stress, especially in patients with prior abuse histories. This evidence fueled the trauma-informed care movement and national efforts, led in the 2000s by groups such as SAMHSA and the precursor to NASMHPD, to minimize coercive practices. The reframing treats restraint as a treatment failure rather than a therapeutic act.
2022-14: Response to Intervention (RTI) is a tiered, evidence-based framework in which struggling students first receive increasingly intensive general-education supports before any special-education referral. It gained traction after the 2004 reauthorization of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), which allowed RTI as an alternative to the old IQ-achievement discrepancy model for identifying learning disabilities. The goal is early help and fewer unnecessary placements.
2022-140: In child psychiatry, minors generally cannot consent to their own evaluation, so obtaining consent from the parent or legal guardian is the necessary first step before any assessment, observation, or records request. This reflects the legal doctrine that parents hold decision-making authority for their children, with limited exceptions such as emancipated or mature minors and emergency care. School-based evaluation does not waive this requirement.
2022-141: Temperament denotes the heritable, biologically based dimensions of personality present early in life, contrasted with character, which is shaped by experience and maturation. The framing here, with automatic responses to danger, novelty, reward, and social approval, comes from C. Robert Cloninger's psychobiological model introduced in the late 1980s and 1990s, whose temperament dimensions included harm avoidance, novelty seeking, reward dependence, and persistence. Cloninger linked each tentatively to neurotransmitter systems.
2022-142: Among the more replicated neurobiological findings in autism is early brain overgrowth: head circumference and total brain volume are often normal or small at birth but increase abnormally fast during roughly the first two to four years of life. This trajectory, highlighted in work by Eric Courchesne in the early 2000s, may reflect excess neurons and reduced developmental pruning. The early overgrowth tends to plateau or normalize later in childhood.
2022-143: Chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing, or ChIP-seq, maps where a protein of interest, such as a transcription factor or modified histone, binds across the genome. The method crosslinks proteins to DNA, fragments the chromatin, pulls down the protein with an antibody, then sequences the attached DNA. ChIP combined with high-throughput sequencing became a foundational epigenomics tool in the late 2000s, central to projects like ENCODE that catalogued functional genomic elements.
2022-144: Family and twin studies place the lifetime risk of schizophrenia in the general population near 1%, rising to roughly 10% for a first-degree relative such as a full sibling. Risk climbs to about 50% for the unaffected identical twin of an affected individual and to nearly half when both parents are affected. These gradient figures, refined by Irving Gottesman's classic aggregations, illustrate the polygenic, substantially heritable architecture of the disorder.
2022-145: G proteins are heterotrimeric switches classified by their alpha subunit. The Gq family couples receptors to phospholipase C-beta, which cleaves PIP2 into the second messengers IP3 and DAG, mobilizing intracellular calcium and activating protein kinase C, the core of the phosphoinositide signaling pathway. By contrast, Gs and Gi raise and lower cyclic AMP. The discovery of G proteins earned Alfred Gilman and Martin Rodbell the 1994 Nobel Prize.
2022-146: Mary Ainsworth, building on John Bowlby's attachment theory, developed the Strange Situation procedure in the 1970s, classifying infants as secure, avoidant, or ambivalent (resistant). The fourth category, disorganized-disoriented, was added later by Mary Main and Judith Solomon in 1986 to capture infants showing contradictory, fearful, or freezing behaviors. Disorganized attachment is the pattern most strongly associated with maltreatment and frightening caregiver behavior, and it predicts later psychopathology.
2022-147: Adoption studies are powerful for separating genetic from environmental contributions, and classic Danish adoption research, notably the work associated with the Copenhagen sample, found that biological relatives of adoptees who died by suicide had elevated suicide rates, while adoptive relatives did not. This supports a heritable component to completed suicide that is partly independent of inherited mood disorder. A family history of suicide is therefore an established, transmissible risk factor.
2022-148: In DSM-5, PTSD is organized into four symptom clusters: intrusion, avoidance, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and marked alterations in arousal and reactivity (Criterion E). The arousal cluster captures the body's persistent hyperactivation, including hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, irritability, recklessness, concentration problems, and sleep disturbance. The exaggerated startle response in particular reflects a sensitized fear circuitry centered on the amygdala that fails to downregulate after trauma.
2022-149: The corpus striatum comprises the caudate nucleus, putamen, and globus pallidus. The caudate and putamen together form the neostriatum (often just called the striatum), separated by fibers of the internal capsule, while the putamen plus globus pallidus form the lentiform nucleus. These basal ganglia structures are central to motor control, and their dopaminergic dysfunction underlies Parkinson disease and Huntington disease, the latter marked by striking caudate atrophy.
2022-15: The arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus is the principal site of neuropeptide Y synthesis and a master hub of appetite regulation. NPY, discovered by Tatemoto and Mutt in 1982 and named for its tyrosine residues at both ends, is one of the most potent orexigenic (appetite-stimulating) peptides known. Arcuate NPY/AgRP neurons sit near the median eminence, sampling circulating leptin and ghrelin to drive feeding.
2022-150: Neuropeptides are short amino-acid chains synthesized from gene transcription and mRNA translation, packaged in large dense-core vesicles, and released from both axon terminals and dendrites. Unlike classical small-molecule transmitters, they are not recaptured by reuptake but are degraded by peptidases, giving longer-lasting effects, and they act through G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers. Substance P, discovered by von Euler and Gaddum in 1931, was among the first neuropeptides identified.
2022-151: The empirical 'good death' literature grew out of palliative care research in the 1990s and 2000s, notably work by Karen Steinhauser and colleagues at Duke who surveyed patients, families, and clinicians. A recurring finding is that beyond pain control, dying people place high value on having a say in how the dying process unfolds, reflecting the broader hospice movement's emphasis on patient control and dignity pioneered by Dame Cicely Saunders.
2022-152: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), sitting in the anterior hypothalamus just above the optic chiasm (hence its name), is the body's master clock. Its pacemaker role was established in the 1970s through lesion studies in rodents that abolished circadian rhythms. It receives light input via the retinohypothalamic tract and entrains peripheral clocks; its molecular machinery of CLOCK/BMAL1 and PER/CRY genes earned Hall, Rosbash, and Young the 2017 Nobel Prize.
2022-153: Community mental health centers were created by the 1963 Community Mental Health Act, signed by John F. Kennedy weeks before his assassination, as the centerpiece of deinstitutionalization. The promised network was never fully funded, and as centers closed, the safety net frayed. Studies link reduced community mental health access to worsened outcomes, including higher suicide mortality, illustrating the unfinished promise of the deinstitutionalization era.
2022-154: The universal/selective/indicated framework comes from a 1994 Institute of Medicine report on preventing mental disorders, refining Gerald Caplan's earlier primary/secondary/tertiary scheme. Universal prevention targets an entire population regardless of individual risk; a billboard campaign reaching all residents fits this tier. Selective prevention targets at-risk subgroups, and indicated prevention targets individuals already showing early signs.
2022-155: Melatonin is synthesized from serotonin in the pineal gland through two enzymes, AANAT and HIOMT, with the pathway running tryptophan to serotonin to melatonin. Aaron Lerner isolated and named melatonin in 1958, deriving the name from its ability to lighten frog skin (melanophore + serotonin). Synthesis is suppressed by light and rises at night, making it the body's chemical signal of darkness.
2022-156: Essential tremor's classic response to alcohol is a near-pathognomonic clue: a small drink often dramatically quiets the action tremor, sometimes leading patients to self-medicate. This 'alcohol responsiveness' helps distinguish it from Parkinsonian rest tremor. The mechanism is thought to involve cerebellar and olivary circuits; the same logic underlies treatment with beta-blockers like propranolol and the anticonvulsant primidone.
2022-157: Friedreich ataxia, described by German physician Nikolaus Friedreich in the 1860s, is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FXN gene encoding frataxin, a protein involved in mitochondrial iron handling. Although the gene is nuclear, frataxin deficiency cripples mitochondrial function, producing ataxia, cardiomyopathy, and diabetes. It is the most common inherited ataxia.
2022-158: The metabolic weight gain of atypical antipsychotics like olanzapine and clozapine is strongly tied to their potent blockade of histamine H1 and serotonin 5-HT2C receptors. 5-HT2C antagonism disrupts hypothalamic appetite regulation, driving hyperphagia. Notably, the appetite-suppressant lorcaserin was a 5-HT2C agonist, the mirror-image strategy, underscoring this receptor's central role in feeding behavior.
2022-159: The evidence hierarchy, formalized by groups like the Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine and the GRADE working group, traditionally places systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials at the apex, above single RCTs, cohort studies, and expert opinion. The term 'evidence-based medicine' was coined by Gordon Guyatt's group at McMaster University around 1991. Pooling RCTs increases statistical power and reduces bias from any single study.
2022-16: Transactional analysis was created by psychiatrist Eric Berne, who popularized it in his 1964 bestseller Games People Play. Its Parent-Adult-Child ego-state model and analysis of social "games" and "scripts" lend themselves to peer-to-peer work, fostering high member interdependence rather than reliance on the leader. Berne trained in classical psychoanalysis but sought a more accessible, egalitarian framework for group settings.
2022-160: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) presents with small firm testes, gynecomastia, tall stature, and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, and is associated with higher rates of autism and learning difficulties. It was described by Harry Klinefelter in 1942, with the XXY karyotype identified in 1959. Because the defect is a whole extra chromosome, a standard karyotype, not sequencing, is the diagnostic test of choice.
2022-161: The safety planning intervention was formalized by Barbara Stanley and Gregory Brown around 2008-2012 as a brief, collaborative alternative to the discredited 'no-suicide contract.' It builds a personalized, stepwise list: warning signs, internal coping, social distractions, people to call, professional contacts, and means restriction. It is now widely used in emergency settings and is endorsed in suicide prevention guidelines.
2022-162: Assertive Community Treatment (ACT) was developed in Madison, Wisconsin in the 1970s by Leonard Stein, Mary Ann Test, and Arnold Marx as the 'Training in Community Living' program. Using a multidisciplinary team with low caseloads, 24/7 availability, and in-vivo services, ACT became one of the most rigorously validated evidence-based practices for severe mental illness, reducing hospitalization and improving housing stability.
2022-163: Among tricyclics, the secondary amines desipramine and nortriptyline are the least anticholinergic, while tertiary amines like amitriptyline and imipramine carry heavy muscarinic burden. Desipramine is the demethylated metabolite of imipramine, and nortriptyline of amitriptyline; this demethylation strips much of the anticholinergic and antihistaminic load, making the secondary amines better tolerated, especially in older patients.
2022-164: Avedis Donabedian's classic 1966 framework divides quality measurement into structure, process, and outcome, and the National Quality Forum adopted these categories. A process measure captures whether a recommended action was performed, such as timely outpatient follow-up after psychiatric discharge, the well-known HEDIS '7-day and 30-day follow-up' metric. Process measures are popular because they are actionable and directly under provider control.
2022-165: The amygdala's role as a rapid, automatic threat detector was illuminated by fMRI studies in the late 1990s, including work by Paul Whalen and colleagues showing amygdala activation to masked, subliminally presented fearful faces that subjects never consciously perceived. This supports Joseph LeDoux's model of a fast subcortical 'low road' for processing emotional salience before conscious awareness.
2022-166: Therapeutic neutrality, articulated by Freud and elaborated by Anna Freud, describes the analyst standing equidistant from the patient's id, ego, superego, and external reality, taking no side in internal conflicts. Anna Freud's phrase about remaining 'equidistant' from the three agencies of the mind captures the stance. It is distinct from abstinence (withholding gratification) and is meant to create a space for the patient's conflicts to emerge.
2022-167: Estrogen modulates dopaminergic systems and appears to influence tardive dyskinesia risk, part of why postmenopausal women carry elevated vulnerability. The relationship between estrogen status and TD reflects the hormone's effects on striatal dopamine receptor sensitivity. TD itself was first widely recognized in the late 1950s as chronic neuroleptic use spread, with Faurbye coining the term in 1964.
2022-168: The left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex is the standard high-frequency rTMS target for depression, based on the hypothesis of left prefrontal hypoactivity in mood disorders. The FDA cleared rTMS for treatment-resistant depression in 2008 (NeuroStar). Originally localized by the '5 cm rule' from the motor cortex, targeting has since been refined using scalp measurements and neuronavigation to the left DLPFC.
2022-169: The NIMH-funded CATIE trial, published in 2005 and led by Jeffrey Lieberman, was a landmark pragmatic study comparing several second-generation antipsychotics with the older perphenazine in schizophrenia. Its clever primary outcome, all-cause discontinuation ('time to stopping the drug'), served as a real-world proxy combining efficacy, tolerability, and patient acceptance. Strikingly, most patients discontinued, and the older drug performed comparably.
2022-17: Early COVID-19 anosmia research showed SARS-CoV-2 attacks not the neurons themselves but the supporting sustentacular cells of the olfactory epithelium, which richly express the ACE2 entry receptor; damage to these support cells disrupts the smell-receptor neurons. This explained why smell often returned as the epithelium regenerated. Anosmia became such a reliable early sign that it was added to official symptom lists in 2020.
2022-170: Long-term potentiation, the persistent strengthening of synapses driven by NMDA-receptor calcium influx and subsequent AMPA receptor trafficking, was discovered by Terje Lomo and Tim Bliss in the rabbit hippocampus around 1973. Widely regarded as the cellular basis of learning and memory, LTP embodies Donald Hebb's 1949 dictum that 'neurons that fire together wire together.'
2022-171: Eligibility for special education in the U.S. is governed by the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), reauthorized in 2004 from the original 1975 Education for All Handicapped Children Act. A student must have one of IDEA's documented disability categories and, because of it, need specialized instruction to make educational progress. The law guarantees a 'free appropriate public education' in the least restrictive environment.
2022-172: Linkage analysis tracks how genetic markers co-segregate with a disorder within family pedigrees, exploiting the fact that loci physically close on a chromosome are inherited together. It was the workhorse for mapping single-gene Mendelian diseases, famously locating the Huntington gene region on chromosome 4 in 1983, before genome-wide association studies became dominant for complex polygenic traits.
2022-173: Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) entered the diagnostic lexicon with DSM-5 in 2013, expanding the old 'feeding disorder of infancy or early childhood.' Unlike anorexia nervosa, ARFID involves no disturbance in body image; restriction stems from sensory aversion (texture, smell), fear of aversive consequences like choking, or low interest in eating, yet can still cause severe weight loss and nutritional deficiency.
2022-174: Dextromethorphan, the cough suppressant in many OTC remedies (the 'DM' in product names), is an NMDA receptor antagonist structurally related to opioids. At high recreational doses it produces dissociative, ketamine- or PCP-like effects, an abuse pattern called 'robotripping' after Robitussin. This NMDA action also underlies its inclusion in the dextromethorphan-bupropion antidepressant approved in 2022.
2022-175: Next-generation (massively parallel) sequencing reads DNA base by base, making it ideal for detecting single-nucleotide point mutations that coarse methods like karyotyping or chromosomal microarray miss. The technology, commercialized in the mid-2000s, slashed the cost of sequencing far below Moore's law, transforming genetic diagnostics. Karyotypes see whole-chromosome changes; NGS resolves changes down to a single base pair.
2022-176: Presbycusis, age-related hearing loss that begins at high frequencies, is most specifically attributed to degeneration of the hair cells of the organ of Corti, especially at the cochlea's basal turn where high-frequency sounds are transduced. The organ of Corti is named for Italian anatomist Alfonso Corti, who described it in 1851. Sensory hair cells, once lost, do not regenerate in mammals.
2022-177: Autism spectrum disorder, consolidated into a single spectrum in DSM-5 (2013), centers on social-communication deficits and restricted, repetitive behaviors, often with sensory hypersensitivity such as covering the ears to noise. The term 'autism' was coined by Eugen Bleuler around 1911 for schizophrenic withdrawal, then independently applied to children by Leo Kanner in 1943 and Hans Asperger in 1944. Stress can amplify rigidity and self-injury in autistic individuals.
2022-178: Conflict of interest is the central ethical concern when industry offers gifts, meals, or speaker dinners to physicians. Research has shown that even small gifts can bias prescribing. The 2010 Physician Payments Sunshine Act, part of the Affordable Care Act, now requires public reporting of pharmaceutical payments to physicians via the Open Payments database, reflecting heightened scrutiny of these relationships.
2022-179: The 12-week repeat fasting glucose recommendation comes from the 2004 consensus statement jointly issued by the American Diabetes Association, American Psychiatric Association, and others on antipsychotic metabolic monitoring. The protocol calls for baseline weight, glucose, and lipids, with fasting glucose and lipids rechecked at roughly 12 weeks after starting an antipsychotic, then periodically, to catch emerging metabolic syndrome.
2022-18: The cholinergic hypothesis of Alzheimer disease centers on degeneration of the nucleus basalis of Meynert and a consequent fall in choline acetyltransferase, the enzyme that synthesizes acetylcholine. This finding from the 1970s drove development of the cholinesterase inhibitors (tacrine, the first, approved 1993, then donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) that remain symptomatic mainstays. The deficit correlates with the severity of cognitive decline.
2022-180: External validity, the generalizability of findings beyond the study sample, is most threatened by a non-representative study population. The internal/external validity distinction was formalized by Donald Campbell and Julian Stanley in their influential 1963 work on experimental design. Tightly controlled trials with narrow inclusion criteria often maximize internal validity at the expense of generalizing to real-world, heterogeneous patients.
2022-181: The flapping tremor seen here is asterixis, a term coined in 1949 by neurologists Adams and Foley, who built it from Greek roots meaning 'not fixed' (a- plus sterixis, 'support'). It reflects brief lapses in postural tone and is the classic bedside sign of hepatic encephalopathy, where rising ammonia and other toxins impair the brain. Though most famous in liver disease, asterixis can also appear in uremia and CO2 retention.
2022-182: Dual loyalty captures the tension a clinician feels when obligations to a patient collide with obligations to a third party such as the state. It became a focus of medical ethics after documented physician complicity in interrogation and abuse, prompting organizations to issue guidelines. In correctional psychiatry the conflict is structural: the same physician serves both the inmate-patient and the custodial institution, complicating confidentiality, treatment, and security duties.
2022-183: Subdural hematomas arise from torn bridging veins in the space between dura and arachnoid, classically after falls in older adults whose age-related brain atrophy stretches those veins. On CT they form a characteristic crescent (concave) shape hugging the brain surface, distinguishing them from the lens-shaped (biconvex) epidural hematoma. Because bleeding is venous and slow, symptoms like confusion can emerge days to weeks after the injury, earning chronic subdurals the nickname 'the great neurologic imitator.'
2022-184: Depersonalization describes feeling detached from one's own body or mental processes, as though observing oneself from outside. The term entered psychiatric language in the late 19th century, with Ludovic Dugas often credited for popularizing 'depersonalisation' around 1898, borrowing a word from the philosopher Amiel's journals. DSM now recognizes depersonalization/derealization disorder, and transient episodes are extremely common, especially during fatigue, stress, or panic.
2022-185: Lewy bodies are intraneuronal inclusions made chiefly of aggregated alpha-synuclein. They are named for Friedrich Lewy (Fritz Heinrich Lewy), who first described them around 1912 while working in Alois Alzheimer's laboratory, originally in Parkinson disease. Alpha-synuclein's central role wasn't confirmed until the late 1990s, placing dementia with Lewy bodies alongside Parkinson disease and multiple system atrophy in the family of synucleinopathies.
2022-186: Transient global amnesia is a striking, self-limited episode of dense anterograde amnesia in which patients repeatedly ask the same orienting questions while remaining alert and able to talk. The syndrome was named by Fisher and Adams in the 1960s. Episodes typically last several hours and resolve completely, often leaving a permanent memory gap for the event; it sometimes follows physical exertion, emotional stress, or immersion in cold water.
2022-187: This reflects diffusion of innovation theory, popularized by Eric Rogers in his 1962 book 'Diffusion of Innovations.' Among the attributes that predict uptake of a new practice, lower complexity (how simple the change seems to adopt) is a key driver, alongside relative advantage, compatibility, trialability, and observability. The framework remains a backbone of implementation science and dissemination research in healthcare.
2022-188: Liothyronine is synthetic T3, the more biologically active thyroid hormone. Its use as an antidepressant augmentation strategy was studied in the large STAR*D trial in the 2000s, where T3 augmentation was compared with lithium add-on for treatment-resistant depression. The hormone is thought to enhance monoaminergic tone, and it is often favored for patients with low energy and psychomotor slowing.
2022-189: Robertsonian translocations fuse two acrocentric chromosomes at their centromeres, and chromosome 14 is the partner most commonly involved when this mechanism causes Down syndrome. The rearrangement is named for American biologist William Rees Brebner Robertson, who described it in grasshoppers in 1916. Unlike trisomy 21 from nondisjunction, the translocation form can be inherited from a balanced-carrier parent, which is why it carries recurrence-risk implications.
2022-19: Oppositional defiant disorder is defined by a persistent pattern of angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behavior, and vindictiveness, distinguishing it from conduct disorder, which involves violating others' rights. DSM-5 reorganized ODD's criteria into those three symptom clusters and emphasized that some defiance is developmentally normal, requiring symptoms beyond what is typical for age. ODD is a recognized developmental precursor to conduct disorder in a subset of children.
2022-190: Restless legs syndrome, also called Willis-Ekbom disease after Thomas Willis (who described it in the 1600s) and Karl-Axel Ekbom (who characterized it in the 1940s), is strongly linked to iron deficiency. Iron is a cofactor for tyrosine hydroxylase in dopamine synthesis, tying the brain-iron hypothesis to the dopaminergic dysfunction in RLS. Checking serum ferritin and supplementing iron is a standard step in management.
2022-191: In Aaron Beck's cognitive model, intermediate beliefs are the rules, attitudes, and assumptions (often 'if-then' conditional statements) that sit between deep core beliefs and the surface-level automatic thoughts. Beck developed cognitive therapy in the 1960s, and his daughter Judith Beck later codified this three-level architecture in her widely used textbooks. These conditional rules shape how a person interprets situations and themselves.
2022-192: Erectile dysfunction in younger and middle-aged men is now recognized as an early sentinel of coronary artery disease, because penile arteries are smaller and show endothelial dysfunction sooner than coronaries. This 'artery size hypothesis' means ED can precede a cardiac event by roughly three to five years, making it a useful prompt for cardiovascular risk assessment in otherwise asymptomatic men.
2022-193: MicroRNAs are short, single-stranded noncoding RNAs (about 22 nucleotides) that silence genes by binding messenger RNA. The first, lin-4, was discovered in the roundworm C. elegans by Victor Ambros and colleagues in 1993, with Gary Ruvkun elucidating its target. Their work on microRNA was honored with the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
2022-194: Mirroring is the developmental process Heinz Kohut placed at the center of self psychology, which he founded in the 1970s. He argued that an empathically attuned caregiver who reflects back the child's feelings (the 'gleam in the mother's eye') allows a cohesive sense of self to form. Failures in this mirroring selfobject function, in Kohut's view, underlie narcissistic vulnerability.
2022-195: Illness anxiety disorder is the DSM-5 successor to most cases formerly called hypochondriasis, a term derived from the ancient Greek 'hypochondrium,' the region below the ribs once thought to be the seat of such complaints. Cognitive behavioral therapy, which targets catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations and reassurance-seeking, has the strongest evidence base as first-line treatment.
2022-196: Histone phosphorylation, particularly of histone H3 at serine 10, peaks during mitosis and is essential for proper chromosome condensation and segregation. The kinase Aurora B drives this modification, and detecting phospho-H3 is a standard laboratory marker of dividing cells. It is one of several reversible histone tail modifications that together form the so-called histone code regulating chromatin.
2022-197: This reflects Irvin Yalom's framework of four existential 'givens,' laid out in his 1980 book 'Existential Psychotherapy': death, freedom, isolation, and meaninglessness. Freedom in Yalom's sense is the burden of responsibility and self-creation, the groundlessness of having to author one's own choices; the patient's frantic note-taking and dread of dependence reflect a struggle to retain agency and control.
2022-198: A competent patient's voluntary waiver is a recognized exception to informed consent: a patient may decline to hear the disclosure and ask the physician to proceed. Modern informed-consent doctrine grew from landmark cases, including Justice Cardozo's 1914 Schloendorff opinion asserting the right to determine what is done to one's body, and the consent standard was sharpened in Canterbury v. Spence (1972). Other true exceptions include emergencies and therapeutic privilege.
2022-199: Phencyclidine, developed in the 1950s as the anesthetic Sernyl, produces psychosis by blocking the NMDA glutamate receptor as a noncompetitive antagonist at the channel's PCP-binding site. Its ability to reproduce both positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia, more faithfully than dopaminergic drugs, helped launch the glutamate (NMDA hypofunction) hypothesis of schizophrenia. Ketamine shares this mechanism.
2022-2: This cluster of simultanagnosia, optic ataxia, and oculomotor apraxia is Balint syndrome, described by Hungarian neurologist Rezso Balint in 1909.
